summary: Autonomous coding agents perform well on many conventional programming tasks, but scientific computing demands a rigorous validation paradigm that extends beyond simple functional test completion: generated code must preserve physical fidelity, differentiable workflows, framework-native semantics, and scalable representations. We introduce Open Research Benchmark for Integrated Tasks in Quantum Computing (ORBIT-Q) to address this gap. At its core, ORBIT-Q contributes a carefully curated suite of complex, research-level quantum workflows that serves as a challenging testbed for modern scientific programming. ORBIT-Q combines a rigorous multi-tier verification pipeline to support two orthogonal comparisons: different agent harness and model configurations at a fixed quantum software framework, and different quantum software frameworks at a fixed agent. In our systematic evaluations, TensorCircuit-NG (TC) exhibits the highest capability and performance efficiency among the evaluated quantum software frameworks under agent-driven programming, and Codex with GPT-5.5 is the strongest tested agent configuration on TC. However, a significant performance and design gap remains between frontier autonomous agents and human expert reference implementations. We further evaluate two efficiency dimensions: agent-side resource use and artifact-side runtime. Together, these results establish ORBIT-Q as a rigorous benchmark for autonomous scientific programming, framework-agent synergy, and quantum software performance.

AI.tldr: ORBIT-Q is a new benchmark for evaluating autonomous coding agents on scientific computing tasks in quantum computing, featuring multi-tier verification and comparisons across agent configurations and software frameworks.
AI.motivation: Existing programming benchmarks focus on simple functional tests, but scientific computing requires code that preserves physical fidelity, differentiable workflows, framework-native semantics, and scalable representations—areas where current evaluations fall short.
AI.method: ORBIT-Q introduces a curated suite of complex quantum workflows with a multi-tier verification pipeline, supporting two orthogonal comparisons: (1) different agent harness/model configurations on a fixed framework, and (2) different quantum software frameworks with a fixed agent.
AI.result: TensorCircuit-NG (TC) shows the highest capability and performance efficiency among frameworks; Codex with GPT-5.5 is the strongest agent configuration on TC. A significant gap remains between frontier agents and human expert implementations.
AI.conclusion: ORBIT-Q serves as a rigorous benchmark for autonomous scientific programming, framework-agent synergy, and quantum software performance, highlighting both progress and remaining challenges in agent-driven scientific computing.

title: Geometric modulation of transition and survival intensities in non-Hermitian systems
summary: The time evolution of non-Hermitian systems is generally nonunitary. Dynamics governed by time-dependent non-Hermitian Hamiltonians lead to a variety of novel phenomena, one of which is state amplification or suppression induced by the complex Berry phase. Here, we extend the framework of geometric modulation to multi-level systems and show that both transition and survival intensities can be modulated. We apply our theory to the non-Hermitian Landau-Zener (LZ) problem. First, we show that, in the half-LZ problem, both the transition and survival probabilities exhibit nonreciprocity due to the complex Berry phase. In the non-Hermitian standard LZ problem, only the survival intensity is known to exhibit nonreciprocity, whereas the transition intensity does not. However, the physical origin of this nonreciprocal behavior remains unclear. In this work, we show that the nonreciprocity originates from the complex Berry phase.

AI.tldr: This paper extends geometric modulation to multi-level non-Hermitian systems, showing that complex Berry phases enable modulation of both transition and survival intensities, and demonstrates that nonreciprocity in non-Hermitian Landau-Zener problems originates from these complex Berry phases.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to understand the physical origin of nonreciprocal behavior in non-Hermitian Landau-Zener problems, specifically why survival intensity exhibits nonreciprocity while transition intensity does not in the standard case, and to extend geometric modulation frameworks to multi-level systems.
AI.method: The authors extend geometric modulation to multi-level non-Hermitian systems and apply their theory to the non-Hermitian Landau-Zener problem, analyzing both the half-LZ and standard LZ problems to examine transition and survival probabilities.
AI.result: In the half-LZ problem, both transition and survival probabilities exhibit nonreciprocity due to the complex Berry phase. In the standard non-Hermitian LZ problem, the complex Berry phase is identified as the origin of the nonreciprocal behavior.
AI.conclusion: The complex Berry phase is the physical origin of nonreciprocity in non-Hermitian Landau-Zener problems, enabling modulation of both transition and survival intensities in multi-level non-Hermitian systems.

title: Quantum Kolmogorov--Arnold representation theorem for continuous unitary-valued maps
summary:
The classical Kolmogorov--Arnold representation theorem states that any continuous multivariate function can be exactly decomposed into a finite composition of univariate continuous functions and addition operations.
  This foundational result has recently inspired the development of Kolmogorov--Arnold Networks (KANs) in classical machine learning, as well as their extensions into the quantum domain (QKANs). In this paper, we establish two quantum analogues of the Kolmogorov--Arnold representation theorem for continuous unitary-valued maps of several variables within an open $1$-neighbourhood of the identity matrix \(O_1(\mathbf{I}) \subset \mathcal{U}(n)\).
  First, we prove a representation theorem that yields an exact additive decomposition inside the matrix exponent of anti-Hermitian-valued maps.
  Second, due to the non-commutative nature of quantum operators, we derive a factorised version expressing the target unitary map as a finite sequential product of univariate matrix exponentials. Finally, we provide a concrete topological counterexample based on the lifting property of \(\mathcal{SU}(2)\) to demonstrate that these local representation theorems cannot be globally extended to the entire unitary group \(\mathcal{U}(n)\) without encountering fundamental structural obstructions.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes two quantum analogues of the Kolmogorov–Arnold representation theorem for continuous unitary-valued maps near the identity, proving an additive decomposition in the exponent and a factorized sequential product form, along with a topological counterexample showing these representations cannot be globally extended to the full unitary group.
AI.motivation: To extend the classical Kolmogorov–Arnold representation theorem (which underlies KANs and QKANs) to the quantum domain by proving analogous representation theorems for continuous unitary-valued maps, and to understand the fundamental limitations of such representations due to non-commutativity and topological obstructions.
AI.method: The authors prove two local representation theorems within an open 1-neighborhood of the identity matrix in U(n): (1) an exact additive decomposition inside the matrix exponent of anti-Hermitian-valued maps; (2) a factorized version expressing the target unitary as a finite sequential product of univariate matrix exponentials. They also construct a topological counterexample using the lifting property of SU(2) to show global extension is impossible.
AI.result: Two local quantum Kolmogorov–Arnold representation theorems are proven for unitary maps near the identity: additive in the exponent space and multiplicative (sequential product) in the unitary group. A concrete counterexample based on SU(2) topology demonstrates that these representations cannot be extended globally to the entire unitary group U(n).
AI.conclusion: Quantum analogues of the Kolmogorov–Arnold representation theorem exist locally around the identity but face fundamental topological obstructions preventing global extension, highlighting an inherent limitation for constructing QKANs over the full unitary group.

title: Self-Specializing Vision-Language Transmon Chip Calibration in a Physics-Grounded Environment
summary: Calibrating a superconducting transmon chip is a sequential decision problem under noise, drift, and a finite budget: an expert must choose experiments, read ambiguous plots, judge fit quality, and revise stale beliefs as the chip drifts. We study whether a vision-language agent can close this loop and specialize itself to one physical device without weight updates, via three co-designed artifacts. The first is a physics-grounded simulation environment for transmon chips: calibration observables derive from circuit-quantized parameters via scqubits, with realistic flux-line distortion, wall-time-scaled and mid-scan drift, and gate leakage, concerns a toy simulator would omit; each tool call advances a modeled clock so drift accrues by wall time, not call count. The second is a vision-language agent that runs the loop end to end, calling tools, reading plots, maintaining a structured notebook, and submitting parameters without hidden truth, scored against hidden parameters and gate fidelities measured on the device. The third is gradient-free online adaptation: a reflector reads truth-free anomaly signatures from past attempts and grows a small, human-readable device note appended to the prompt, admitted by a paired-snapshot accept gate that isolates strategy improvement from drift. On a hard-tier chip under budget pressure, six iterations raised the worst-case CZ fidelity from 0.678 to 0.787 and cut its variance, reproducing at four-qubit scale; a single accepted note raised CZ fidelity from 0.678 to 0.913 on its paired snapshot. A planted-fault study confirms the note is causal, diagnosing a hardware fault truth-free, its principal value raising the failure floor and cutting variance. The agent, scoring, and reward transfer to real hardware via a measurement-backend swap; only the accept gate is a simulation affordance, reducing to a held-out-slice or repeat-and-average form.

AI.tldr: A vision-language agent autonomously calibrates a superconducting transmon chip by closing the experimental loop via three co-designed components: a physics-grounded simulation environment with realistic noise and drift, an end-to-end agent that reads plots and submits parameters without hidden truth, and gradient-free online adaptation that grows a human-readable device note through anomaly detection. Six iterations raised worst-case CZ fidelity from 0.678 to 0.787, with one accepted note achieving 0.913 on a paired snapshot, and the approach transfers to real hardware.
AI.motivation: Superconducting transmon chip calibration is a sequential decision problem under noise, drift, and finite budget, requiring experts to choose experiments, interpret ambiguous plots, and revise beliefs as the chip drifts—a process that has not been closed by an autonomous vision-language agent without weight updates.
AI.method: Three co-designed artifacts: (1) a physics-grounded simulation using scqubits with realistic flux-line distortion, wall-time-scaled drift, and gate leakage; (2) a vision-language agent that runs the loop end-to-end, calling tools, reading plots, maintaining a notebook, and submitting parameters scored against hidden ground truth; (3) gradient-free online adaptation via a reflector that writes anomaly signatures into a human-readable device note, admitted by a paired-snapshot accept gate that isolates strategy improvement from drift.
AI.result: On a hard-tier chip under budget, six iterations raised worst-case CZ fidelity from 0.678 to 0.787 and cut variance; one accepted note raised CZ fidelity to 0.913 on its paired snapshot. A planted-fault study confirms the note is causal and truth-free. Results reproduce at four-qubit scale.
AI.conclusion: The vision-language agent can autonomously calibrate transmon chips without weight updates, and the approach transfers to real hardware via a measurement-backend swap, with the accept gate reducible to a held-out-slice or repeat-and-average form for physical deployment.

title: Broadband Characterization of Polarization Mode Dispersion for Quantum Communication Channels
summary: We present a method for characterizing polarization fiber channels carrying broadband quantum signals, where narrowband filtering would waste photon flux. Wavelength-dependent polarization mode dispersion (PMD) maps each input state to a trajectory on the Poincaré sphere; we show that the singular value decomposition of the band-averaged rotation matrix yields, in closed form, the optimal input states, the mutually unbiased measurement bases, and their infidelities. The three singular values provide a compact, bandwidth-dependent channel signature that separates first- from higher-order PMD, and the resulting 5%-infidelity bandwidth gives a practical filtering budget. We characterize deployed fiber links in Masdar City and demonstrate PMD mitigation by concatenating two channels through a single polarization controller.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a method for characterizing polarization fiber channels carrying broadband quantum signals, using SVD of the band-averaged rotation matrix to yield optimal input states, mutually unbiased measurement bases, and infidelities. It provides a compact channel signature, demonstrates a 5%-infidelity bandwidth for filtering budget, and validates with deployed fiber links in Masdar City, showing PMD mitigation by concatenating two channels through a single polarization controller.
AI.motivation: Existing narrowband filtering approaches waste photon flux when characterizing polarization fiber channels for broadband quantum signals, motivating the need for a method that works directly in the broadband regime without sacrificing photon efficiency.
AI.method: The method uses wavelength-dependent PMD to map input states to trajectories on the Poincaré sphere. The singular value decomposition (SVD) of the band-averaged rotation matrix is applied to compute optimal input states, mutually unbiased measurement bases, and their infidelities in closed form. The three singular values serve as a compact channel signature separating first-order from higher-order PMD.
AI.result: The singular values yield a bandwidth-dependent channel signature that separates first- and higher-order PMD. A 5%-infidelity bandwidth is identified as a practical filtering budget. The method was experimentally validated on deployed fiber links in Masdar City, demonstrating PMD mitigation by concatenating two channels through a single polarization controller.
AI.conclusion: The SVD-based approach provides an efficient, closed-form characterization of broadband polarization channels for quantum signals, enabling practical PMD mitigation and filtering budget determination without wasting photon flux from narrowband filtering.

title: Quantum Annealing for Dynamic Portfolio Optimization under Realistic Transaction Costs
summary: This paper investigates and compares quantum and classical investment strategies for portfolio construction under realistic trading and allocation constraints. The study considers a multi-period portfolio re-balancing setting in which asset weights are subject to lower and upper bounds, class-level exposure restrictions, and turnover limitations. On the quantum side, the portfolio selection problem is reformulated as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) model through a finite binary encoding of asset weights, and subsequently embedded into a constrained quadratic model (CQM) solved by a hybrid quantum-classical optimization workflow. On the classical side, benchmark allocation strategies are introduced to provide an economically meaningful reference for performance assessment. The proposed framework jointly evaluates portfolio efficiency from two complementary perspectives: business performance, measured through return, volatility, and a measure of the trade-off between them, the Sharpe ratio; and computational performance, assessed through solver structure, constraint handling, and hardware execution characteristics. The resulting comparison provides a rigorous basis for understanding the practical role of quantum annealing in constrained portfolio optimization, while clarifying both its modeling advantages and its current implementation limitations relative to established classical approaches.

AI.tldr: This paper compares quantum (QUBO/CQM via hybrid quantum-classical solver) and classical investment strategies for multi-period portfolio rebalancing under realistic constraints (weight bounds, class exposure, turnover limits), evaluating both business performance (return, volatility, Sharpe ratio) and computational performance (solver structure, constraint handling, hardware execution).
AI.motivation: To rigorously assess the practical role of quantum annealing in constrained portfolio optimization by comparing quantum and classical approaches under realistic trading and allocation constraints.
AI.method: The portfolio selection problem is reformulated as a QUBO model using finite binary encoding of asset weights, embedded into a constrained quadratic model (CQM) solved by a hybrid quantum-classical optimization workflow. Classical benchmark allocation strategies are introduced for comparison.
AI.result: Joint evaluation of business performance (return, volatility, Sharpe ratio) and computational performance (solver structure, constraint handling, hardware execution) across quantum and classical approaches.
AI.conclusion: The comparison provides a rigorous basis for understanding quantum annealing's practical role in constrained portfolio optimization, clarifying its modeling advantages and current implementation limitations relative to classical approaches.

title: A Galton-Watson estimate for Dyson series
summary: We consider the question of convergence of particular series of integrals, which are labeled by rooted trees. Necessary and sufficient criteria for convergence are obtained, together with an explicit expression for the sum. The technique used is strongly reminiscent of the generating function approach of Galton and Watson to branching processes. The interest in these series derives from the Dyson series expansion for the perturbation of a free quantum dynamics by a local potential: the convergence of the series imlies that the perturbed dynamics exists and is unitarily equivalent with the free one.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the convergence of series of integrals indexed by rooted trees, establishing necessary and sufficient criteria along with explicit sum formulas, drawing parallels to Galton-Watson branching processes' generating functions, with applications to Dyson series in quantum dynamics where convergence implies existence and unitary equivalence of perturbed and free dynamics.
AI.motivation: The study is motivated by the Dyson series expansion for perturbing free quantum dynamics by a local potential; establishing convergence of this series is crucial to guarantee that the perturbed dynamics exists and remains unitarily equivalent to the free dynamics.
AI.method: The paper uses techniques reminiscent of generating function approaches from Galton-Watson branching processes, analyzing series of integrals labeled by rooted trees to derive necessary and sufficient convergence criteria and explicit summation formulas.
AI.result: Necessary and sufficient criteria for convergence of the tree-labeled series of integrals were obtained, along with an explicit expression for the sum.
AI.conclusion: The convergence of the analyzed series implies that the perturbed quantum dynamics exists and is unitarily equivalent to the free dynamics, providing a rigorous foundation for the Dyson series expansion.

title: Generating one-way computations with flow: flow-preserving rewriting that ignores the interpretation
summary:
The one-way model is a universal model of quantum computation, driven by successive adaptive single-qubit measurements on an entangled resource state. Measurements are non-deterministic, yet if the computation satisfies one of several related families of conditions known as 'flows', the computation can be made deterministic overall by modifying later measurements depending on the outcomes of earlier ones. Flow properties also enable efficient translation from one-way computations to circuits, motivating research into rewriting one-way computations while preserving the existence of flow. Existing approaches to flow-preserving rewriting are used for compilation or optimisation and preserve both the interpretation and the existence of flow.
  Here, we broaden our perspective to consider flow-preserving rewriting that does not necessarily preserve the interpretation, with applications to creating test instances for software that works with flow, as well as to generating ansätze for quantum machine learning. We show that a family of just three flow-preserving rewrite rules suffices to generate any diagram with flow from a trivial diagram with the desired number of inputs and outputs. This rule set is nearly the same as the complete set of flow- and interpretation-preserving rewrite rules for one-way computations in which all measurements are Pauli; and just a small subset of the flow- and interpretation-preserving rewrite rules for arbitrary measurements.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that three flow-preserving rewrite rules can generate any diagram with flow from a trivial diagram, broadening the use of such rules beyond preserving interpretation to applications like test instance creation and quantum machine learning ansätze generation.
AI.motivation: Existing flow-preserving rewriting techniques for one-way quantum computations preserve both the interpretation and flow. The authors seek to broaden this perspective by considering flow-preserving rewriting that does not necessarily preserve interpretation, enabling new applications such as generating test instances for flow-handling software and creating ansätze for quantum machine learning.
AI.method: The authors identify a family of just three flow-preserving rewrite rules and prove that this rule set suffices to generate any diagram with flow from a trivial diagram with the desired number of inputs and outputs. They compare this rule set to existing complete sets of flow- and interpretation-preserving rewrite rules for Pauli measurements and for arbitrary measurements.
AI.result: A set of three flow-preserving rewrite rules is sufficient to generate any diagram with flow from a trivial diagram. This rule set is nearly identical to the complete set of flow- and interpretation-preserving rewrite rules for Pauli-measured one-way computations, and is a small subset of those for arbitrary measurements.
AI.conclusion: Flow-preserving rewriting without interpretation preservation is feasible with a minimal rule set of three rules, enabling new applications in test instance generation and quantum machine learning ansätze creation for one-way quantum computations.

title: False vacuum decay in long-range interacting quantum systems
summary: We formulate false-vacuum decay in a mixed-field Ising chain with $1/r^α$ interactions as a spatially nonlocal Euclidean $φ^4$ theory featuring a fractional spatial kinetic term $\sim |q|^σ$, where $σ=α-1$. The nonlocal bounce is anisotropic in space-time and develops algebraic spatial tails, challenging the standard thin-wall picture of a compact droplet. Combining thin-wall arguments with numerical solutions of the full nonlocal saddle, we show that these tails preserve the leading thin-wall exponents, manifesting instead in subleading corrections. For $0<σ<1$, the lifetime exponent scales with the energy bias $h$ of the metastable state as $B\sim h^{-1/σ}$; for $1<σ<2$, the leading Coleman scaling $B\sim h^{-1}$ is recovered, while long-range effects are retained in the subdominant term $\sim h^{σ-2}$. Our results show that tunable long-range interactions fundamentally reshape bubble nucleation and alter false-vacuum decay in quantum simulators.

AI.tldr: This paper studies false-vacuum decay in a mixed-field Ising chain with long-range interactions, showing that the nonlocal bounce develops algebraic spatial tails that preserve leading thin-wall exponents but modify subleading corrections, with lifetime scaling depending on the interaction range parameter σ.
AI.motivation: To understand how tunable long-range interactions reshape bubble nucleation and false-vacuum decay in quantum simulators, challenging the standard thin-wall picture of compact droplets.
AI.method: Formulates false-vacuum decay as a spatially nonlocal Euclidean φ⁴ theory with fractional spatial kinetic term ~|q|^σ (σ=α-1), combining thin-wall arguments with numerical solutions of the full nonlocal saddle.
AI.result: For 0<σ<1, lifetime exponent B ~ h^{-1/σ}; for 1<σ<2, leading Coleman scaling B ~ h^{-1} is recovered with subdominant term ~ h^{σ-2}. Algebraic spatial tails preserve leading thin-wall exponents but manifest in subleading corrections.
AI.conclusion: Tunable long-range interactions fundamentally reshape bubble nucleation and alter false-vacuum decay in quantum simulators.

title: Comparing and learning figures of merit for quantum circuit compilation
summary: To make quantum algorithms executable on a particular quantum device, they need to be compiled into circuits that respect constraints of the quantum hardware. This compilation usually involves multiple steps, where many hardware-compatible circuits are generated, and the best circuit is selected. To say which circuit is best, the quality of a circuit is generally quantified by a $\textit{figure of merit}$ (FoM). For FoMs, there is a trade-off between ease of calculation and accuracy in predicted execution quality. Commonly used FoMs, e.g., the number of gates, circuit depth, etc., are easy to evaluate, but do not directly capture the effects of circuit structure and noise. On the other end of the spectrum are FoMs that require full circuit execution and take a prohibitively long time to evaluate. One example is the probability of successful trials (PST), i.e., the probability of obtaining the initial state after running the quantum circuit followed by its inverse. Here, we investigate advantages and disadvantages of different FoMs, and formulate the properties of an ideal FoM. Based on our results, we propose wPST, a weighted version of the PST that accounts for individual qubits, not just the whole state. To quickly predict PST and wPST, we design machine learning models that take into account both the quantum circuit and quantum hardware data. In numerical simulations and experiments on quantum processors, we find that our machine learning-predicted FoMs outperform commonly used FoMs, increasing the correlation with the true PST or wPST by over 50%. To make our model useful for quantum compilers, we devise a two-step process to predict the wPST for non-transpiled quantum circuits: first, we predict the additional quantum gates required for the given quantum circuit, and then we predict the wPST, accounting for coherence times in the quantum device.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates figures of merit (FoMs) for quantum circuit compilation, proposes wPST (weighted probability of successful trials) as an improved FoM, and develops machine learning models to predict wPST/PST efficiently, achieving over 50% improvement in correlation with true values over traditional FoMs.
AI.motivation: Existing figures of merit (FoMs) for evaluating quantum circuit quality face a trade-off between ease of calculation and accuracy. Simple metrics like gate count or circuit depth fail to capture noise and circuit structure effects, while accurate FoMs like PST require prohibitive full circuit execution. There is a need for a FoM that balances computational efficiency with predictive accuracy.
AI.method: The authors propose wPST, a weighted version of PST that accounts for individual qubit behavior rather than just the global state. They design machine learning models that incorporate both quantum circuit features and hardware data to predict PST and wPST without full execution. For non-transpiled circuits, a two-step process first predicts additional gates needed, then predicts wPST while accounting for coherence times.
AI.result: Machine learning-predicted FoMs outperform commonly used FoMs by over 50% in correlation with true PST or wPST, validated through numerical simulations and experiments on real quantum processors.
AI.conclusion: wPST is a more accurate figure of merit than traditional metrics, and machine learning enables its efficient prediction, making it practical for use in quantum compilers to select better circuits during compilation.

title: Complexity of Normalized Persistence Problems for Topological Data Analysis and Local Hamiltonians
summary: Topological data analysis (TDA) is a machine learning technique that uses topology to extract patterns from data and has shown the potential to exhibit quantum advantage. A key concept in TDA is persistent homology, which measures the robustness of topological information at different lengthscales. In this paper, we introduce and study the problem of normalized persistence, a practically motivated and easily interpretable version of persistent homology that counts the fraction of holes that persist at different lengthscales. We prove that a variant of normalized persistence is $\mathsf{DQC}_1$-hard and contained in $\mathsf{BQP}$, giving evidence of an exponential quantum speedup for TDA under the standard assumption that $\mathsf{DQC}_1 \not\subseteq \mathsf{BPP}$. These are the first $\mathsf{DQC}_1$-hardness results that are directly applicable to TDA instances. We also find a close connection between normalized persistence and the complexity of estimating spectral quantities in the low-energy subspace of local Hamiltonians. We study a family of such problems, including a low-energy normalized subtrace and spectral density. We show that these are $\mathsf{DQC}_1$-hard for $O(1)$-local Hamiltonians, strengthening previous results that required log-local interactions. We also introduce a variant of $\mathsf{DQC}_1$ with perfect completeness ($\mathsf{SDQC}_1$) to characterize the hardness of problems normalized by an exact kernel. This includes normalized persistence for $O(1)$-local Hamiltonians, which we show is $\mathsf{SDQC}_1$-hard.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces normalized persistence, a practically motivated variant of persistent homology in topological data analysis, proves it is DQC₁-hard and in BQP (suggesting exponential quantum speedup), and establishes connections to estimating low-energy spectral quantities of local Hamiltonians, including new DQC₁-hardness results for O(1)-local Hamiltonians and the introduction of SDQC₁ for problems with exact kernel normalization.
AI.motivation: To provide formal complexity-theoretic evidence for exponential quantum advantage in topological data analysis by studying a practically interpretable variant of persistent homology called normalized persistence, and to explore its connections to spectral estimation of local Hamiltonians.
AI.method: The paper proves complexity classifications: showing normalized persistence variants are DQC₁-hard (and thus likely not efficiently solvable classically) while contained in BQP, and establishing similar hardness for low-energy normalized subtrace and spectral density problems for O(1)-local Hamiltonians. It also introduces a new complexity class SDQC₁ (DQC₁ with perfect completeness) to characterize problems normalized by exact kernel.
AI.result: Normalized persistence is DQC₁-hard and in BQP, giving first DQC₁-hardness results directly applicable to TDA instances. Low-energy normalized subtrace and spectral density are DQC₁-hard for O(1)-local Hamiltonians (improving prior log-local results). Normalized persistence for O(1)-local Hamiltonians is SDQC₁-hard.
AI.conclusion: The work provides strong complexity-theoretic evidence that topological data analysis can achieve exponential quantum speedup (under standard assumptions), and establishes tight connections between TDA and spectral properties of local Hamiltonians, while introducing new complexity classes to capture the exact-kernel normalization regime.

title: Quantum Probability and Quantum Information Theory
comment: 43 pages, 11 figures. Course given at the 2006 summer school in Trieste on Quantum Information, Computation and Cryptography. Elements of this course will appear in a book of Burkhard Kümmerer and the author on quantum Markov chains
summary: This is an introductory course on quantum probability and quantum information, based on matrix algebras.

AI.tldr: An introductory course on quantum probability and quantum information using matrix algebras.
AI.motivation: To provide an accessible introduction to quantum probability and quantum information theory through the framework of matrix algebras, likely aiming to bridge classical probability and quantum mechanics.
AI.method: The paper presents a course structured around matrix algebras, using them as the mathematical foundation to explain concepts in quantum probability and quantum information.
AI.result: The abstract does not specify empirical results; it describes the scope and pedagogical approach of a course.
AI.conclusion: The course offers a matrix-algebra-based introduction to quantum probability and quantum information.

title: Dissipative preparation and stabilization of d-mode multinomial cat states
summary: Engineering dissipation with tailored steady states has become a powerful approach for preparing and stabilizing quantum states. In this framework, engineered dissipative processes continuously steer a system towards desired target states while suppressing unwanted noise. However, extending this idea to multimode systems is challenging and remains largely unexplored, although this class of states is a powerful resource for quantum sensing and quantum information processing applications. Here, we propose a general method to design the required dissipative processes for the generation of multimode cat states in bosonic systems. We show that the engineered dissipation prepares such states from the vacuum with high fidelity and robustly stabilizes them against decoherence. As a result, their lifetime is extended by several orders of magnitude compared to natural decay times, which in turn enhances their applications in quantum techonologies. We specifically focus on the preparation and stabilization of two-mode binomial cat states and discuss a pathway for the implementation in superconducting circuit. However, our scheme can also scale up to arbitrary d-mode multinomial cat states associated to $\mathfrak{su}(d\ge2)$ algebras, and thus, our scalable framework provides a feasible route towards stabilizing compact nonclassical states.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a general method for engineering dissipation to generate and stabilize multimode cat states in bosonic systems, demonstrating high-fidelity preparation from vacuum and extended lifetimes, with scalability to arbitrary d-mode multinomial cat states.
AI.motivation: Extending engineered dissipation from single-mode to multimode systems is challenging and largely unexplored, despite multimode cat states being powerful resources for quantum sensing and quantum information processing.
AI.method: A general method to design dissipative processes for generating multimode cat states in bosonic systems, specifically demonstrated for two-mode binomial cat states and scalable to arbitrary d-mode multinomial cat states associated with su(d≥2) algebras.
AI.result: Engineered dissipation prepares multimode cat states from vacuum with high fidelity and robustly stabilizes them against decoherence; their lifetime is extended by several orders of magnitude compared to natural decay times.
AI.conclusion: The scalable framework provides a feasible route towards stabilizing compact nonclassical states, with a pathway for implementation in superconducting circuits.

title: High Success Probability, Fidelity, and Purity Nonlinear Optical Two-Qubit Gates on Chip
summary: Optical two-qubit gate with high success probability, fault-tolerant fidelity, and high-purity outputs is a fundamental yet unsolved challenge, essential for large-scale optical quantum computing toward quantum advantage. Here, we propose a feasible scheme for such gate using thin-film lithium niobate platform, enabling \c{hi}(2) nonlinear photon-photon interaction with 100% efficiency. By decoupling photon interaction and qubit flip operations, fidelity ceiling is removed, and output state purity is recovered by spectral-phase pre-compensation based on a full-spectral photon interaction model, yielding a CNOT gate with 84% success probability, 93% purity, and unity fidelity.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a feasible CNOT gate scheme on thin-film lithium niobate using χ(2) nonlinear photon-photon interaction with 100% efficiency. By decoupling interaction and qubit flip operations, it achieves 84% success probability, 93% purity, and unity fidelity.
AI.motivation: A high-success-probability, fault-tolerant, high-purity optical two-qubit gate is essential for large-scale optical quantum computing but remains an unsolved challenge.
AI.method: Uses thin-film lithium niobate platform with χ(2) nonlinearity for efficient photon-photon interaction; decouples photon interaction from qubit flip operations; applies spectral-phase pre-compensation based on a full-spectral photon interaction model to restore output state purity.
AI.result: A CNOT gate with 84% success probability, 93% purity, and unity fidelity.
AI.conclusion: The proposed scheme removes the fidelity ceiling and recovers output purity, advancing toward scalable optical quantum computing with practical feasibility.

title: An End-to-End Multi-Stage Kill-Chain Attack on Quantum Neural Networks: Demonstration on Trapped-Ion Hardware
summary: We demonstrate an end-to-end, multi-stage attack against a quantum neural network (QNN) model that is executed on a trapped-ion quantum computer. Our chain combines side-channel reconnaissance, crosstalk characterization, adversarial example generation, and a physical crosstalk attack that realizes the adversarial perturbation on the device. We cover the full attack chain on ion traps and report the corresponding superconducting-hardware experiments in the appendix. We discuss implications for QaaS providers and hardware mitigations.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a full, multi-stage attack chain against a quantum neural network (QNN) on a trapped-ion quantum computer, combining side-channel reconnaissance, crosstalk characterization, adversarial example generation, and a physical crosstalk attack. It also includes superconducting-hardware experiments in the appendix and discusses implications for QaaS providers and hardware mitigations.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that quantum neural network models on real quantum hardware (trapped-ion) are vulnerable to practical, end-to-end adversarial attacks exploiting physical crosstalk, highlighting security risks for QaaS providers.
AI.method: The attack chain consists of: (1) side-channel reconnaissance to gather device parameters, (2) crosstalk characterization to map unintended interactions between qubits, (3) adversarial example generation leveraging the crosstalk model, and (4) a physical crosstalk attack that applies the adversarial perturbation on the trapped-ion device. Superconducting hardware experiments are reported in the appendix.
AI.result: The authors successfully executed the full attack chain on trapped-ion quantum hardware, showing that adversarial perturbations can be realized via crosstalk, and validated similar effects on superconducting hardware (reported in appendix).
AI.conclusion: QNNs on current quantum hardware are vulnerable to multi-stage physical attacks using crosstalk, necessitating security considerations and hardware-level mitigations for QaaS platforms.

title: Measurements Number Scaling in the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm for MaxCut: A Statistical Analysis
summary: We provide a statistical analysis of the measurement (shot) requirements of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) for the MaxCut problem. We derive sufficient conditions on the number of shots per cost operator evaluation to: (a) estimate the expected cost to within a relative error $δ$ and a confidence $1-ε$, and (b) ensure SGD-based parameter optimization converges to a target relative suboptimality level with high probability. In addition, we provide an explicit bound on the number of SGD iterations required to reach the target accuracy. Our analysis reveals an unexpected scaling phenomenon: for specific graph classes, which we formally characterize, the total shot budget needed to achieve a fixed relative-performance metric decreases as the instance size grows. This result complements earlier cost function concentration arguments regarding parameter optimization redundancy, thereby highlighting the potential for high-performance, low-overhead QAOA implementations for large-scale MaxCut instances. To assist practitioners, we translate our analytical findings into practical rules of thumb for shot-budget allocation and validate these results with numerical simulations, offering new insights into the interplay between graph size, structural complexity, and resource requirements in QAOA.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a statistical analysis of shot requirements for QAOA on MaxCut, deriving sufficient conditions for estimation accuracy and SGD convergence, revealing that for certain graph classes the total shot budget decreases as instance size grows, and offering practical rules of thumb validated numerically.
AI.motivation: To understand and quantify the measurement (shot) requirements for QAOA on MaxCut, addressing the gap between theoretical promise and practical resource constraints, particularly for large-scale instances.
AI.method: Statistical analysis deriving sufficient conditions on shots per cost operator evaluation for (a) estimating expected cost within relative error δ and confidence 1-ε, and (b) ensuring SGD-based parameter optimization converges to target suboptimality; explicit bound on SGD iterations; theoretical characterization of graph classes with favorable scaling.
AI.result: Unexpected scaling phenomenon: for specific graph classes, total shot budget needed for fixed relative performance decreases as instance size grows. Provides explicit bounds on SGD iterations and practical rules of thumb for shot allocation.
AI.conclusion: Highlights potential for high-performance, low-overhead QAOA implementations on large-scale MaxCut instances, complementing prior cost concentration arguments and offering new insights into resource-graph size interplay.

title: Nested-Loop Trajectory-Informed Variational Quantum Solver for Interior-Point OPF
summary: Optimal power flow (OPF) solved by an interior-point method (IPM) requires repeatedly solving Newton linear systems. When variational quantum linear solvers (VQLS) are used, each IPM iteration involves an additional nested inner variational optimization loop, which can significantly slow the overall quantum-assisted IPM convergence. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a dual-level trainable quantum IPM framework for OPF that leverages early solver-generated trajectories rather than relying on single-point prediction. The key observation is that early IPM iterates provide informative primal-dual, slack, and barrier-variable evolution about the path to optimality, while early VQLS parameter updates provide useful information about the later variational search. At the quantum-solver level, a trainable parameter model uses a short prefix of the VQLS parameter trajectory to project the remaining variational search toward a lower-cost region. At the OPF-solver level, a second trainable model uses early primal-dual IPM iterates to project a later central path state, which is restored to an admissible point before IPM refinement continues. Simulation studies show that the proposed approach reduces the number of variational updates by up to $95\%$ while maintaining OPF objective values close to the classical IPM reference. A 2-bus demonstration on real quantum hardware is also included to validate the implementation of the proposed workflow.

AI.tldr: A dual-level trainable quantum IPM framework for OPF that uses early trajectories from both VQLS and IPM to predict later states, reducing variational updates by up to 95% while maintaining accuracy close to classical benchmarks, with validation on real quantum hardware.
AI.motivation: Classical IPM for OPF requires repeated Newton linear system solves; VQLS introduces nested inner variational loops that significantly slow convergence. The paper aims to reduce this computational burden.
AI.method: Proposes a dual-level trainable framework: (1) at the quantum-solver level, a trainable parameter model uses a short prefix of VQLS parameter trajectory to project the remaining variational search; (2) at the OPF-solver level, a second trainable model uses early primal-dual IPM iterates to project a later central path state, which is then restored to an admissible point.
AI.result: Reduces the number of variational updates by up to 95% while maintaining OPF objective values close to the classical IPM reference. A 2-bus demonstration on real quantum hardware validates the implementation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed dual-level trainable quantum IPM framework effectively accelerates quantum-assisted OPF by leveraging early trajectory information, achieving significant reduction in variational updates with minimal accuracy loss.

title: Symmetry-Protected Quantum Synchronization in Squeezed-Bath-Engineered Superradiance
summary: A squeezed dissipative bath converts the coupling phase of a bipartite unconventional Dicke model into a control parameter that suppresses both static superradiant thresholds, opening a window where only a Hopf instability survives and the two spin ensembles synchronize completely via the shared cavity mode. The squeezed bath preserves a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ parity symmetry, so conventional broken-symmetry diagnostics vanish identically. We certify the synchronized state instead through parity-even, information-theoretic witnesses: a 30\% photon-number suppression, a Husimi-$Q$ lobe-count change, a 64\% suppression of spin--spin mutual information, and a robust discord-to-mutual-information ratio $D/I = 0.50 \pm 0.05$, confirmed by full quantum master-equation simulations. These results establish parity-even witnesses as a general, entanglement-free route to certifying quantum synchronization in symmetry-protected driven-dissipative systems.

AI.tldr: A squeezed dissipative bath in a bipartite unconventional Dicke model suppresses static superradiant thresholds, leaving only a Hopf instability where two spin ensembles synchronize via a shared cavity mode. The synchronized state is certified not by conventional broken-symmetry diagnostics (which vanish due to $\mathbb{Z}_2$ parity symmetry) but by parity-even, information-theoretic witnesses: 30% photon-number suppression, Husimi-$Q$ lobe-count change, 64% suppression of spin-spin mutual information, and a discord-to-mutual-information ratio of $0.50 \pm 0.05$. This establishes parity-even witnesses as a general, entanglement-free route to certifying quantum synchronization in symmetry-protected driven-dissipative systems.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that quantum synchronization can be certified in symmetry-protected dissipative systems without relying on broken-symmetry order parameters, using information-theoretic parity-even witnesses instead.
AI.method: The authors study a bipartite unconventional Dicke model with a squeezed dissipative bath, analyze static and dynamic (Hopf) instabilities, and use full quantum master-equation simulations to compute parity-even witnesses: photon-number suppression, Husimi-$Q$ lobe-count changes, mutual information suppression, and the discord-to-mutual-information ratio.
AI.result: A 30% photon-number suppression, a Husimi-$Q$ lobe-count change, a 64% suppression of spin-spin mutual information, and a robust $D/I = 0.50 \pm 0.05$ ratio are observed, confirming synchronization despite vanishing conventional broken-symmetry diagnostics.
AI.conclusion: Parity-even, information-theoretic witnesses provide a general, entanglement-free framework for certifying quantum synchronization in symmetry-protected driven-dissipative systems.

title: Specifying the operational meaning of quantum reference frames
summary: In their strongest usage, quantum reference frames have been described as referring to "the measurements performed by a superposed lab", "the perspective of a quantum particle", "the point of view of a superposed observer", etc. While exciting, these operational proposals have remained brief and ambiguous, leading to misinterpretations and criticism. Here, we provide a detailed specification and defense of the notion of a position-superposed lab or observer. We argue that this requires no exotic claims about quantum physics and raises no greater interpretive difficulty than ordinary quantum measurements. We then derive several consequences of taking this operational meaning seriously. We stress that the position-superposed observers that define quantum references frames are different from, and considerably less problematic than, the outcome-superposed observers considered in Wigners' friend scenarios. In particular, we show that outcomes obtained by a position-superposed observer may (without decohering the superposition) be broadcast to a well-localised one, in contrast with Wigner's friend scenarios, which require the outcomes to remain internal to the system at hand. Finally, we defend the possibility to roleplay a quantum reference frame from a classical reference frame.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a detailed specification and defense of position-superposed observers (quantum reference frames), distinguishing them from problematic Wigner's friend scenarios, and showing that their outcomes can be broadcast to well-localised observers without decoherence.
AI.motivation: The notion of quantum reference frames (superposed labs/observers) has been used ambiguously and received criticism; the authors aim to clarify, defend, and specify what this operational concept truly entails without exotic claims.
AI.method: Conceptual analysis and defense of position-superposed observers within standard quantum mechanics, distinguishing them from outcome-superposed observers in Wigner's friend scenarios.
AI.result: Position-superposed observers can broadcast measurement outcomes to well-localised observers without decohering the superposition, unlike Wigner's friend scenarios where outcomes must remain internal.
AI.conclusion: Position-superposed observers raise no greater interpretive difficulty than ordinary quantum measurements; roleplaying a quantum reference frame from a classical reference frame is possible; these observers are fundamentally different from and less problematic than outcome-superposed observers.

title: Matter-Field Exchange Generates Entanglement, Not Classical Gravity
summary: Aziz and Howl have argued that a hybrid theory with quantum matter and a classical gravitational field can generate entanglement between two massive systems. In their construction, the branch-dependent contribution appears at fourth order through propagators of the quantum matter field in a fixed classical gravitational potential. We analyse this mechanism within the same perturbative QFT framework and show that the effect should not be interpreted as classical gravity mediating entanglement in the sense relevant to BMV-type witnesses. The non-separable term relies on a quantum-matter exchange channel between the two interferometers and is present only when the two systems are modelled as excitations of the same matter field. If distinct, non-interconverting matter fields describe the systems, the corresponding cross-propagator is absent and the Aziz-Howl entangling diagram vanishes. The effect relies on coherent propagation amplitudes of the quantum matter field between the two interferometers, together with postselection onto the original localised branch subspace. Moreover, the inference of entanglement is made after projecting the full QFT evolution onto a restricted final subspace containing the original localised $N$-particle branch states. This projection removes precisely the sectors that would record matter-field contamination, mode deformation, or exchange between the two interferometers. We therefore argue that the Aziz-Howl mechanism is a matter-sector cross-talk effect in a classical background, not entanglement mediated by classical gravitational degrees of freedom. Having identified the channel responsible for the Aziz-Howl contribution, we predict that it can be eliminated by using distinct, non-interconverting matter species in the two interferometers, or by inserting a barrier that suppresses matter-field propagation between them.

AI.tldr: The paper critically analyzes the Aziz-Howl mechanism, arguing it does not demonstrate classical gravity mediating entanglement. Instead, the effect arises from quantum matter-field exchange between interferometers and postselection onto restricted localised-branch states. The authors propose eliminating the effect by using distinct non-interconverting matter species or inserting a barrier to suppress matter propagation.
AI.motivation: To assess whether the Aziz-Howl mechanism genuinely demonstrates entanglement mediated by a classical gravitational field, as opposed to a quantum matter-sector artifact, which has implications for BMV-type entanglement witnesses and tests of quantum gravity.
AI.method: Perturbative QFT analysis of the Aziz-Howl construction, examining the diagrammatic structure of the entangling contribution, the role of matter-field propagators between interferometers, and the effect of postselection onto restricted N-particle branch subspaces.
AI.result: The Aziz-Howl entangling term arises from quantum matter-field exchange between two interferometers, requiring they be excitations of the same matter field; the effect vanishes for distinct non-interconverting species. Postselection onto the original localised branch subspace removes sectors that would record matter contamination or exchange.
AI.conclusion: The Aziz-Howl mechanism is a matter-sector cross-talk effect in a classical background, not entanglement mediated by classical gravitational degrees of freedom. The effect can be eliminated by using distinct matter species or inserting a barrier.

title: Design of an Electrically Tunable Microtoroid for Frequency Selection of Polarization-Entangled Photons
summary: Encoding quantum information into discrete optical frequencies, or "frequency bins," uses different colors of light as additional information channels, allowing each photon to carry more information than polarization alone. We present a computational design for an electrically tunable silica microtoroid that selects desired frequency channels after a polarization-entangled photon pair has been generated without disturbing the photons' polarization entanglement. In the proposed architecture, the 750 nm signal photon passes through the microtoroid, while its entangled 880 nm partner bypasses the resonator and serves as a reference for the selected frequency channel. The principal challenge is resonator birefringence: because horizontally and vertically polarized light resonate at slightly different frequencies, the selected frequency can reveal the photon's polarization state and weaken the quantum correlation between the photon pair. We solve this problem by adding a small lithium-niobate tuning element controlled with a single applied voltage. The voltage shifts the resonator so that it responds almost identically to horizontally and vertically polarized light, reducing the remaining mismatch to only 0.286 optical linewidths across nine frequency channels. The photons remain strongly entangled after passing through the device, with a concurrence of C = 0.969, a Bell-state fidelity of F = 0.981, and a Bell parameter of S_max = 2.785. If the relative timing between the frequency channels is also controlled, the same device can generate a nine-channel polarization-frequency hyperentangled state with an effective dimension of K = 8.97. This computational design provides a compact, electrically tunable bridge between polarization-entangled photon sources and future high-capacity quantum photonic systems.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a computational design for an electrically tunable silica microtoroid that can select frequency channels from polarization-entangled photon pairs without disturbing entanglement, overcoming resonator birefringence via a lithium-niobate tuning element, achieving high concurrence (0.969), Bell-state fidelity (0.981), and enabling nine-channel hyperentangled states.
AI.motivation: To enable frequency-bin encoding for polarization-entangled photon pairs without degrading quantum correlations, specifically solving the problem of resonator birefringence that would otherwise reveal polarization information and weaken entanglement.
AI.method: A silica microtoroid resonator with an electrically tunable lithium-niobate element; the 750 nm signal photon is routed through the resonator while the 880 nm partner bypasses it; the voltage shifts the resonator to equalize response for H and V polarizations, reducing mismatch to 0.286 linewidths across nine channels.
AI.result: Concurrence C=0.969, Bell-state fidelity F=0.981, Bell parameter S_max=2.785. With timing control, a nine-channel polarization-frequency hyperentangled state with effective dimension K=8.97 is achievable.
AI.conclusion: The design provides a compact, electrically tunable bridge between polarization-entangled sources and high-capacity frequency-multiplexed quantum photonic systems.

title: Dynamical zero modes, boundary dependence, and numerical instability in dynamical quantum phase transitions
summary: Boundary conditions are usually expected to cause only finite-size corrections to bulk quantities, but this expectation can fail for dynamical quantum phase transitions. In this work, we show that such boundary dependence is encoded in dynamical zero modes (DZMs) of the Loschmidt matrix, which are defined as singular vectors whose singular values vanish in the thermodynamic limit. Using the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) and extended SSH models as examples, we find that the time interval where the Loschmidt rate functions (LRFs) under periodic and open boundary conditions differ coincides with the emergence of DZMs in the open-boundary Loschmidt matrix. These modes carry the boundary-dependent contribution: removing them from the open-boundary LRF recovers the periodic-boundary result. We further show that these DZMs lead to finite-precision numerical instability, since their finite-size singular values decay exponentially with system size and eventually become unresolved in fixed-precision arithmetic. A reliable small-size branch before this loss of precision can be used to estimate the thermodynamic LRF by linear extrapolation. Our results identify DZMs as both a diagnostic of boundary-dependent LRFs and the origin of the associated numerical instability.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that boundary-condition dependence in dynamical quantum phase transitions is encoded in dynamical zero modes (DZMs) of the Loschmidt matrix. Using SSH models, the authors demonstrate that DZMs cause differences between periodic and open boundary Loschmidt rate functions, and that removing them recovers the periodic-boundary result. DZMs also cause finite-precision numerical instability due to exponential decay of singular values.
AI.motivation: To understand why boundary conditions, which typically cause only finite-size corrections, can qualitatively affect dynamical quantum phase transitions, and to identify the mathematical structure responsible for this boundary dependence.
AI.method: Introduced dynamical zero modes (DZMs) as singular vectors of the Loschmidt matrix with vanishing singular values in the thermodynamic limit. Analyzed SSH and extended SSH models under periodic and open boundary conditions, compared Loschmidt rate functions (LRFs), and performed linear extrapolation from finite-size data.
AI.result: DZMs emerge precisely when open- and periodic-boundary LRFs differ; removing DZMs from the open-boundary LRF recovers the periodic-boundary result. Finite-size DZM singular values decay exponentially, causing numerical instability in fixed-precision arithmetic.
AI.conclusion: DZMs serve as both a diagnostic of boundary-dependent Loschmidt rate functions and the origin of the associated numerical instability. Reliable small-size extrapolation can estimate the thermodynamic LRF before precision loss occurs.

title: Superposed circular motion Unruh effect in (3+1) dimensions
summary: Using a recently-introduced quantum control model for Unruh-DeWitt detectors in superpositions of classical trajectories, we investigate the response of a detector interacting with a massless scalar quantum field in (3+1) dimensions along a superposition of circular trajectories. We present numerical results for the transition probability and effective temperature of such a detector in four distinct geometric scenarios: (a) concentric, vertically-stacked trajectories, (b) planar, horizontally-displaced trajectories, (c) static central point and surrounding circular trajectory, and (d) concentric, planar circular trajectories. For Gaussian switching functions that are much broader than the acceleration timescale, in case (a) we find only minor deviations from the well-known, effectively thermal response of a single circular trajectory, whereas in case (c) we find a significant reduction in the effective temperature and greater variation with energy gap. We conclude with a discussion of a potential analogue implementation in ultracold atom systems.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates Unruh-DeWitt detectors following superpositions of circular trajectories in (3+1)D scalar quantum fields, finding that trajectory geometry significantly affects transition probabilities and effective temperatures, with potential ultracold atom analogue implementations.
AI.motivation: To extend quantum control models for Unruh-DeWitt detectors to superpositions of classical trajectories, specifically circular trajectories, and understand how trajectory geometry affects the detector's response to quantum vacuum fluctuations.
AI.method: Numerical analysis of transition probabilities and effective temperatures for Unruh-DeWitt detectors in four geometric scenarios of circular trajectory superpositions, using Gaussian switching functions broader than the acceleration timescale in (3+1)D massless scalar quantum field theory.
AI.result: Case (a) shows minor deviations from thermal response of a single circular trajectory; case (c) shows significant reduction in effective temperature and greater energy-gap dependence; the other cases exhibit intermediate behavior.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory superposition geometry qualitatively alters detector response, and potential analogue implementations in ultracold atom systems are discussed.

title: Semiclassical Langevin dynamics of long-range dissipative time crystals
summary: We develop a semiclassical Langevin approach to study finite-size effects in dissipative time-crystalline spin systems. For a spin-$1/2$ model with power-law Lindblad operators, we find finite-size oscillations exponentially decaying in time, and their decay rate decreases algebraically with system size in the long-range regime. The scaling exponent of this decay time provides a direct diagnostic of the robustness of the time-crystalline, and we find that this robustness extends beyond the range of power-law dissipation exponents where the system dynamics is mean-field in the thermodynamic limit. We also apply our approach to a spin-one model with local dissipation and long-range Hamiltonian interactions, formulating it in terms of Gell-Mann variables. In this case, finite-size stability is quantified through the deviation time from the mean-field behavior and the behavior of the dominant Fourier peak. We find that both quantities scale as a power law with the system size -- marking thereby a time-crystal behavior -- when the exponent of the power-law interaction is below a certain threshold, that turns out to be in agreement with previous cumulant-expansion findings. Our results show that semiclassical Langevin dynamics provides a useful finite-size probe of dissipative time crystals in regimes beyond exact Lindblad simulations.

AI.tldr: The authors develop a semiclassical Langevin approach to study finite-size effects in dissipative time-crystalline spin systems, finding that finite-size oscillations decay exponentially with size-dependent rates, and demonstrate that this method probes time-crystal robustness in regimes beyond exact Lindblad simulations.
AI.motivation: To study finite-size effects in dissipative time-crystalline spin systems, particularly probing robustness beyond the thermodynamic limit and beyond the reach of exact Lindblad simulations.
AI.method: A semiclassical Langevin approach is developed. For a spin-1/2 model with power-law Lindblad operators, finite-size oscillations are analyzed. For a spin-one model with local dissipation and long-range Hamiltonian interactions, Gell-Mann variables are used.
AI.result: Finite-size oscillations decay exponentially in time with a decay rate that decreases algebraically with system size in the long-range regime. The scaling exponent of decay time diagnoses time-crystal robustness. For the spin-one model, deviation time from mean-field and dominant Fourier peak scale as power laws with system size, marking time-crystal behavior when the interaction exponent is below a threshold consistent with cumulant-expansion findings.
AI.conclusion: The semiclassical Langevin dynamics provides a useful finite-size probe of dissipative time crystals, extending beyond the range where exact Lindblad simulations are feasible.

title: Driving collective RPA modes by a time-dependent Dyson map
summary: We study a time-dependent non-Hermitian generalisation of the Schütte-Da~Providência model describing a bosonic mode coupled to collective particle-hole excitations. Using a time-dependent Dyson map, we construct a Hermitian counterpart and reduce the collective fermionic sector by means of the random phase approximation (RPA). The resulting dynamics is mapped to two time-dependent harmonic-oscillator branches with instantaneous RPA frequencies $W_\pm(t)$. We determine the corresponding stability regions and compute transition probabilities between instantaneous oscillator states. In first-order instantaneous-basis perturbation theory the leading transition $n\to n+2$ is proportional to $\dot W_j/W_j$, showing that it is purely nonadiabatic and absent in the time-independent case. We compare this result with exact Lewis-Riesenfeld transition amplitudes within the RPA approximation. Numerical examples show that different components of the Dyson map provide distinct driving mechanisms: the scaling parameter modulates the effective coupling, while the squeezing parameter acts through a moving-boundary contribution. In both cases the induced collective transitions exhibit parametric-resonance peaks and sideband structures.

AI.tldr: A time-dependent non-Hermitian generalization of the Schütte-Da Providência model is studied. Using time-dependent Dyson maps and RPA, the system reduces to two time-dependent harmonic oscillators. Leading nonadiabatic transitions n→n+2 scale with Ẇⱼ/Wⱼ, and numerical examples reveal parametric-resonance peaks and sideband structures driven by Dyson map components.
AI.motivation: To extend the Schütte-Da Providência model (bosonic mode coupled to collective particle-hole excitations) to a time-dependent non-Hermitian framework, enabling the study of nonadiabatic transitions and parametric effects absent in the static case.
AI.method: (1) Introduce a time-dependent non-Hermitian generalization. (2) Construct a time-dependent Dyson map to obtain a Hermitian counterpart. (3) Reduce the fermionic sector via RPA, yielding two time-dependent harmonic-oscillator branches with instantaneous RPA frequencies W±(t). (4) Compute transition probabilities using first-order instantaneous-basis perturbation theory and exact Lewis-Riesenfeld transition amplitudes. (5) Perform numerical examples to analyze driving mechanisms from scaling and squeezing parameters.
AI.result: The leading transition n→n+2 is proportional to Ẇⱼ/Wⱼ, confirming it is purely nonadiabatic and absent in the time-independent case. Numerical results show parametric-resonance peaks and sideband structures; the scaling parameter modulates effective coupling, while the squeezing parameter contributes via a moving-boundary effect.
AI.conclusion: The time-dependent non-Hermitian generalization reveals nontrivial nonadiabatic collective transitions beyond the static RPA approach, with Dyson map components providing distinct physical driving mechanisms that could be relevant for open quantum systems and time-dependent quantum many-body dynamics.

title: Daylight quantum keyless private communication for free-space links
summary: Quantum key distribution (QKD) is the most established approach in quantum communication. However, long-distance free-space implementations, particularly satellite links, remain challenging, especially during the day due to daylight background noise. Quantum keyless private communication (QKPC) is a quantum communication protocol that enables information-theoretic security with simpler system requirements, improved robustness against noise, and without the need for secret key distribution. QKPC and QKD are complementary, with QKPC enabling free-space links where QKD is impractical, while QKD provides channel monitoring for applications that require eavesdropping detection. Here, we report a complete implementation of QKPC in a daylight free-space experiment over a 90 m rooftop link, using an experimentally simple setup. Our demonstration includes all stages of the protocol, from encoding and synchronization to message decoding, operates entirely without auxiliary classical synchronization channels, and is implemented offline through post-processing. This work demonstrates the feasibility of practical and scalable quantum communication over high-noise daylight links and highlights the potential of QKPC as a complementary solution to QKD for future ground-based and space-based communication systems.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the first complete experimental demonstration of Quantum Keyless Private Communication (QKPC) over a 90 m daylight free-space rooftop link, achieving information-theoretic security without secret key distribution and using a simple setup without auxiliary classical synchronization channels.
AI.motivation: Long-distance free-space QKD, especially satellite links, remains challenging during daytime due to daylight background noise. QKPC offers an alternative with simpler system requirements and better noise robustness, but had not been experimentally demonstrated in a complete daylight free-space setting.
AI.method: The authors implemented a complete QKPC protocol over a 90 m rooftop free-space link in daylight, including encoding, synchronization, and message decoding stages, operating entirely without auxiliary classical synchronization channels, using offline post-processing.
AI.result: Successful demonstration of QKPC over a 90 m daylight free-space link with an experimentally simple setup, operating without auxiliary classical synchronization channels.
AI.conclusion: QKPC is feasible and practical for high-noise daylight links, serving as a complementary solution to QKD for future ground-based and space-based quantum communication systems.

title: Thermalization hierarchy from irreducible degrees of freedom
summary: The decomposition of the Hilbert space of a quantum many-body system into the irreducible representations of its bond and commutant algebras yields a finer structure of dynamically isolated subspaces than the mere decomposition into symmetry sectors. While it has been recognized that subspaces associated with low bond-irrep dimensions $D_λ$ tend to violate the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH), here we show that $D_λ$ controls thermalization continuously across the full spectrum of dynamical subspaces. Using SU(2)-symmetric spin-1/2 chains as a paradigmatic example, we demonstrate that $\mathrm{log} \ D_λ$ quantitatively accounts for the average eigenstate entanglement entropy within each sector, establishing a thermalization hierarchy that interpolates from exact quantum many-body scars at $D_λ=1$ to volume-law ergodic states at large $D_λ$. To make this concrete, we introduce the notion of irreducible degrees of freedom (IDOF), defined as the number of independently-varying spatial coordinates parametrizing a many-body state within a given bond-algebra sector, which provides a microscopic interpretation of $D_λ$ and of the resulting thermalization hierarchy. Finally, we show that by selectively breaking symmetries while preserving chosen bond-algebra sectors, one can embed families of nonthermal eigenstates at prescribed entanglement levels into an otherwise ergodic spectrum, generalizing restricted spectrum-generating algebras from towers of individual states to entire dynamical subspaces.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the bond algebra's irreducible representation dimension $D_λ$ continuously controls thermalization in quantum many-body systems, from exact scars ($D_λ=1$) to ergodic states (large $D_λ$), quantified by eigenstate entanglement entropy via $\log D_λ$, introducing irreducible degrees of freedom (IDOF) as a microscopic interpretation.
AI.motivation: To establish that the bond algebra's irreducible representation dimension $D_λ$ provides a continuous, quantitative measure of thermalization across dynamical subspaces, going beyond the binary scar-vs-ergodic classification.
AI.method: Using SU(2)-symmetric spin-1/2 chains, the authors analyze the bond-algebra and commutant algebra decomposition, compute eigenstate entanglement entropy as a function of $D_λ$, introduce irreducible degrees of freedom (IDOF) as the count of independently-varying spatial coordinates per sector, and demonstrate selective symmetry breaking to embed nonthermal states.
AI.result: $\log D_λ$ quantitatively predicts the average eigenstate entanglement entropy within each sector; sectors with $D_λ=1$ are exact quantum many-body scars, while large $D_λ$ yields volume-law ergodic states, creating a continuous thermalization hierarchy.
AI.conclusion: Bond-algebra sectors provide a finer structure than symmetry sectors, with $D_λ$ serving as a universal control parameter for thermalization; the IDOF concept gives a microscopic interpretation; selective symmetry breaking enables engineering nonthermal subspaces at prescribed entanglement levels within an ergodic spectrum.

title: The arrival position problem in quantum mechanics
summary: The problem of making unambiguous probabilistic predictions about experiments involving waiting "always on" detectors remains a challenge for quantum theory. While most research on this problem studies arrival time, i.e., predicting the distribution of when detection events occur, this paper studies the arrival position problem, which is the complementary challenge of predicting the distribution of where detection events occur. Despite the widespread recognition of the arrival time problem, the inability of standard quantum theory to address the arrival position problem remains a pervasive theoretical blind spot. In this paper, we compare quantitative arrival position predictions derived from prominent proposed solutions to the screen problem. As we show, these models yield distinguishable predictions even in relatively simple experiments achievable with current technology. Notably, many of these discrepancies persist even in the far-field limit, where standard semiclassical approximations are typically assumed to be valid.

AI.tldr: The paper compares different proposed solutions to the arrival position problem (predicting where detection occurs on a screen), finding that they yield distinguishable predictions even in simple, realizable experiments and in the far-field limit where semiclassical approximations are expected to hold.
AI.motivation: Standard quantum theory lacks a framework for making unambiguous probabilistic predictions about "arrival position" (where a particle hits a screen). While arrival time problems are well-studied, the arrival position problem is a pervasive theoretical blind spot that this paper aims to address.
AI.method: The paper quantitatively compares predictions from multiple prominent proposed solutions to the screen problem, testing them across simple experimental setups achievable with current technology, including the far-field limit.
AI.result: Different models yield distinguishable predictions even in simple experiments. These discrepancies persist in the far-field limit, where standard semiclassical approximations are typically assumed to be valid.
AI.conclusion: The arrival position problem is a measurable and experimentally addressable issue; existing models can be distinguished empirically, challenging the assumption that semiclassical approximations are adequate in the far-field regime.

title: A Pulsed Live-Cell Quantum Microscope for Entangled Solid State and Biological Qubits
summary: Two revolutions in quantum sensing are converging on the same microscope stage. Biological qubits have emerged as genetically encoded, optically addressable quantum systems inside live cells. Solid state spin based qubits have been entangled and used as nanoscale correlator magnetometers, delivering sensitivity and spatial-resolution gains that single-spin probes cannot reach. Here we report a pulsed quantum microscope that enables simultaneous quantum state manipulation of both qubit technologies in live cells. The platform combines nanosecond-gated optical excitation at 450 nm and 520 nm, three-dimensional diffraction-limited addressing by galvo beam scanning and piezo objective focus, rapidly switched static and radio-frequency magnetic fields, single-photon timing with picosecond resolution, and microwave control for frequencies from DC to 5 GHz, including the 2.87 GHz resonance of solid state spins, the 500 MHz to 800 MHz resonance of radical pairs in biological qubits, and any future qubit resonance in the GHz range. Live cell imaging with simultaneous biological and solid state nanoparticle qubits in the same cell demonstrates the power of this technique for multiplexed quantum sensing.
