We anticipate this approach will open new opportunities for researchers to explore quantum sensing in live cells, and, ultimately, entanglement between a solid-state qubit and a protein-hosted spin qubit.

AI.tldr: A pulsed quantum microscope is developed that simultaneously manipulates both biological qubits (genetically encoded in live cells) and solid-state spin qubits (nanoparticles), enabling multiplexed quantum sensing with nanosecond optical gating, diffraction-limited addressing, and wideband microwave control (DC-5 GHz). Live cell imaging demonstrates the co-existence and operation of both qubit types, paving the way toward entanglement between solid-state and protein-hosted spin qubits.
AI.motivation: To bridge two converging quantum sensing revolutions—biological qubits (genetically encoded, optically addressable quantum systems in live cells) and solid-state spin qubits (used as entangled nanoscale correlator magnetometers)—by creating a single microscope platform that can simultaneously manipulate and read out both qubit technologies in living cells.
AI.method: A pulsed quantum microscope integrating nanosecond-gated optical excitation at 450 nm and 520 nm, 3D diffraction-limited addressing via galvo beam scanning and piezo objective focus, rapidly switched static and RF magnetic fields, single-photon timing with picosecond resolution, and broadband microwave control (DC-5 GHz, covering 2.87 GHz solid-state spin resonance and 500-800 MHz biological radical-pair resonance).
AI.result: Demonstrated live cell imaging with simultaneous operation of biological qubits and solid-state nanoparticle qubits within the same cell, validating the platform's capability for multiplexed quantum sensing.
AI.conclusion: This approach opens new opportunities for exploring quantum sensing in live cells and ultimately achieving entanglement between a solid-state qubit and a protein-hosted spin qubit.

title: Device-independent Quantum Key Distribution in the commuting operator framework
comment: See also the concurrent independent work by Correa da Silva, Fröb, Lechner, and L. Sangaletti, which is being released simultaneously
summary:
Device-independent quantum key distribution (DIQKD) is arguably the gold standard for secure quantum communication, as it aims to rely only on observed input-output statistics of an uncharacterized device which is only assumption to obey the laws of quantum physics. A corresponding security analysis hence demands a description of a quantum experiment from a most general perspective. Under close inspection, existing proof techniques do not always meet this goal as they tend to rely on subtile assumptions on a tensor product structure of the underlying Hilbert space and a 'hidden but finite' dimensionality. In this work, we collect the tools needed for a full analysis of DIQKD in the commuting operator framework, which avoids these subtilities and provides the arguably most general view on a quantum experiment. We rigorously proof the common assumption that in DIQKD measurements can be w.l.o.g. assumed to be projective. Furthermore, we show that task of computing key rates can be casted as a non-commutative polynomial optimization (NPO) problem to which the Navascués-Pironio-Acín (NPA) hierarchy gives a correct and converging relaxation.
  As a tool, we generalize the integral representation for the relative entropy by Frenkel [Quantum 7, 1102 (2023)] to general von Neumann algebras and apply techniques from Kossmann and Schwonnek [arXiv: 2411.04858] for the approximation in an NPO program.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a rigorous security analysis framework for Device-Independent Quantum Key Distribution (DIQKD) using the commuting operator model, proving that measurements can be assumed projective without loss of generality and that key rate computation reduces to a non-commutative polynomial optimization problem solvable via the NPA hierarchy.
AI.motivation: Existing DIQKD proof techniques rely on subtle assumptions (tensor product Hilbert space structure, hidden finite dimensionality) that are not fully general. The authors aim to provide the most general security analysis using the commuting operator framework, which avoids these limitations.
AI.method: The authors adopt the commuting operator framework for DIQKD analysis, rigorously prove that measurements can be assumed projective without loss of generality, formulate key rate computation as a non-commutative polynomial optimization (NPO) problem, generalize Frenkel's integral representation for relative entropy to von Neumann algebras, and apply approximation techniques from Kossmann and Schwonnek.
AI.result: The paper shows that the NPA hierarchy provides a correct and converging relaxation for the DIQKD key rate problem in the commuting operator framework, and establishes the projective measurement assumption as rigorous.
AI.conclusion: The commuting operator framework enables a fully rigorous DIQKD security analysis without tensor product or dimensionality assumptions, with computable key rates via NPO/NPA methods.

title: Macroscopic Quantum Interference of the Center-of-Mass Motion of Levitated Superconducting Microparticles enabled by Magnetic Higher-Order Traps
summary: We show how magnetostatic higher-order multipole traps can be used to generate macroscopic quantum interference of the motion of levitated superconducting microparticles. An appropriate combination of multipolar magnetic fields offers great versatility in constructing various trap potentials, including anharmonic trap potentials such as Duffing or double-well types. Crucially, the anharmonic trap potentials realize a nonlinearity on the order of hundred times the zero-point motion, i.e., on a length scale below nanometers. These anharmonic potentials allow for the generation of quantum features of the center-of-mass motion of a magnetically levitated superconducting microparticle. Importantly, they can be easily generated with a static arrangement of coils, requiring only that the current running through them is tunable. We propose protocols exploiting the versatility of the magnetic trap landscape to generate non-Gaussian motional states. We solve the dynamics of the center-of-mass motion of the particle in phase space and analyze its parameter dependence. Furthermore, we give a recipe to distinguish classical from quantum behavior in a statistically meaningful way through measurement of the position of the particle. Our results open a path to accessing the quantum regime of the center-of-mass motion of objects with masses larger than picogram, i.e., $10^{13}$ atomic mass units. This will enable fundamental physics experiments for studying the transition between quantum and classical behavior, exploring the intersection between quantum physics and gravity as well as probing of certain types of dark matter.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates how magnetostatic higher-order multipole traps can generate macroscopic quantum interference in levitated superconducting microparticles, using anharmonic trap potentials (Duffing or double-well) with nonlinearity ~100× zero-point motion to create non-Gaussian motional states, enabling quantum regime access for objects >picogram mass for fundamental physics tests.
AI.motivation: To access the quantum regime of center-of-mass motion for macroscopic objects (>picogram mass) using magnetostatic multipole traps, enabling studies of quantum-classical transition, quantum-gravity intersection, and dark matter detection.
AI.method: Combination of multipolar magnetic fields to construct versatile anharmonic trap potentials (Duffing/double-well); static coil arrangements with tunable currents; phase-space dynamics analysis of center-of-mass motion; protocols for generating non-Gaussian motional states.
AI.result: Achieved nonlinearity on order of ~100× zero-point motion (sub-nanometer scale); demonstrated ability to generate quantum interference of macroscopic motion; provided recipe for statistically distinguishing classical from quantum behavior via position measurement.
AI.conclusion: Opens path to accessing quantum regime for objects >10^13 atomic mass units, enabling fundamental experiments on quantum-classical transition, quantum gravity, and dark matter probing.

title: From the Hong-Ou-Mandel Effect to Quantum Sensing: Interference of Nonclassical Light with Partial Distinguishability and Noise
comment: Parts of this PhD thesis are adapted from the following works: arxiv.org/abs/2602.00071, arxiv.org/abs/2504.02893 and arxiv.org/abs/2301.02192
summary: This thesis explores the interference of nonclassical states of light, particularly Fock and Gaussian states, in noisy linear interferometers, with applications to quantum information and quantum sensing. Using the phase-space formalism, analytical tools based on generating functions are developed to describe quantum optical interference in a unified way. For multiphoton Fock states, new zero probability events (suppression laws) are identified beyond the previously derived symmetry permutation principle, revealing rich interference structures that is degraded with photon distinguishability. For Gaussian states, the Hafnian-based description of Gaussian Boson Sampling is extended to include partial distinguishability via the overlap matrix of the internal state of the photons. Finally, the link between these interference effects and quantum multiparameter estimation is examined for the simultaneous estimation of phase and loss. This study shows that while probe incompatibility can vanish for optimized non-Gaussian states and some two-mode Gaussian states, at high photon number, measurement incompatibility remains a fundamental constraint even in this limit.

AI.tldr: This thesis develops analytical tools based on generating functions in phase-space formalism to study nonclassical light interference in noisy linear interferometers, identifying new suppression laws for Fock states, extending Hafnian-based description of Gaussian Boson Sampling to partial distinguishability, and analyzing fundamental constraints in quantum multiparameter estimation of phase and loss.
AI.motivation: To understand how nonclassical states of light (Fock and Gaussian states) behave in noisy linear interferometers, with applications to quantum information and quantum sensing, particularly addressing the gap in unified analytical descriptions of interference phenomena and the fundamental limitations in multiparameter estimation.
AI.method: Phase-space formalism with generating functions as analytical tools for unified description; symmetry-based analysis for suppression laws in multiphoton Fock states; Hafnian-based matrix description extended via overlap matrix for partial distinguishability in Gaussian Boson Sampling; quantum multiparameter estimation theory for simultaneous phase and loss estimation.
AI.result: Discovery of new zero probability events (suppression laws) beyond the symmetry permutation principle for Fock states; successful extension of Hafnian framework to handle partial distinguishability in Gaussian Boson Sampling; identification that probe incompatibility can vanish for optimized non-Gaussian and some two-mode Gaussian states, but measurement incompatibility remains a fundamental constraint even at high photon numbers.
AI.conclusion: The unified phase-space framework effectively describes quantum optical interference; rich interference structures exist beyond known symmetry principles but degrade with distinguishability; measurement incompatibility is a more persistent fundamental limitation than probe incompatibility in quantum multiparameter estimation.

title: The influence of the transverse electric field on accelerating vortex state in the axisymmetric electric field
summary: The relativistic vortex states of massive charged particles propagating in non-uniform axisymmetric electric field are studied. Starting from the stationary-state equation after the relativistic Foldy-Wouthuysen (FW) transformation and employing the paraxial approximation, the coupled evolution equations for the beam width, wavefront curvature, and Gouy phase are derived. The equations are solved numerically for a quadratic electrostatic potential, an immersion lens, and an einzel lens. The essential influence of the transverse field on beam evolution is demonstrated. The results provide a relativistic quantum framework for controlling accelerated vortex particle beams using electrostatic fields.

AI.tldr: The paper studies relativistic vortex states of massive charged particles in non-uniform axisymmetric electric fields, deriving coupled evolution equations under paraxial approximation after FW transformation, and numerically solving them for quadratic potential, immersion lens, and einzel lens configurations, showing transverse field effects on beam evolution.
AI.motivation: To provide a relativistic quantum framework for controlling accelerated vortex particle beams using electrostatic fields.
AI.method: Starting from stationary-state equation after relativistic Foldy-Wouthuysen (FW) transformation, employing paraxial approximation to derive coupled evolution equations for beam width, wavefront curvature, and Gouy phase; numerical solutions for quadratic electrostatic potential, immersion lens, and einzel lens.
AI.result: Demonstrated the essential influence of transverse field on beam evolution; obtained numerical solutions for three electrostatic configurations.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a relativistic quantum framework for controlling accelerated vortex particle beams using electrostatic fields.

title: Entanglement-Assisted Timing Optimization for Discriminating Amplitude-Damping Dynamics
summary: We analyze minimum-error discrimination of two qubit dynamical processes generated by phase-covariant amplitude-damping Lindbladians in a single-use scenario. The optimization involves both the input probe, possibly entangled with an isolated ancilla, and the interrogation time. For unassisted probes we obtain a closed expression for the optimal trace-norm distinguishability at fixed time, with distinct interior and boundary branches. For entanglement-assisted probes, the common phase covariance of the two channels reduces the diamond-norm optimization to a one-parameter Schmidt family. The resulting formula gives transparent sufficient conditions for fixed-time entanglement advantage and separates this local advantage from advantage after global optimization over time. We exhibit examples in which the best unassisted strategy is approached only asymptotically, whereas an entangled probe achieves a strictly smaller error probability at finite time.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes optimal discrimination between two qubit dynamical processes (phase-covariant amplitude-damping Lindbladians) using single-use strategies, deriving closed-form distinguishability expressions for unassisted probes and a Schmidt-family reduction for entanglement-assisted probes, with conditions for entanglement advantage.
AI.motivation: To understand minimum-error discrimination of two quantum dynamical processes (channels) generated by phase-covariant amplitude-damping Lindbladians, optimizing over input probes, ancilla entanglement, and interrogation time.
AI.method: Closed-form optimization of trace-norm distinguishability for unassisted probes at fixed time (interior/boundary branches); reduction of diamond-norm optimization to one-parameter Schmidt family for entanglement-assisted probes leveraging phase covariance.
AI.result: Obtained closed expression for optimal trace-norm distinguishability for unassisted probes; derived formula for entanglement-assisted case giving transparent sufficient conditions for fixed-time entanglement advantage; found examples where unassisted optimality is only asymptotic while entangled probes achieve strictly lower error at finite time.
AI.conclusion: Entanglement can provide a strict advantage in discriminating two quantum dynamical processes, separable from the advantage gained by global time optimization; some channels require infinite time for optimal unassisted discrimination but finite time with entanglement.

title: Gorini-Kossakowski-Sudarshan-Lindblad equation in different bases: application to driven-dissipative two- and multilevel systems
summary: An open quantum system can be described by a master equation, of which one of the most popular is the Gorini-Kossakowski-Sudarshan-Lindblad (GKSL) equation. We revisit description of driven-dissipative quantum systems focusing on the appropriate choice of the system's basis and the respective transformations. We consider the GKSL equation in different bases and calculate the dynamics for a qubit and for a qudit. An appropriate choice of the basis is a fundamental problem for theoretical consideration of open quantum systems and provides an opportunity to obtain the desired evolution in practice.

AI.tldr: This paper reexamines the GKSL master equation for open quantum systems, focusing on how the choice of basis affects the description and dynamics of driven-dissipative systems, with examples for qubit and qudit systems.
AI.motivation: To revisit the appropriate choice of basis for describing driven-dissipative quantum systems via the GKSL equation, as basis selection is fundamental for both theoretical analysis and practical realization of desired evolution.
AI.method: The authors analyze the GKSL master equation in different bases, calculating the dynamics for a qubit and a qudit to demonstrate the impact of basis transformations on the system's description.
AI.result: The choice of basis significantly affects the form and interpretation of the GKSL equation; appropriate basis selection enables obtaining desired dissipative dynamics for qubit and qudit systems.
AI.conclusion: Basis choice is a fundamental problem for open quantum systems, offering both theoretical insight and practical control over engineered dissipative evolution.

title: Perturbed quantum billiards on the hyperbolic plane
summary: We study the emergence of generic quantum chaos from an arithmetic billiard in the hyperbolic plane. Starting from an arithmetic triangle, we introduce small area-preserving geometric perturbations and compute long consecutive sequences of eigenvalues and eigenstates. The spectral statistics show a perturbation-dependent crossover from Poisson-like arithmetic behaviour to the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble (GOE), with the crossover scale moving to higher wavenumbers as the perturbation decreases. To characterize the nearest-neighbour spacing distribution, we compare the data with Brody and generalized-gamma fits. The generalized-gamma form is used only as a two-parameter diagnostic, allowing the small- and intermediate-spacing structure to vary independently from the large-spacing tail, rather than as a universal crossover law. For the weakest perturbation, we also compare the data with an effective block-GOE model, which diagnoses residual block-like structure deep into the computed spectral range. We complement the spectral analysis with Poincaré-Husimi representations of the eigenstates and quantify phase-space localization using an entropy-based measure. Its distribution is well described by Beta distributions whose width decays as a power law in the wavenumber. Before the spectral crossover, the localization statistics retain memory of the near-arithmetic regime. After the GOE regime is reached, the localization-fluctuation widths collapse onto a common decay law, sigma(Beta) ~ k^{-eta}, with eta approximately 0.37--0.38. These results provide a combined spectral and eigenfunction-level picture of the arithmetic-to-GOE crossover in hyperbolic quantum billiards.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the transition from arithmetic (Poisson-like) to chaotic (GOE) behavior in hyperbolic quantum billiards via geometric perturbations, analyzing spectral statistics and eigenstate localization in both regimes.
AI.motivation: To understand how generic quantum chaos emerges from arithmetic (non-generic) quantum systems in hyperbolic geometry, particularly the crossover between distinct spectral and eigenstate statistics.
AI.method: Introducing small area-preserving geometric perturbations to arithmetic triangles, computing long eigenvalue/eigenstate sequences, comparing spectral statistics with Brody and generalized-gamma fits, using an effective block-GOE model for weak perturbations, and analyzing Poincaré-Husimi eigenstate representations with entropy-based localization measures.
AI.result: Perturbation-dependent Poisson-to-GOE crossover with scale shifting to higher wavenumbers as perturbation decreases; localization fluctuation widths collapse onto a universal power-law decay σ(β) ~ k^{-η} with η ≈ 0.37–0.38 after reaching the GOE regime; Beta distributions describe localization statistics well.
AI.conclusion: The combined spectral and eigenfunction analysis provides a comprehensive picture of the arithmetic-to-GOE crossover in hyperbolic quantum billiards, revealing universal and non-universal features across the transition.

title: A regularization method for quantum neural networks using data symmetry
summary: Leveraging data symmetries has recently become a key strategy in quantum neural networks (QNNs) to improve generalization and training efficiency. In this study, we propose a novel regularization method for QNNs based on input data symmetry. By introducing a penalty term that encourages the model to align with data symmetry, our method enables improved training speed and generalization. This symmetry-based regularization is simple to implement and does not require prior knowledge of the symmetry group. We validate its effectiveness through numerical experiments on both classification tasks and quantum generative adversarial networks. Empirical results demonstrate faster convergence and lower test errors. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical generalization bound using Rademacher complexity and conjecture a condition under which models with symmetry exhibit better generalization. Our findings highlight the potential of symmetry-aware regularization in enhancing the performance of QML models.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a symmetry-based regularization method for quantum neural networks that improves training speed and generalization without requiring prior knowledge of the symmetry group, validated on classification and quantum GAN tasks with theoretical generalization bounds via Rademacher complexity.
AI.motivation: Leveraging data symmetries in QNNs to improve generalization and training efficiency, motivated by the success of symmetry-aware methods in classical ML and the need for better regularization techniques in quantum machine learning.
AI.method: Introduces a penalty term that encourages QNN outputs to align with input data symmetries, without requiring explicit knowledge of the symmetry group; empirically tested on classification tasks and quantum generative adversarial networks; theoretically analyzed using Rademacher complexity to derive generalization bounds.
AI.result: Faster convergence and lower test errors empirically; theoretical generalization bound derived; condition conjectured under which symmetry-aware models generalize better.
AI.conclusion: Symmetry-aware regularization enhances QML model performance, offering a simple and effective approach to improving QNN training and generalization.

title: Matter-wave Induced Transparenc
summary: Electromagnetically induced transparency suppresses optical absorption through destructive interference, playing a central role in light-matter interaction and quantum information science. We report matter-wave induced transparency, where atomic collisional interactions induce transmission through a lossy molecular potential for the incident atomic scattering waves. Using cesium Bose-Einstein condensates and modulation-induced Feshbach resonances, we realize a three-level atom-molecule coupled system with unprecedented flexibility. Under the dark state condition, a narrow and tunable transparency window appears within a broad dissipative collisional resonance. The transparency window linewidth is controlled by modulation-induced coupling. And scattering pathways are selectable via multifrequency Floquet modulation. These results establish an interference-based route for exploring programmable nonequilibrium and non-Hermitian physics, steering quantum chemistry and precision measurements.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the observation of matter-wave induced transparency (MWIT) in a three-level atom-molecule coupled system using cesium Bose-Einstein condensates and modulation-induced Feshbach resonances, where atomic collisional interactions induce transmission through a lossy molecular potential, creating a narrow, tunable transparency window within a broad dissipative collisional resonance.
AI.motivation: To realize an atomic analog of electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) using matter waves and atomic collisional interactions, enabling new control over dissipative collisional resonances and exploring programmable nonequilibrium and non-Hermitian physics.
AI.method: Using cesium Bose-Einstein condensates with modulation-induced Feshbach resonances to create a three-level atom-molecule coupled system, with dark state conditions and multifrequency Floquet modulation to control scattering pathways and transparency window linewidth.
AI.result: A narrow and tunable transparency window appears within a broad dissipative collisional resonance under dark state conditions, with linewidth controlled by modulation-induced coupling and selectable scattering pathways via multifrequency Floquet modulation.
AI.conclusion: This establishes an interference-based route for exploring programmable nonequilibrium and non-Hermitian physics, with implications for steering quantum chemistry and precision measurements.

title: Algebra of quantum mechanics via classical phonons. I: The Schrodinger equation as the Newtonian equation of motion and quantum observables as classical averages
summary: The Schrodinger equation for a single spinless particle is formally obtained via a classical phonon model, namely the Frenkel-Kontorova model. Starting from a one-dimensional lattice of coupled harmonic oscillators, we show that the continuous limit of the corresponding Newtonian equation of motion yields the Klein-Gordon equation for a real-valued field. By introducing a complex-valued change of variables mixing the real-valued displacement and velocity fields, and by separating fast and slow time scales, the Klein-Gordon equation is written as the Schrodinger equation within the non-relativistic limit. This complex change of variable also allows to rewrite classical global observables of the phonon field, such as the total energy or momentum, as the corresponding quantum observables. Additionally, we show that when a friction force is incorporated into the classical model, the corresponding Klein-Gordon equation can be rewritten as a Schrodinger equation with a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian. While the global approach is limited here to the non-relativistic regime and does not address the measurement problem, quantization or relativistic effects, it nonetheless illustrates how quantum algebra and complex-valued wave functions can be exactly reproduced using classical dynamics. The relativistic regime for a spinless particle and the link between commutators and Poisson brackets is addressed in the second part of this series.

AI.tldr: This paper derives the Schrödinger equation from a classical phonon model (Frenkel-Kontorova) by taking the continuum limit of coupled harmonic oscillators to obtain the Klein-Gordon equation, then using a complex change of variables and time-scale separation to recover the Schrödinger equation in the non-relativistic limit. It also shows that adding friction yields a non-Hermitian Schrödinger equation.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that quantum mechanical structures (complex wave functions, quantum algebra) can emerge purely from classical dynamics of a phonon field, without invoking quantization or the measurement problem.
AI.method: Starting from a 1D Frenkel-Kontorova model (coupled harmonic oscillators), the continuum limit of Newton's equations yields the Klein-Gordon equation for a real field. A complex change of variables mixing displacement and velocity fields, combined with separation of fast and slow time scales, transforms the Klein-Gordon equation into the Schrödinger equation in the non-relativistic limit. Classical observables (energy, momentum) are shown to map to quantum observables via the same transformation. Friction is introduced to produce a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian.
AI.result: The Schrödinger equation (including a non-Hermitian variant with friction) is exactly reproduced from classical phonon dynamics. Classical global observables map to quantum expectation values.
AI.conclusion: Quantum algebra and complex wave functions can be exactly reproduced using classical dynamics in the non-relativistic regime, though the approach does not address quantization, measurement, or relativistic effects. Relativistic extensions and the commutator-Poisson bracket connection are deferred to a second part.

title: On estimating operator norm distance, with optimal trace distance estimation when one state is pure
comment: 28 pages, 2 algorithms. To appear in ESA 2026
summary:
We investigate the computational complexity of estimating the operator norm distance ${\rm T}_{\infty}(ρ_0,ρ_1)$, defined via the operator norm $\|A\|_{\infty} = σ_{\max}(A)$, given ${\rm poly}(n)$-size state-preparation circuits of $n$-qubit quantum states $ρ_0$ and $ρ_1$. We provide efficient quantum estimators for the operator norm distance whose complexity is independent of the rank (and thus the dimension) of the states:
  1. When one state is pure, we establish an optimal quantum estimator using $Θ(1/ε)$ queries to the state-preparation circuits. Consequently, for constant additive error, say $ε=1/5$, our estimator runs in ${\rm poly}(n)$ time. Since the operator norm distance ${\rm T}_{\infty}(|ψ\rangle\!\langleψ|,ρ)$ is exactly half of the trace distance ${\rm T}(|ψ\rangle\!\langleψ|,ρ)$, our result also gives rank-independent query complexity for estimating both quantities, whereas the approaches due to van Apeldoorn, Cornelissen, Gily{é}n, and Nannicini (SODA 2023) and Wang and Zhang (TIT 2024) have query complexity scaling at least linearly with ${\rm rank}(ρ)$, which can be $\exp(n)$ in general.
  2. For general quantum states, we also provide a quantum estimator using $\widetilde{O}(1/ε^{3/2})$ queries to the state-preparation circuits, which shows that the corresponding promise problem is ${\sf BQP}$-complete and improves the ${\sf QMA}$ upper bound sketched by Liu and Wang (ESA 2025). Together with an $Ω(1/ε)$ quantum query complexity lower bound, this leaves only square-root room for improvement.
  The key intuition behind our estimators is that, when one state is pure, the pure state $|ψ\rangle$ has overlap at least $1/2$ with the top unit eigenvector of $|ψ\rangle\!\langleψ|-ρ$, reflecting a structural feature specific to the operator norm distance.

AI.tldr: The paper develops efficient quantum algorithms for estimating the operator norm distance between quantum states, with rank-independent query complexity. For one pure state, they achieve optimal Θ(1/ε) queries (poly(n) time for constant ε). For general states, they use Õ(1/ε^{3/2}) queries, showing BQP-completeness and improving prior QMA upper bounds, with only quadratic gap from the Ω(1/ε) lower bound.
AI.motivation: To efficiently estimate the operator norm distance T_∞(ρ₀,ρ₁) between n-qubit quantum states using state-preparation circuits, with query complexity independent of state rank (which can be exponentially large), overcoming limitations of prior approaches that scale at least linearly with rank.
AI.method: (1) For pure vs. arbitrary state: Uses the structural insight that the pure state has overlap ≥1/2 with the top eigenvector of the difference, enabling optimal Θ(1/ε) query estimator. (2) For general states: Provides an Õ(1/ε^{3/2}) query estimator, showing BQP-completeness of the promise problem.
AI.result: Optimal quantum estimator with Θ(1/ε) queries when one state is pure (poly(n) time for constant ε); general-state estimator with Õ(1/ε^{3/2}) queries, establishing BQP-completeness and improving the QMA upper bound; Ω(1/ε) quantum query lower bound.
AI.conclusion: Operator norm distance estimation admits rank-independent quantum algorithms with near-optimal query complexity, leaving only a quadratic gap (from 1/ε to 1/ε^{3/2}) for the general case.

title: Algebra of quantum mechanics \textit{via} classical phonons. II: Klein-Gordon dynamics, the Heisenberg formalism, the Dirac canonical commutation rule and the Poincaré algebra through the continuous Poisson bracket formalism
summary: In the first part of this series we have shown how the Schrodinger equation for a single particle and the corresponding non relativistic quantum observables can be obtained from a purely classical phonon model through the Newtonian equations of motion. In this work we focus instead on how the classical Hamiltonian formalism applied to the same phonon system allows to recover the feature of relativistic quantum mechanics for a single spinless particle. Using the classical nature of the phonon model, we naturally define continuous Poisson brackets between classical observables, which allows to recover the dynamics of such observables, i.e. the Ehrenfest relations associated to real-valued Klein-Gordon fields. The Poisson brackets also permits to obtain the generic form of constants of motions, thus generalizing the concept of inner products and momentum on Klein-Gordon fields. We then connect the formalism of real-valued classical functionals with that of hermitian operators and complex-valued wave functions. This is done through the introduction of a non-local complex-valued change of variables which allows to rewrite the real-valued Klein-Gordon equation in a form akin to the Schrodinger equation, and the classical observables as quantum expectation values. Then, we show how this change of variables allows to rewrite the classical Poisson brackets as commutators of hermitian operators. This points out the strict equivalence between the Heisenberg formalism and the formalism of classical Poisson bracket. Eventually, we illustrate how the Poisson brackets allows to recover the transformations of Poincaré group in 1+1 dimension together with its algebra. The latter makes the link between the Lorentz invariant inner product of Mostafazadeh and the Casimir invariant associated to the mass of particle.

AI.tldr: This paper extends a classical phonon model to recover relativistic quantum mechanics for a single spinless particle, showing that classical Poisson brackets on real-valued Klein-Gordon fields yield Ehrenfest relations, constants of motion, and through a non-local complex change of variables, reproduce the Heisenberg formalism and Poincaré group algebra in 1+1 dimensions.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that relativistic quantum mechanics (specifically for a single spinless particle described by Klein-Gordon fields) can be derived from a purely classical phonon model using Hamiltonian formalism, thereby bridging classical mechanics and relativistic quantum theory.
AI.method: Applying classical Hamiltonian formalism to a phonon model; defining continuous Poisson brackets between classical observables; introducing a non-local complex-valued change of variables to map real-valued Klein-Gordon fields to complex wavefunctions and classical observables to quantum expectation values; rewriting Poisson brackets as commutators of Hermitian operators.
AI.result: Recovered Ehrenfest relations for real-valued Klein-Gordon fields; generalized inner products and momentum on Klein-Gordon fields via constants of motion; established equivalence between classical Poisson brackets and Heisenberg commutators; recovered Poincaré group transformations and algebra in 1+1 dimensions; linked Lorentz-invariant inner product to Casimir mass invariant.
AI.conclusion: The classical Hamiltonian formalism applied to a phonon model is strictly equivalent to the Heisenberg formalism of relativistic quantum mechanics for a spinless particle, with classical Poisson brackets mapping directly to operator commutators and the Poincaré group structure emerging naturally.

title: Disentangling Haldane Phase by Generalized Clifford Circuits
summary: Disentangling transformations play a central role in the classical simulation of quantum many-body systems, yet their analytic structure and underlying mechanism remain largely unexplored. Here, we study the structure of the disentangler in the Haldane phase of spin-1 systems using generalized Clifford circuits. To this end, we extend the Clifford-circuit-augmented matrix product states (CAMPS)-based density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) method to spin-1 systems. Within this framework, we find that the local disentanglers optimized for the Haldane phase implement the generalized Kramers--Wannier (KW) transformation, and we analytically verify its optimality for the Affleck--Kennedy--Lieb--Tasaki (AKLT) state. Beyond reducing entanglement, the KW transformation maps the Haldane phase to a phase with spontaneously broken $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ symmetry. This mapping is distinct from the Kennedy--Tasaki transformation and provides a new unitary route from symmetry-protected topological order to symmetry breaking.

AI.tldr: The paper studies disentanglers in the Haldane phase of spin-1 systems using generalized Clifford circuits, extending CAMPS-based DMRG to spin-1. Local disentanglers optimized for the Haldane phase are found to implement the generalized Kramers-Wannier (KW) transformation, which is analytically verified as optimal for the AKLT state. This KW transformation maps the Haldane phase to a spontaneously broken ℤ₂ symmetry phase, offering a new unitary route from SPT order to symmetry breaking, distinct from the Kennedy-Tasaki transformation.
AI.motivation: To uncover the analytic structure and underlying mechanism of disentanglers in quantum many-body systems, specifically within the Haldane phase of spin-1 systems.
AI.method: Extends the Clifford-circuit-augmented matrix product states (CAMPS)-based density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) method to spin-1 systems, using generalized Clifford circuits to study the structure of local disentanglers in the Haldane phase.
AI.result: Local disentanglers optimized for the Haldane phase implement the generalized Kramers-Wannier (KW) transformation; this transformation is analytically verified as optimal for the AKLT state.
AI.conclusion: The KW transformation maps the Haldane phase to a phase with spontaneously broken ℤ₂ symmetry, providing a new unitary route from symmetry-protected topological (SPT) order to symmetry breaking, distinct from the known Kennedy-Tasaki transformation.

title: Orthogonality Edges in Strong-Coupling Quantum Work Statistics
summary: Strong coupling to a reservoir can do more than shift, broaden, or dress the work peaks of a driven quantum system. When the reservoir is infrared singular, a sudden change of a local control parameter can alter the boundary condition seen by infinitely many low-energy modes, converting a quasiparticle-like threshold line into a many-body edge. We demonstrate this mechanism for the inclusive work distribution of the biased spin-boson model under a sudden bias inversion. In the independent-boson limit, the problem is exactly solvable and gives a sharp infrared classification: a super-Ohmic bath can retain a finite elastic threshold weight, whereas Ohmic and sub-Ohmic baths extinguish the elastic line through boundary orthogonality. At the Ohmic fixed point, the same exponent controls both the vanishing elastic residue and the low-work continuum. We then ask how this edge is resolved away from the static-boundary limit. Using displaced-basis exact diagonalization of logarithmically discretized baths, we find that finite tunnelling leaves an edge-like continuum over the accessible energy window, while separating two operational diagnostics of the threshold: the cumulative-continuum exponent extracted from $z$-interleaved spectra lies above the elastic-overlap exponent extracted from $z$-averaged overlaps, $θ_C>θ_Z$. We interpret this separation as a finite-energy crossover away from the static-boundary fixed point, not as evidence for a new asymptotic fixed point. The separation survives fitting-window variation, oscillator-cutoff checks, spectrum-size checks, and leave-one-$z$-out tests, while time-domain characteristic functions provide a compatible but non-decisive diagnostic. Finally, the same threshold edge controls the sampling cost of Jarzynski-type exponential averages, making rare low-work events increasingly important at low temperature.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how an infrared-singular reservoir transforms the work distribution of a driven quantum system from a quasiparticle peak into a many-body edge, using the biased spin-boson model with sudden bias inversion. It provides exact results in the independent-boson limit, classifies bath types (super-Ohmic retains finite elastic weight; Ohmic/sub-Ohmic extinguish it), and uses displaced-basis exact diagonalization to show that finite tunneling creates an edge continuum with two distinct threshold exponents (θ_C > θ_Z), interpreted as a finite-energy crossover rather than a new fixed point.
AI.motivation: To understand how infrared-singular reservoirs fundamentally alter the work distribution of driven quantum systems beyond simple broadening or dressing, and to classify the threshold behavior across different bath spectral densities.
AI.method: Analytic solution in the independent-boson limit; displaced-basis exact diagonalization with logarithmically discretized baths; extraction of cumulative-continuum and elastic-overlap exponents via z-interleaved spectra and z-averaged overlaps; time-domain characteristic function analysis; leave-one-z-out and finite-size checks.
AI.result: Super-Ohmic baths retain finite elastic weight; Ohmic/sub-Ohmic baths extinguish the elastic line; finite tunneling produces two distinct exponents (θ_C > θ_Z) that separate diagnostic measures; this separation is robust across fitting-window, cutoff, spectrum-size, and leave-one-out tests; the threshold edge controls Jarzynski sampling cost.
AI.conclusion: The separation of threshold exponents is a finite-energy crossover away from the static-boundary fixed point, not a new asymptotic fixed point. The edge structure has practical implications for the cost of Jarzynski exponential averaging at low temperature.

title: A Semantic Framework for Reproducible Variational Quantum Algorithm Execution Records
summary: Variational quantum algorithms are hybrid quantum-classical workflows whose results depend on many interacting choices, including the ansatz, Hamiltonian, optimizer, backend, shot count, noise model, mitigation method, random seed, stopping criteria, and software versions. In current practice, this information is often scattered across code, configuration files, logs, backend metadata, and paper descriptions, making executions difficult to reproduce, compare, debug, and reuse. This paper proposes an ontology-supported framework for representing Variational Quantum Algorithm (VQA) execution records as structured and machine-readable software engineering artifacts. The framework defines a Web Ontology Language (OWL) ontology for modeling the main entities involved in VQA experimentation, including algorithms, circuits, ansatzes, Hamiltonians, optimizers, backends, noise models, mitigation techniques, execution steps, software environments, measurement outcomes, and results. It further combines the ontology with Shapes Constraint Language (SHACL) constraints for validating completeness and consistency, and SPARQL Protocol and RDF Query Language (SPARQL) competency queries for retrieving reproducibility-relevant information. We demonstrate the approach using Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) execution records, including a valid record and intentionally incomplete or inconsistent examples. The results show that the framework can represent complete VQA execution contexts, detect missing or malformed metadata, and support query-based inspection of information needed for reproducible quantum software experimentation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an ontology-supported framework (using OWL, SHACL, and SPARQL) to represent Variational Quantum Algorithm execution records as structured, machine-readable artifacts, enabling reproducibility, validation, and query-based inspection of experimental metadata.
AI.motivation: VQA execution information is currently scattered across code, config files, logs, and metadata, making experiments difficult to reproduce, compare, debug, and reuse.
AI.method: The framework defines an OWL ontology for modeling VQA entities (algorithms, circuits, ansatzes, Hamiltonians, optimizers, backends, noise models, mitigation techniques, execution steps, software environments, measurement outcomes, results), combined with SHACL constraints for validation and SPARQL queries for retrieving reproducibility-relevant information.
AI.result: Demonstrated using VQE execution records, the framework successfully represents complete VQA execution contexts, detects missing or malformed metadata, and supports query-based inspection for reproducible quantum software experimentation.
AI.conclusion: The framework effectively addresses reproducibility challenges in VQA experimentation by providing structured, validated, and queryable execution records.

title: Verification of Quantum Computations: Hardware-Efficient Security Proofs
comment: Habilitation à diriger des recherches presented on June 23, 2026 at Ecole Normale Supérieure --- 91 pages
summary:
How can a user with limited quantum resources verify the output of an untrusted, fully quantum server? This manuscript provides a conceptual synthesis of some recent developments toward answering this question under statistical (information-theoretic) security. Rather than duplicating the dense technical proofs of the underlying publications, our focus here is on the physical motivations, the structural connections between different protocols, and the path toward hardware-efficient implementation.
  We begin by introducing a modular, composable framework that partitions verification into three distinct, independent primitives: remote state preparation, trap-based deviation detection, and error-correcting embedding. Using this framework, we show how the demanding hardware requirements of early protocols can be systematically relaxed. We review schemes that eliminate the spatial overhead, remove the need to prepare computational-basis dummy states, and replace single-photon sources with trusted local rotations or weak coherent pulses. Finally, we examine how these techniques scale, both to asymmetric multi-party settings and to the delegation of fully fault-tolerant computations in the presence of gate-level noise. This document is intended as a guide to the architectural principles of practical quantum verification.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a conceptual synthesis of recent developments in statistically secure quantum verification, introducing a modular framework with three primitives (remote state preparation, trap-based deviation detection, and error-correcting embedding) to systematically relax hardware requirements and enable practical verification of untrusted quantum servers by resource-limited users.
AI.motivation: To enable a user with limited quantum resources to verify the output of an untrusted, fully quantum server under statistical (information-theoretic) security, and to provide a guide to the architectural principles of practical quantum verification rather than dense technical proofs.
AI.method: Introduces a modular, composable framework partitioning verification into three independent primitives: remote state preparation, trap-based deviation detection, and error-correcting embedding. Reviews schemes that eliminate spatial overhead, remove the need for computational-basis dummy states, and replace single-photon sources with trusted local rotations or weak coherent pulses.
AI.result: Demonstrates how demanding hardware requirements of early protocols can be systematically relaxed. Examines scaling to asymmetric multi-party settings and delegation of fully fault-tolerant computations under gate-level noise.
AI.conclusion: The modular framework provides a path toward hardware-efficient implementation of quantum verification, with techniques that scale to multi-party settings and fault-tolerant computations.

title: Stellar Braid Monodromy of Finite-Rank Non-Gaussian Photonic States
summary: Finite-rank non-Gaussian bosonic states admit a holomorphic description in the Bargmann representation: after a zero-free Gaussian factor is separated off, their non-Gaussian structure is encoded by a finite stellar divisor. This article introduces a topological refinement of stellar rank for regular parameterized families of such states. Rather than only counting the zeros of the stellar divisor, we follow their motion under deformations of the state and record the associated braid monodromy. In the finite-Fock chart, a regular degree-r stellar state is represented by a monic polynomial with r simple zeros. The regular stratum is biholomorphic to the unordered configuration space of r points in the complex plane, and its fundamental group is the Artin braid group on r strands. Thus braid monodromy is an intrinsic invariant of loops in the regular finite-rank stellar state space. We then extend the construction to admissible finite stellar divisors of the form E_tau,mu(z) P(z); the zero-free Gaussian parameters form a contractible fiber over the same configuration-space base. Experimentally motivated finite-Fock families, especially the cubic subspace spanned by the first four Fock states, provide concrete laboratories, while trinomial slices yield explicit discriminants and local half-twists. The resulting invariant is post-tomographic and applies to preparation loops and parameterized families; it complements Wigner negativity, stellar rank, approximate stellar rank, and other scalar diagnostics of non-Gaussianity.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a topological refinement of stellar rank for finite-rank non-Gaussian bosonic states, using braid monodromy from the motion of zeros in the Bargmann representation to capture loop-level structure beyond counting stellar zeros.
AI.motivation: Existing non-Gaussianity diagnostics (stellar rank, Wigner negativity) are scalar or discrete and miss topological/loop-level structure in parameterized families of states. The authors aim to introduce a richer invariant capturing braiding of stellar zeros under deformations.
AI.method: The regular stratum of degree-r stellar states is shown to be biholomorphic to the unordered configuration space of r points in the complex plane, whose fundamental group is the Artin braid group. Braid monodromy is computed from loops in state space. The construction extends to admissible finite stellar divisors with Gaussian prefactors. Concrete examples use cubic subspace (first four Fock states) and trinomial slices to compute discriminants and half-twists.
AI.result: Braid monodromy is an intrinsic invariant of loops in regular finite-rank stellar state space. The zero-free Gaussian parameters form a contractible fiber, so the topology reduces to the configuration space base. Explicit discriminants and local half-twists are demonstrated in low-dimensional Fock subspaces.
AI.conclusion: Braid monodromy provides a post-tomographic, topological invariant for preparation loops and parameterized families of non-Gaussian states, complementing existing scalar diagnostics like stellar rank and Wigner negativity.

title: The Delayed Stabilizer ZX-Calculus
summary: Many stabilizer quantum error-correcting codes are built from a finite pattern repeated across space or time, such as lattice codes, translation-invariant graph states, and quantum convolutional codes. Ordinary stabilizer ZX-diagrams capture only finite truncations of such systems, obscuring the repeated structure that defines them. We introduce the delayed stabilizer ZX-calculus, a finite graphical language for these infinite, translation-invariant processes. It extends the odd-prime-dimensional stabilizer ZX-calculus with a single new generator, the delay, which feeds data from one time step to the next. We equip the calculus with two semantics. In the first semantics, we interpret the behaviour of a delayed ZX-diagram as an equivalence class of sequences of quantum channels; where two sequences are identified if they have the same information content. We show that the behaviour of a delayed ZX-diagram uniquely determines an infinite stabilizer group. In the second semantics, we interpret the delay as a formal variable, encoding the translation-invariant families of Pauli operators as generating functions. This allows us to represent a delayed ZX-diagram in terms of a tableau of generating functions, from which the infinite stabilizer group can be recovered. Finally, we give a complete axiomatization of the delayed stabilizer ZX-calculus, featuring generalised Euler decomposition and colour change rules. Using generalised forms of local complementation and pivoting, we reduce every diagram to a unique normal form. This establishes soundness, universality, and completeness for the generating tableau semantics.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the delayed stabilizer ZX-calculus, a graphical language for infinite, translation-invariant stabilizer quantum error-correcting codes, with two semantics (equivalence classes of channel sequences and generating functions), a complete axiomatization, and a unique normal form via generalized local complementation and pivoting.
AI.motivation: Ordinary stabilizer ZX-diagrams can only capture finite truncations of infinite, translation-invariant quantum codes (lattice codes, graph states, convolutional codes), obscuring their repeated structure. The authors aim to provide a finite graphical language that directly represents these infinite periodic systems.
AI.method: The paper extends the odd-prime-dimensional stabilizer ZX-calculus with a single new generator called the delay, which feeds data across time steps. Two semantics are developed: (1) an equivalence class of sequences of quantum channels distinguished by information content; (2) a generating function semantics treating delay as a formal variable, encoded via a tableau of generating functions. A complete axiomatization is provided with generalized Euler decomposition, color change rules, local complementation, and pivoting, reducing every diagram to a unique normal form.
AI.result: The behavior of a delayed ZX-diagram uniquely determines an infinite stabilizer group. The generating function semantics allows representation via a tableau from which the infinite stabilizer group can be recovered. The axiomatization yields soundness, universality, and completeness for the generating tableau semantics, with every diagram reducible to a unique normal form.
AI.conclusion: The delayed stabilizer ZX-calculus provides a finite, complete graphical language for infinite translation-invariant stabilizer codes, bridging the gap between finite diagrammatic reasoning and infinite quantum error-correcting structures.

title: Detection methods for optimal target reflectivity estimation with two-mode squeezed vacuum probes
summary: Target reflectivity estimation using a two-mode squeezed vacuum (TMSV) probe offers a theoretical advantage over classical schemes, but realizing this potential under the measurement constraints of microwave platforms remains a central challenge. In this work, we study the precision limits for target reflectivity estimation across different energy and loss regimes, while accounting for realistic measurement restrictions. We characterize the optimal measurements and identify a transition in their structure: above a specific reflectivity threshold, a parametric amplifier receiver is optimal, whereas below it, the optimal observables are two-mode squeezing generators. We then study the performance of Gaussian measurements. When restricted to standard local homodyne detection, the TMSV probe is highly non-optimal. However, we show that suitable non-local Gaussian measurements can closely approach the quantum Cramér-Rao bound at the large noise limit. These results demonstrate that near-optimal quantum target reflectivity estimation is achievable in various relevant noisy regimes, even under the restriction of Gaussian measurements.

AI.tldr: This paper studies quantum target reflectivity estimation using two-mode squeezed vacuum probes under realistic microwave measurement constraints, identifies optimal measurement transitions based on reflectivity thresholds, and shows that non-local Gaussian measurements can approach the quantum Cramér-Rao bound in noisy regimes.
AI.motivation: While TMSV probes offer theoretical advantages for target reflectivity estimation, realizing this potential under the measurement constraints of microwave platforms remains a central challenge. This work aims to bridge that gap by studying precision limits under realistic conditions.
AI.method: The authors characterize optimal measurements for target reflectivity estimation across different energy and loss regimes, identify a transition in optimal measurement structure (parametric amplifier receiver above a reflectivity threshold, two-mode squeezing generators below it), and analyze the performance of Gaussian measurements including local homodyne detection and non-local Gaussian measurements.
AI.result: Standard local homodyne detection with TMSV probes is highly non-optimal, but suitable non-local Gaussian measurements can closely approach the quantum Cramér-Rao bound in the large noise limit. Near-optimal estimation is achievable under realistic measurement restrictions.
AI.conclusion: Near-optimal quantum target reflectivity estimation is achievable in various relevant noisy regimes even under the restriction of Gaussian measurements, demonstrating practical feasibility for microwave platforms.

title: Robust self-test of the maximally entangled state of two-qubits without assuming unitary observables
summary: Standard device-independent self-testing uses Naimark dilation to assume projective measurements, masking the operational limitations of realistic non-unitary observables. We establish a robust pure self-test for the singlet and Pauli observables that entirely circumvents dilation of the measurement apparatus. Assuming a pure state to model an untrusted source, we regularize the physical non-projective operators and derive an analytic $\mathcal{O}(\sqrtε)$ robustness bound. Our results suggest that device-independent certification of real implementations is significantly more demanding than standard projective models imply.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a robust pure self-test for singlet and Pauli observables without relying on Naimark dilation to assume projective measurements, instead regularizing non-projective operators directly, and finds that device-independent certification is significantly more demanding than standard projective models suggest.
AI.motivation: Standard device-independent self-testing relies on Naimark dilation to assume projective measurements, which masks the operational limitations of realistic non-unitary observables in experimental implementations.
AI.method: The authors establish a robust pure self-test for the singlet and Pauli observables that circumvents dilation of the measurement apparatus. Assuming a pure state for the untrusted source, they regularize physical non-projective operators and derive an analytic O(√ε) robustness bound.
AI.result: Derived an analytic O(√ε) robustness bound for self-testing without Naimark dilation, showing that device-independent certification is significantly more demanding than standard projective models imply.
AI.conclusion: Device-independent certification of real implementations is significantly more demanding than standard projective models imply, highlighting the limitations of the traditional Naimark dilation approach in practical settings.

title: Quantum simulation of gauge theories on dynamical spacetimes via Floquet-induced matrix models
comment: 12 pages with 6 figures, with an additional 6 pages of appendices and 2 additional figures, as well as 12 pages of supplementary info
summary: Quantum simulations of gauge theories are typically built on spatial lattices, an approach that has enabled major progress at the cost of requiring fixed background geometries and obscuring the treatment of curved and dynamical spacetimes. Large-$N$ matrix models offer an alternative, encoding spacetime geometry and gauge fields in the commutation structure of a set of Hermitian matrices, with the classical continuum emerging smoothly at large matrix dimensions. Here we introduce a Floquet framework that makes these models directly accessible to programmable quantum platforms. We show that Euclidean path integral weights of a Yang-Mills matrix models are reproduced, at leading order in the coupling, by the ensemble-averaged fidelities of Haar-random states evolved under periodic sequences of matrix operators. The observables for the simulated matrix model can then be accessed through established randomized benchmarking protocols in terms of the Loschmidt echo. The encoding requires exponentially fewer qubits than canonically quantized approaches. Numerically, we validate the fidelity-weight correspondence, demonstrate parallelized quantum circuits that sample the path-integral measure, and identify the deconfinement transition of an $SU(2)$ gauge field on both flat and expanding cosmological backgrounds. By avoiding a fixed spacetime lattice, the framework preserves continuous symmetries and unitarity on dynamical geometries, opening quantum simulation to field and spacetime dynamics beyond the reach of conventional lattice methods.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a Floquet framework for quantum simulation of large-N matrix models, enabling the study of gauge theories on dynamical spacetimes without fixed spatial lattices, validated numerically for SU(2) gauge fields on flat and expanding backgrounds.
AI.motivation: Conventional lattice-based quantum simulations of gauge theories require fixed background geometries, making it difficult to treat curved and dynamical spacetimes. The authors aim to overcome this limitation by leveraging large-N matrix models, which naturally encode spacetime geometry in matrix commutation structures.
AI.method: The authors introduce a Floquet framework where Euclidean path integral weights of Yang-Mills matrix models are reproduced at leading order in coupling by ensemble-averaged fidelities of Haar-random states evolved under periodic sequences of matrix operators. Observables are accessed via randomized benchmarking protocols in terms of the Loschmidt echo. The encoding requires exponentially fewer qubits than canonical quantization approaches.
AI.result: Numerical validation of the fidelity-weight correspondence is demonstrated, along with parallelized quantum circuits that sample the path-integral measure. The framework successfully identifies the deconfinement transition of an SU(2) gauge field on both flat and expanding cosmological backgrounds.
AI.conclusion: By avoiding a fixed spacetime lattice, the framework preserves continuous symmetries and unitarity on dynamical geometries, opening quantum simulation to field and spacetime dynamics beyond conventional lattice methods.

title: A Lie-Jordan Geometric Formulation of Lindblad Dynamics
summary: We develop a Lie-Jordan geometric formulation of finite-dimensional open quantum dynamics, building on the algebraic framework introduced in our previous work (arXiv:2606.26477). The Hilbert-Schmidt operator space is endowed with an orthonormal Hermitian basis, in which the commutator and anticommutator are encoded by the structure tensors \(C_{μν}{}^λ\) and \(B_{μν}{}^λ\). Within this formulation, the von Neumann and Gorini-Kossakowski-Lindblad-Sudarshan equations admit a direct component representation. Our central result is the identification of a basis-independent universal trilinear dissipative map, \( \mathcal D(X,Y)Z=XZY-\frac12\{YX,Z\}, \) whose components define a universal operator-space tensor depending only on the Lie-Jordan structure tensors. The physical dissipator is obtained by contracting this tensor with the expansion coefficients of the Lindblad operators and the Kossakowski matrix, thereby separating the universal algebraic structure from the model-dependent physical information. We further show that the combinations \((B+C)\) and \((B-C)\) generate internal left and right transports, allowing the elementary dissipative map to be expressed as a left-right bimodule action corrected by an ordered Jordan contribution. The universal map satisfies basis-independent trace and Hermitian-conjugation identities, from which trace preservation, Hermiticity preservation of the complete dissipator, and the reality of its component representation in a Hermitian Hilbert-Schmidt basis follow. We also derive its Hilbert-Schmidt adjoint and illustrate the formalism for a qubit with pure dephasing and amplitude-damping channels. This construction provides a tensorial and affine-geometric interpretation of the universal superoperator structure derived in arXiv:2606.26477 while keeping the algebraic and model-dependent sectors explicitly separated.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a Lie-Jordan geometric formulation of finite-dimensional open quantum dynamics, identifying a universal basis-independent trilinear dissipative map that separates algebraic structure from model-dependent physical information, and demonstrating its properties for trace/Hermiticity preservation.
AI.motivation: To provide a tensorial and affine-geometric interpretation of the universal superoperator structure from prior work, while explicitly separating the algebraic sector from model-dependent physical information in open quantum dynamics.
AI.method: The Hilbert-Schmidt operator space is endowed with an orthonormal Hermitian basis; commutator and anticommutator are encoded by structure tensors C and B. A universal trilinear dissipative map D(X,Y)Z is identified, whose components are expressed solely in terms of Lie-Jordan structure tensors. Physical dissipators are obtained by contracting this tensor with Lindblad operator coefficients and the Kossakowski matrix.
AI.result: Identification of a basis-independent universal trilinear dissipative map; demonstration that (B+C) and (B-C) generate internal left/right transports; the dissipative map is expressed as a left-right bimodule action with ordered Jordan correction; trace/Hermiticity preservation identities are derived; Hilbert-Schmidt adjoint is computed; formalism is illustrated for qubit dephasing and amplitude-damping channels.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a clean geometric separation between universal algebraic superoperator structure and model-specific physical parameters, offering an affine-geometric interpretation consistent with the previous algebraic derivation.

title: Frozen-Tree Sampling Refutes Quantum Advantage of Random Circuit Sampling
summary: Random circuit sampling of bitstrings from a Haar-random quantum state is widely believed to be classically intractable, and has therefore been implemented as a primary benchmark for demonstrating quantum advantage. Here, we challenge this premise by proposing an efficient classical frozen-tree sampling algorithm that exploits the conditional scale invariance of Haar-random quantum states [Oh, arXiv:2602.19448]. The frozen-tree sampler draws bitstrings of $n$ qubits in $O(n)$ time per sample. Moreover, its output probability $p_F(x)$ is statistically identical to the probability $p_C(x)$ of a random quantum circuit, since both are independent instances of the same Dirichlet distribution. Consequently, no statistical test acting on samples alone can distinguish the classical frozen-tree sampler from a quantum random circuit. The claimed quantum advantage of random circuit sampling therefore does not withstand scrutiny: its hardness lies not in sampling from the Dirichlet distribution, which is classically efficient, but in identifying a specific circuit realization.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an efficient classical "frozen-tree sampling" algorithm that exploits the conditional scale invariance of Haar-random quantum states. This algorithm draws n-qubit bitstrings in O(n) time per sample, producing outputs statistically identical to random quantum circuits (same Dirichlet distribution). Therefore, no statistical test can distinguish samples from the classical frozen-tree sampler versus a quantum random circuit, undermining the claimed quantum advantage of random circuit sampling.
AI.motivation: To challenge the premise that random circuit sampling of bitstrings from a Haar-random quantum state is classically intractable and serves as a valid benchmark for quantum advantage.
AI.method: The authors propose a classical frozen-tree sampling algorithm that leverages the conditional scale invariance property of Haar-random quantum states. The algorithm draws n-qubit bitstrings in O(n) time per sample.
AI.result: The output probability p_F(x) of the frozen-tree sampler is statistically identical to p_C(x) of a random quantum circuit, as both are independent instances of the same Dirichlet distribution. No statistical test acting solely on samples can distinguish between them.
AI.conclusion: The claimed quantum advantage of random circuit sampling does not withstand scrutiny; the hardness lies not in sampling from the Dirichlet distribution (which is classically efficient) but in identifying a specific circuit realization.

title: Wei-Norman approach for non-Hermitian driven spin-$S$ systems and its application to defect freezing
summary: In the theoretical study of nonequilibrium non-Hermitian systems, obtaining exact analytical solutions for their nonadiabatic dynamics is highly desirable yet often challenging. In this work, we identify a class of non-Hermitian quantum systems where this difficulty can be substantially reduced. Employing the Wei-Norman approach, we show that for a spin-$S$ subject to a general non-Hermitian time-dependent drive, the matrix elements of the evolution operator can be expressed in closed analytical forms (via Jacobi polynomials) in terms of the corresponding spin-$1/2$ model. This approach is straightforward and accessible to nonspecialists in Lie algebra. As an application, we investigate a specific nonequilibrium non-Hermitian phenomenon known as defect freezing, i.e., the existence of excitations in the adiabatic limit, in spin-$S$ extensions of the $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model under linear quenches. We derive exact analytical expressions for the momentum-resolved excitation probabilities and the total excitation densities. Our results reveal that defect freezing occurs exclusively in momentum sectors that traverse the $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetry-broken region -- and thus pass through a pair of higher-order exceptional points (EPs) -- during the quench; notably, the excitation density exhibits a singularity at a critical value of the non-Hermiticity parameter. This work enriches the analytical toolkit for nonadiabatic dynamics in multi-level non-Hermitian systems and provides quantitative, testable predictions for defect freezing across higher-order EPs, possibly accessible on platforms such as electric circuit networks and photonic lattices.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an analytical framework for nonadiabatic dynamics in a class of non-Hermitian quantum systems using the Wei-Norman approach, enabling closed-form expressions for evolution operator matrix elements of a spin-S under arbitrary time-dependent non-Hermitian driving in terms of spin-1/2 counterparts via Jacobi polynomials. Applying this to spin-S PT-symmetric SSH models under linear quenches, the authors derive exact excitation probabilities and densities, showing defect freezing occurs only in momentum sectors crossing PT-broken regions with higher-order exceptional points, and revealing a singularity in excitation density at a critical non-Hermiticity parameter.
AI.motivation: Obtaining exact analytical solutions for nonadiabatic dynamics in nonequilibrium non-Hermitian systems is highly desirable but often challenging; this work aims to reduce this difficulty for a specific class of systems.
AI.method: The Wei-Norman approach is employed to express evolution operator matrix elements of a spin-S under general non-Hermitian time-dependent drive in closed analytical forms (via Jacobi polynomials) in terms of the corresponding spin-1/2 model.
AI.result: (1) Exact analytical expressions for momentum-resolved excitation probabilities and total excitation densities in spin-S PT-symmetric SSH models. (2) Defect freezing occurs only in momentum sectors traversing the PT-symmetry-broken region with higher-order EPs. (3) Excitation density exhibits a singularity at a critical non-Hermiticity parameter.
AI.conclusion: This work enriches the analytical toolkit for nonadiabatic dynamics in multi-level non-Hermitian systems and provides quantitative, testable predictions for defect freezing across higher-order EPs, potentially accessible on platforms like electric circuit networks and photonic lattices.

title: Coherent quantum control of dark excitons in hybrid metal organic chalchogenolates
comment: 16 pages, includes main and supplemental, submitted (2026)
summary: Artificial atom-like systems are a promising candidate for next generation quantum processing. Among them, dark excitons exhibit one of the longest lifetimes at high temperatures. Here, we demonstrate coherent control of dark excitonic states in metal-organic chalcogenolates (MOChas) by using an ultrafast pulse shaper at room temperature. These dark exciton states are optically accessed via two-photon absorption and directly read out with a four-wave mixing process. The system is described by a non-perturbative, two-photon Hamiltonian based on well-known atomic physics and applied to a three level system comprised of two dark excitons. Empirical and theoretical state specific optical access is shown via a simple optical pulse shape. The developed Hamiltonian-based description is a first step towards a quantum processing platform using three-level systems and two photon transitions, one example being dark excitons in the MOCha silver benzeneselenolate (mithrene). Simple conditions for gate operations are laid out and described.

Dark excitons are accessed via two-photon absorption and read out via four-wave mixing. A non-perturbative, two-photon Hamiltonian based on atomic physics describes the three-level system, laying groundwork for quantum processing using dark excitons in MOChas like mithrene.

The motivation is to achieve coherent control over these states and develop a theoretical framework for quantum operations using two-photon transitions in three-level systems.

Dark excitons are optically accessed via two-photon absorption and read out via four-wave mixing. A non-perturbative, two-photon Hamiltonian based on atomic physics describes the three-level system comprised of two dark excitons.

title: A Cross-Platform Analysis of High-Performance Quantum Error Correction Codes
summary: The theory of quantum error correction was established decades ago. Yet the limitation of the quantum computing platforms in terms of noise level and available physical qubit count persists, which greatly hinders the development of scalable quantum computing systems. In this paper, we present analytical estimates of logical error rates of advanced QEC codes across leading hardware platforms and distributed quantum computing systems using a simple but unified framework. The analysis captures two dominant contributors to logical error: code structure and two-qubit gate overhead. The framework provides a fast estimate of logical error rates and identification of dominating factors in different hardware platforms, such as circuit volume, routing overhead, inter-QPU operations, or asymmetric noise protection. We show that several qualitative trends observed in larger-scale simulations can be reproduced and interpreted analytically within this framework. We further demonstrate that the framework can be used to find the sweet spot design region of distributed QEC, which is critical for the design of distributed quantum computing systems.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an analytical framework for estimating logical error rates of quantum error correction (QEC) codes across hardware platforms and distributed quantum computing systems, focusing on two dominant contributors: code structure and two-qubit gate overhead.
AI.motivation: Despite decades of quantum error correction theory, scalable quantum computing remains hindered by noise and limited qubit counts. A unified analytical framework is needed to quickly estimate logical error rates and identify dominant factors without costly large-scale simulations.
AI.method: The authors develop a simple but unified analytical framework that captures logical error contributions from code structure and two-qubit gate overhead. It considers platform-specific factors such as circuit volume, routing overhead, inter-QPU operations, and asymmetric noise protection.
AI.result: The framework reproduces qualitative trends observed in larger-scale simulations and enables identification of dominating error factors across different hardware platforms. It can also find the sweet spot design region for distributed QEC.
AI.conclusion: The analytical framework provides a fast, interpretable tool for estimating logical error rates and guiding the design of distributed quantum computing systems, particularly in identifying optimal operating regions.

title: Controlling Atom Array in an Ultra-high-cooperativity Optical Cavity
summary: Neutral-atom array and cavity quantum electrodynamics offer complementary strengths for quantum science: scalable, reconfigurable qubit architectures and strong coherent light-matter coupling. Combining them in a single platform requires an optical cavity with simultaneously high cooperativity, sufficient mode volume to accommodate atom array, and ample side optical access for atom trapping, imaging, cooling, and rearrangement, a combination that is challenging to achieve. Here we realize an atomic array integrated with a millimeter-scale Fabry--Pérot cavity whose optically-characterized single-atom cooperativity reaches $η_{\mathrm{cav}}=125\pm13$. Atom-cavity transmission spectra of trapped atoms yield an effective spectroscopic cooperativity $η_{\mathrm{spec}}=112.3\pm3.3$, providing an in-situ verification of strong coupling in the integrated platform, and we demonstrate simultaneous coupling of up to 16 individually trapped atoms to the antinode of the cavity mode.
