The key technical advance is a two-step mirror-fabrication method combining precision mechanical shaping and carbon-dioxide laser polishing, which produces concave fused-silica mirrors with sub-millimeter radii of curvature and residual roughness below 2 Å. Our results establish a regime of cavity-integrated atomic array that simultaneously provides high cooperativity, large mode volume, and flexible manipulation of individual atoms, opening opportunities for cavity-assisted quantum state readout and long-range entanglement-engineering in atom-array platforms.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates the integration of a neutral-atom array with a millimeter-scale Fabry-Pérot cavity, achieving high cooperativity (η_cav=125±13, η_spec=112.3±3.3), strong coupling, and simultaneous coupling of up to 16 individually trapped atoms, enabled by a two-step mirror fabrication method combining mechanical shaping and CO2 laser polishing.
AI.motivation: Combining neutral-atom arrays (scalable, reconfigurable qubits) with cavity QED (strong coherent light-matter coupling) in a single platform is challenging because it requires an optical cavity with simultaneously high cooperativity, sufficient mode volume for an atomic array, and ample side optical access for atom manipulation.
AI.method: A two-step mirror-fabrication method combining precision mechanical shaping and carbon-dioxide laser polishing to produce concave fused-silica mirrors with sub-millimeter radii of curvature and residual roughness below 2 Å, enabling a millimeter-scale Fabry-Pérot cavity integrated with an atomic array.
AI.result: Optically-characterized single-atom cooperativity reaches η_cav=125±13; effective spectroscopic cooperativity η_spec=112.3±3.3; simultaneous coupling of up to 16 individually trapped atoms to the cavity mode antinode.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes a regime of cavity-integrated atomic arrays that simultaneously provides high cooperativity, large mode volume, and flexible individual atom manipulation, opening opportunities for cavity-assisted quantum state readout and long-range entanglement engineering in atom-array platforms.

title: Circuit Design Informed Adaptive Variational Quantum Algorithms
summary: Resource-efficient computation is of central importance in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era, where decoherence, gate errors, and restricted qubit connectivity severely limit the reliable execution of quantum algorithms. In this work, we demonstrate that incorporating circuit design considerations is crucial for developing resource-efficient variational quantum algorithms. By focusing on the Hadamard test circuit architecture, hardware-aware qubit connectivity, and problem-specific adaptive framework, we analyze how circuit design constraints can systematically reduce the measurement overhead associated with repeated evaluations of the candidate gate pool in adaptive algorithms. Specifically, we demonstrate reductions in the required measurement resources ranging from at least 25% to as high as 50% - 55%. To assess the effectiveness of our approach, we investigate the ground state problem of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation. Overall, our work contributes to resource-friendly strategies for quantum computation and underscores that algorithmic frameworks should systematically integrate circuit design constraints with hardware-aware and problem-specific structures to enhance the practical feasibility of quantum devices in the NISQ era.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that integrating circuit design considerations (Hadamard test architecture, hardware-aware qubit connectivity, adaptive frameworks) into variational quantum algorithms can reduce measurement overhead by 25-55%, using the nonlinear Schrödinger equation ground state problem as a test case.
AI.motivation: Resource-efficient computation is critical in the NISQ era due to decoherence, gate errors, and restricted qubit connectivity that limit reliable quantum algorithm execution.
AI.method: Incorporates circuit design considerations—specifically Hadamard test circuit architecture, hardware-aware qubit connectivity, and a problem-specific adaptive framework—to systematically reduce measurement overhead from repeated candidate gate pool evaluations in adaptive algorithms.
AI.result: Demonstrates reductions in required measurement resources ranging from at least 25% to as high as 50-55%.
AI.conclusion: Algorithmic frameworks should systematically integrate circuit design constraints with hardware-aware and problem-specific structures to enhance the practical feasibility of quantum devices in the NISQ era.

title: Realizing Next-Nearest-Neighbor Coupling and Peierls Phase in Circuits
summary: We really design the trimerized circuits for the non-Hermitian one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger models. There are three models, the initial one just considers the nearest neighbor coupling, the enhanced one is extended to contain the next-nearest-neighbor coupling, and the final one is reenhanced by introducing the Peierls phase. We investigate the dynamics of the circuit Laplacians with respect to the models, find that the topological states appear in the initial model and the response intervals are substantially affected by the next-nearest-neighbor coupling channels and the Peierls phase. These results are practically demonstrated by numerical simulations and experimental measurements. As a conclusion, the trimerized circuits can provide an adjustable and simple platform to investigate new topological physical states.

AI.tldr: This paper designs trimerized circuits for non-Hermitian 1D SSH models (initial, enhanced with next-nearest-neighbor coupling, and reenhanced with Peierls phase), studies circuit Laplacian dynamics, and finds topological states influenced by coupling channels and Peierls phase, validated by simulations and experiments.
AI.motivation: To design trimerized circuits as an adjustable and simple platform for investigating new topological physical states in non-Hermitian systems.
AI.method: Three trimerized circuit models of non-Hermitian 1D SSH models are designed: (1) initial with nearest-neighbor coupling; (2) enhanced with next-nearest-neighbor coupling; (3) reenhanced with Peierls phase. Circuit Laplacian dynamics are analyzed, and results are validated via numerical simulations and experimental measurements.
AI.result: Topological states emerge in the initial model. The response intervals are substantially affected by the next-nearest-neighbor coupling channels and the Peierls phase. Results are confirmed by both simulations and experiments.
AI.conclusion: Trimerized circuits provide an adjustable and simple platform for investigating new topological physical states.

title: Analytic properties of cross-click operators in passive multi-basis photodetection: monotonicity, exact convergence rates, and dimension reduction for quantum key distribution
summary: Cross-click operators, the POVM elements for simultaneous clicks in detectors assigned to different measurement bases, are used in QKD and entanglement-verification analyses with realistic threshold detectors to bound multiphoton contributions. Earlier applications verified the needed growth of the minimum eigenvalue $f^{(n)}$ on the $n$-photon subspace only numerically over finite sectors. This work gives an analytic characterization for passive linear-optical analyzers with arbitrary efficiency mismatch and dark counts. The key observation is that every silence operator is the second quantization $Γ(A)$ of an explicit single-photon contraction $A$, whose $n$-photon restriction is $A^{\otimes n}$ on $\mathrm{Sym}^n$. This yields: (i) monotonicity $f^{(n+1)}\ge f^{(n)}$; (ii) two-sided exponential bounds $\max_b γ_b|A_b|^n \le 1-f^{(n)} \le \sum_b γ_b|A_b|^n$, which determine the exact asymptotic convergence rate from single-photon spectral data; (iii) for ideal detectors and $n\ge1$, the exact formula $f^{(n)}=1-\sum_b p_b^n$; and (iv) an exact factorization $1-f^{(n_A,n_B)}=(1-f_A^{(n_A)})(1-f_B^{(n_B)})$ for the two-party cross-click operator. The results apply to polarization, time-bin, and spatial-mode analyzers within the stated threshold-detector model. As an application, we obtain closed-form photon-number weight bounds used in detection-efficiency-mismatch analyses, replacing finite-sector Fock-space numerics by formulas valid for all photon numbers.

AI.tldr: This paper provides an analytic characterization of cross-click operators for passive linear-optical analyzers, deriving exact formulas and bounds for their minimum eigenvalues on n-photon subspaces, with applications to QKD and entanglement verification.
AI.motivation: Earlier work on cross-click operators in QKD and entanglement-verification analyses relied only on numerical verification over finite sectors. An analytic characterization was needed to rigorously bound multiphoton contributions and extend results to all photon numbers.
AI.method: The key insight is that every silence operator can be expressed as the second quantization Γ(A) of an explicit single-photon contraction operator A. The n-photon restriction then becomes A⊗n on Sym^n. This framework enables analytic computation of eigenvalues and bounds using single-photon spectral data.
AI.result: Four main results: (i) monotonicity f^{(n+1)} ≥ f^{(n)}; (ii) two-sided exponential bounds relating f^{(n)} to spectral data of single-photon operators; (iii) exact formula f^{(n)}=1-∑_b p_b^n for ideal detectors; (iv) exact factorization for two-party cross-click operators. Also yields closed-form photon-number weight bounds for detection-efficiency-mismatch analyses.
AI.conclusion: The analytic characterization replaces finite-sector Fock-space numerics with formulas valid for all photon numbers, applicable to polarization, time-bin, and spatial-mode analyzers under threshold-detector models with arbitrary efficiency mismatch and dark counts.

title: Genuine Multipartite Entanglement between Logical Qubits via Cross-Code Lattice Surgery
summary: Universal quantum computers are expected to generate arbitrary complex quantum states of logical qubits encoded in many physical qubits. This capability hinges on a fault-tolerantly implemented universal gate set, which no single quantum error-correction code admits transversally but which becomes accessible by joining complementary codes via lattice surgery. Here we report on the experimental generation and certification of logical genuine multipartite entanglement in a trapped-ion quantum processor using a transversally implemented universal logical gate set. The gate set is accessed via lattice surgery across two different codes and comprises a Hadamard gate on a four-qubit surface code and a doubly controlled Pauli-$Z$ ($\overline{\mathrm{CCZ}}$) gate on an eight-qubit 3D colour code. To showcase this lattice-surgery toolbox, we generate both stabiliser (Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger) and non-stabiliser ($|\overline{\mathrm{CCZ}}\rangle$) states of three logical qubits and verify their genuine multipartite entanglement--a form of correlation beyond statistical mixtures of bipartite entanglement across any bipartition. We further use these cross-code primitives to demonstrate arbitrary rotations of single logical qubits via a $\overline{\mathrm{CCZ}}$-based resource gadget accessing the full universal gate set through lattice surgery. Together, these demonstrations showcase the core building blocks of an architecture for fault-tolerant quantum computation and its ability to generate complex logical quantum states.

AI.tldr: Experimental demonstration of a universal logical gate set via lattice surgery across two different quantum error-correction codes (surface code and 3D color code) on a trapped-ion processor, generating and certifying genuine multipartite entanglement in logical qubits, including both stabilizer (GHZ) and non-stabilizer (|CCZ⟩) states.
AI.motivation: No single quantum error-correction code admits a universal gate set transversally, but universal fault-tolerant computation requires such a gate set. Lattice surgery across complementary codes offers a path to this goal, and experimental validation is needed.
AI.method: Implementation of a transversal universal logical gate set via lattice surgery between a 4-qubit surface code (Hadamard gate) and an 8-qubit 3D color code (doubly controlled Pauli-Z gate). Demonstrations include generation of logical GHZ states (stabilizer) and |CCZ⟩ states (non-stabilizer), with genuine multipartite entanglement certification.
AI.result: Successful generation and certification of genuine multipartite entanglement in logical GHZ and |CCZ⟩ states of three logical qubits. Demonstration of arbitrary single-logical-qubit rotations via a CCZ-based resource gadget enabling the full universal gate set through lattice surgery.
AI.conclusion: The lattice-surgery toolbox provides the core building blocks for fault-tolerant quantum computation, demonstrating the ability to generate complex logical quantum states with a universal gate set across complementary codes.

title: Weak ergodicity breaking without nonthermal eigenstates
summary: The typical mechanisms of ergodicity breaking in isolated interacting quantum systems, such as many-body localization and quantum many-body scars, originate from the nonthermal nature of the underlying eigenstates. Here, in the absence of nonthermal eigenstates, we identify a mechanism for collective revivals of multiparticle Wannier states (MWSs) associated with nearly linear bands in a spatially modulated Bose-Hubbard lattice. The MWSs, as superpositions of multiparticle Bloch states within individual energy bands, give rise to band-resolved Wannier-sector fragmentation. The key idea is that spatially periodic modulation folds and separates energy bands of a simple lattice into several sub-bands, among which nearly linear sub-bands inherit the linear segments of the original bands. Although multiparticle Bloch states satisfy the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH), the MWSs in the nearly linear band still exhibit long-lived collective revivals, due to emergent equally spaced energy levels. Our work provides a route to weak ergodicity breaking in which long-lived revivals arise from spectral phase coherence among ETH-satisfying eigenstates rather than from scar-like nonthermal eigenstates.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a mechanism for weak ergodicity breaking via collective revivals of multiparticle Wannier states in a modulated Bose-Hubbard lattice, arising from spectral phase coherence among ETH-satisfying eigenstates rather than nonthermal eigenstates.
AI.motivation: To find mechanisms of ergodicity breaking that do not rely on nonthermal eigenstates (e.g., MBL or quantum scars), exploring how collective revivals can emerge from spectral phase coherence among otherwise thermal eigenstates.
AI.method: The authors introduce a spatially modulated Bose-Hubbard lattice, where periodic modulation folds and separates energy bands into sub-bands, including nearly linear sub-bands. They construct multiparticle Wannier states (MWSs) as superpositions of Bloch states within individual bands, leading to band-resolved Wannier-sector fragmentation.
AI.result: Multiparticle Bloch states satisfy the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH), yet MWSs built from nearly linear bands exhibit long-lived collective revivals due to emergent equally spaced energy levels, demonstrating weak ergodicity breaking.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a route to weak ergodicity breaking where long-lived revivals originate from spectral phase coherence among ETH-satisfying eigenstates, offering an alternative to scar-like nonthermal eigenstate mechanisms.

title: Chromatic Completeness and the Independence of Geometric Obstruction
summary: We establish a strict logical separation between two distinct phenomena in orthogonality hypergraphs: chromatic completeness, the possibility of assigning a single globally consistent nondegenerate spectrum to all contexts, and geometric coordinatizability, the existence of a faithful orthogonal representation by rays. A strong chromatic number larger than the Hilbert-space dimension obstructs only the former. It does not, by itself, obstruct the existence of a faithful orthogonal representation. We make this separation explicit by comparing two three-dimensional examples with the same strong chromatic number. A completed 25-ray version of the Yu-Oh configuration has strong chromatic number four and nevertheless possesses an explicit faithful orthogonal representation in R^3. Conversely, Greechie's G_{32} hypergraph also has strong chromatic number four, and has a separating and unital set of two-valued states, but we give an elementary algebraic proof that it admits no faithful orthogonal representation in C^3. The obstruction in G_{32} is therefore not chromatic but projective-geometric: the incidence relations force two distinct atoms to collapse onto the same ray.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a logical separation between chromatic completeness (global consistent spectrum assignment) and geometric coordinatizability (faithful orthogonal representation) in orthogonality hypergraphs, demonstrating they are distinct phenomena through two 3D examples with identical strong chromatic numbers but different representability.
AI.motivation: To clarify the relationship between chromatic properties and geometric realizability of orthogonality hypergraphs, specifically whether a large strong chromatic number necessarily prevents faithful orthogonal representations in Hilbert spaces.
AI.method: Comparative analysis of two three-dimensional orthogonality hypergraphs (completed 25-ray Yu-Oh configuration and Greechie's G32 hypergraph) that share the same strong chromatic number (four), using algebraic proofs to examine their representability.
AI.result: The 25-ray Yu-Oh configuration has strong chromatic number 4 yet admits a faithful orthogonal representation in R^3. Greechie's G32 also has strong chromatic number 4 and a separating unital set of two-valued states, but provably admits no faithful orthogonal representation in C^3.
AI.conclusion: A strong chromatic number larger than Hilbert-space dimension obstructs chromatic completeness but not necessarily geometric coordinatizability. The obstruction in G32 is projective-geometric (incidence relations forcing atom collapse) rather than chromatic.

title: Optimal estimation of quantum boundary effect in cosmic string space-time
summary: The presence of a cosmic string modifies vacuum fluctuations, making the evolution of a two-level polarizable atom position dependent. Such modifications produce effects on the atomic dynamics analogous to those induced by a reflecting boundary. We show that these quantum boundary effects can be estimated by performing a sequence of $N$ measurements on a single probe atom. For a fixed total probe time, the precision limit is attained by preparing each probe in its optimal initial state, performing the corresponding optimal measurement, and shortening the probe time of each probe. The optimal measurement is uniquely determined by the probe's initial state, and the precision limit obtained with the atom initially in the excited state is four times higher than that for an equal-weight superposition state. The estimation precision displays damped oscillatory behavior as the atom-boundary or atom-string separation increases. While polarization parallel to the reflecting boundary is always optimal in the boundary case, the optimal polarization in cosmic-string space-time depends on both the atom-string separation and the deficit angle. For small deficit angles and sufficiently large separations, polarization along the cosmic-string direction becomes inferior to the other polarization directions.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that quantum boundary effects (from cosmic strings or reflecting boundaries) can be estimated via a sequence of N measurements on a single two-level atom, where optimal precision depends on initial state (excited state gives 4× better precision than superposition), measurement choice, and probe duration; precision oscillates with separation, and optimal polarization differs between cosmic-string and boundary scenarios.
AI.motivation: To understand how vacuum fluctuations modified by a cosmic string affect atomic dynamics analogously to a reflecting boundary, and to develop a quantum metrology framework for estimating these effects using a single probe atom.
AI.method: The authors analyze a two-level polarizable atom interacting with modified vacuum fluctuations in cosmic-string spacetime (and compared to a reflecting boundary). They consider sequential projective measurements (N measurements) on a single atom with fixed total probe time, optimizing initial states, measurement bases, and probe duration to achieve precision limits.
AI.result: The optimal initial state (excited state) yields 4× better precision than an equal-weight superposition state. Precision exhibits damped oscillations with atom-string/boundary separation. For reflecting boundaries, polarization parallel to the boundary is always optimal. In cosmic-string spacetime, the optimal polarization depends on both the deficit angle and atom-string separation; for small deficit angles and large separations, polarization along the cosmic string becomes suboptimal.
AI.conclusion: Quantum boundary effects from cosmic strings can be estimated via sequential measurements on a single atom, with distinct optimal strategies compared to reflecting boundaries, revealing spacetime-dependent polarization preferences.

title: Incompatibility assisted Zeno-like confinement enables unbounded sharing of nonlocality
summary: To enable sequential sharing of Bell-nonlocality by an unbounded number of copies, each copy must satisfy two requirements. First, the measurements must be incompatible to extract nonlocality. Second, the post-processsed state, obtained as an equal mixture of the two post-measurement states, must remain nonlocal. We show that the incompatibility requirements impose nontrivial constraints on the choice of the initial nonlocal state and the amount of measurement noise required to ensure that the post-processed state remains nonlocal for an unbounded number of copies. We establish this result for two measurement scenarios, namely, when each copy performs unsharp measurements corresponding to a pair of anti-commuting Pauli observables, and when each copy performs probabilistic projective measurements (PPMs) of a pair of anti-commuting Pauli observables. Furthermore, we show that, in the asymptotic limit, the nonlocal post-processed states of all the copies are almost identical, leading to a quantum Zeno-like confinement within the nonlocal region.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the sequential sharing of Bell-nonlocality across an unbounded number of copies, showing that incompatibility of measurements and preservation of nonlocality in post-processed states impose constraints. Using unsharp measurements or probabilistic projective measurements (PPMs) of anti-commuting Pauli observables, the authors demonstrate that in the asymptotic limit, post-processed states become almost identical, resembling a quantum Zeno-like confinement within the nonlocal region.
AI.motivation: To understand how Bell-nonlocality can be sequentially shared by an unbounded number of copies, and to identify the necessary conditions (measurement incompatibility and nonlocality preservation in post-processed states) and the constraints they impose on the initial state and measurement noise.
AI.method: The study considers two measurement scenarios: (1) unsharp measurements corresponding to a pair of anti-commuting Pauli observables, and (2) probabilistic projective measurements (PPMs) of a pair of anti-commuting Pauli observables. It analyzes the constraints on the initial nonlocal state and measurement noise needed for the post-processed state (equal mixture of two post-measurement states) to remain nonlocal for an unbounded number of copies.
AI.result: The incompatibility requirements impose nontrivial constraints on the choice of the initial nonlocal state and the amount of measurement noise. In the asymptotic limit, nonlocal post-processed states of all copies become almost identical, leading to a quantum Zeno-like confinement within the nonlocal region.
AI.conclusion: Sequential sharing of Bell-nonlocality by an unbounded number of copies is possible under specific conditions, with a quantum Zeno-like effect confining states within the nonlocal region as the number of copies grows.

title: Fundamental limits on state preparation for an open qubit
summary: We analytically determine the ultimate limits of state preparation in two-level open quantum systems driven by coherent control. For a dissipative qubit governed by a GKSL master equation, we give an exact characterization of the reachable set in the Bloch ball. Dissipation excludes a region of states in the Bloch ball which cannot be approached even under arbitrarily strong coherent driving, and we prove that this region has a nontrivial geometry whose boundary is a surface of revolution around the $x$-axis which is analytic except for two conical singularities. We derive a closed-form control protocol for moving on this boundary, and construct an explicit protocol that steers the system arbitrarily close to any prescribed boundary state. These results provide a complete geometric constructive description of reachable qubit states in the standard dissipative environment, establishing fundamental bounds on controllability and state-preparation fidelity for open two-level quantum systems.

AI.tldr: The paper analytically characterizes the reachable set of states in the Bloch ball for a dissipative qubit under coherent control, revealing a forbidden region with nontrivial geometry bounded by a surface of revolution (analytic except for two conical singularities). It provides closed-form control protocols to move on this boundary and steer arbitrarily close to any boundary state, establishing fundamental controllability limits.
AI.motivation: To determine the ultimate limits of state preparation in two-level open quantum systems driven by coherent control, specifically for dissipative qubits governed by GKSL master equations.
AI.method: Analytical derivation of the reachable set in the Bloch ball under GKSL dynamics; geometric characterization of the forbidden region's boundary as a surface of revolution with two conical singularities; closed-form control protocol design for boundary traversal and state steering.
AI.result: Dissipation excludes a nontrivial region of Bloch sphere states unreachable even under arbitrarily strong coherent driving; the reachability boundary is analytic except at two conical singularities; explicit protocols exist to approach any boundary state arbitrarily closely.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a complete geometric, constructive description of reachable qubit states in a standard dissipative environment, establishing fundamental bounds on controllability and state-preparation fidelity for open two-level quantum systems.

title: Supersymmetry and Entanglement in the Generalized Dirac Oscillator
summary: The supersymmetric properties of the generalized Dirac oscillator allow us to determine the entanglement entropy between the spin and the continuous variable in a purely algebraic manner. The entanglement has a relativistic origin and disappears in the nonrelativistic limit. The entanglement entropy attains its maximal value in the limit of infinite energy.

AI.tldr: The paper uses supersymmetric properties of the generalized Dirac oscillator to algebraically determine spin-continuous variable entanglement entropy, which has relativistic origin, vanishes in the nonrelativistic limit, and reaches maximum at infinite energy.
AI.motivation: To understand the relativistic origin of entanglement between spin and continuous variables in the generalized Dirac oscillator using supersymmetric algebraic methods.
AI.method: Exploits supersymmetric properties of the generalized Dirac oscillator to compute entanglement entropy algebraically.
AI.result: Entanglement entropy can be determined purely algebraically; it has relativistic origin, disappears in the nonrelativistic limit, and attains maximal value in the infinite energy limit.
AI.conclusion: The entanglement between spin and continuous variable in the generalized Dirac oscillator is a purely relativistic effect, fully characterizable via supersymmetric algebra.

title: Purcell effect and quantum Zeno effect suppressed self-discharging of quantum battery
summary: Quantum batteries (QB), as an energy storage and transfer device, not only show obvious advantages compared to classical electrochemical batteries, but also have important applications in quantum information. Self-discharging is a central obstacle to storing useful work in open QB, especially when the charger itself provides an unavoidable loss channel. Here we show that such charger-induced loss can be converted into a protection mechanism by combining Purcell effect with quantum Zeno effect. We reveal that the virtual photon process and the Purcell effect can induce the strong coupling regime to the quantum Zeno regime, in which the stronger the dissipation of the charger, the weaker the self-discharging effect of the QB. As a result, the dissipation caused by the charger to the QB can be suppressed four orders of magnitude in our scheme. Meanwhile, the quantum Zeno effect induced by the Purcell effect can also avoid the energy backflow between the QB and the charger. Owing to the significantly suppressed dissipation, the stored energy of QB can be charged to a nearly full state and the stored energy is almost converted into extractable work, which greatly improves the energy conversion efficiency.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that charger-induced dissipation in open quantum batteries can be transformed into a protection mechanism via Purcell effect and quantum Zeno effect, suppressing self-discharging by four orders of magnitude and enabling near-full charging with high energy conversion efficiency.
AI.motivation: Self-discharging in open quantum batteries is a major obstacle to storing useful work, especially when the charger itself introduces unavoidable loss channels. The authors aim to convert this loss into a beneficial protection mechanism.
AI.method: The authors combine the Purcell effect with the quantum Zeno effect to transition from a strong coupling regime to a quantum Zeno regime. The virtual photon process and Purcell effect enable stronger charger dissipation to suppress self-discharging more effectively.
AI.result: The charger-induced dissipation on the quantum battery is suppressed by four orders of magnitude. The quantum Zeno effect prevents energy backflow between battery and charger. The stored energy reaches a nearly full state and is almost entirely converted into extractable work, greatly improving energy conversion efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Charger-induced loss can be converted into a protection mechanism; stronger dissipation of the charger leads to weaker self-discharging of the quantum battery, offering a practical route to high-efficiency quantum energy storage.

title: Topological properties and Majorana Multiplicity in Zigzag Kitaev Chain
comment: 11 pages , 11 figures, to be submitted to journal soon. Comments will be appreciated
summary: We investigate the spectral and topological properties of a zigzag Kitaev chain constructed from two diagonally coupled one dimensional Kitaev chains with a zero and finite superconducting pairing phase difference. Using a Bogoliubov-de Gennes formulation, we analyze the energy spectrum, distribution of Majorana zero modes (MZMs), the quasi-particle dispersion, and the winding number, respectively. For a zero phase difference, the resulting energy spectrum shows topological phases with two, four MZMs, and trivial regions. The phases of gap closure determine the topological phase boundaries. In particular, for the phase difference between $φ=π$, the degeneracy of MZMs is partially lifted, leading to modified topological phases compared to the case $φ=0$. The topological and trivial phase boundaries are further confirmed by evaluating the quasi-particle dispersion and the topological invariant, namely the winding number. We show that the zigzag Kitaev chain contributes independently to the total winding number $ν= 1$ and $2$, giving rise to distinct topological phases that support two and four MZMs. The $ν= 0$ gives rise to a trivial region. The energy spectrum of systems corroborates the analytical phase boundaries and reveals characteristics associated with hybridization, enabling us to obtain the complete phase diagram of the zigzag model. Our results establish the zigzag Kitaev chain as a minimal platform for engineering MZM quantum computations, with potential applications in the study of topological phases and Majorana based qubit physics.

AI.tldr: This paper studies a zigzag Kitaev chain (two diagonally coupled 1D Kitaev chains) and shows that varying the superconducting pairing phase difference (φ=0 vs φ=π) produces distinct topological phases supporting zero, two, or four Majorana zero modes (MZMs), with phase boundaries confirmed via energy spectrum, quasi-particle dispersion, and winding number calculations.
AI.motivation: To investigate how the superconducting pairing phase difference affects the spectral and topological properties of a zigzag Kitaev chain, and to establish it as a minimal platform for MZM-based quantum computation.
AI.method: Bogoliubov-de Gennes (BdG) formulation to analyze energy spectrum, MZM distribution, quasi-particle dispersion, and winding number topological invariant.
AI.result: For φ=0: topological phases with two or four MZMs and trivial regions exist. For φ=π: partial lifting of MZM degeneracy yields modified topological phases. The total winding number ν=1,2 correspond to two and four MZMs respectively; ν=0 gives trivial region. Complete phase diagram obtained.
AI.conclusion: The zigzag Kitaev chain serves as a minimal platform for engineering MZM quantum computations and studying topological phases and Majorana-based qubit physics.

title: Noise-Aware Synthesis of Quantum LDPC Encoder Circuits via Two-Sided Hamming Descent
summary:
Quantum low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes are a promising route to fault-tolerant quantum computation, but their use requires efficient preparation of encoded states. Standard encoder constructions generate circuits through fixed algebraic procedures, yet the resulting circuit can contain substantial redundancy. We formulate LDPC encoder preparation as a circuit-resynthesis problem: given the linear-reversible matrix implemented by the encoder's CNOT block, we seek a lower-cost equivalent circuit that can be routed efficiently on the target hardware and which mitigates noise. We propose a novel optimization approach referred as two-sided Hamming descent and a noise-aware optimization pipeline for this task.
  Across several families of Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) LDPC encoders, including Bivariate Bicycle, hypergraph-product, and entanglement-assisted codes, the proposed pipeline produces substantially smaller and shallower encoder circuits than the standard constructions and the synthesis baselines considered, cutting gate counts by 53.8% in aggregate across the benchmark and by up to 68% on the Bivariate Bicycle family. The gains remain visible after routing, where the two-qubit depth is reduced by up to 71% and translate into higher-fidelity state preparation under circuit-level noise. On the Bivariate Bicycle family, live-range scheduling further reduces routed preparation failure by up to 13.7% without adding two-qubit gates to the selected circuit. These results indicate that encoder-matrix resynthesis, combined with hardware-calibrated selection and scheduling, is an effective compiler-level tool for preparing quantum LDPC code states.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a circuit-resynthesis approach for optimizing quantum LDPC encoder preparation by reducing redundancy in CNOT blocks, achieving substantial reductions in gate counts (53.8% aggregate, up to 68% on Bivariate Bicycle codes), depth (up to 71%), and improved state-preparation fidelity under noise.
AI.motivation: Quantum LDPC codes require efficient preparation of encoded states for fault-tolerant computation, but standard encoder constructions produce circuits with substantial redundancy that increase noise susceptibility and hardware routing costs.
AI.method: Formulates LDPC encoder preparation as a circuit-resynthesis problem targeting the linear-reversible matrix of the CNOT block; proposes two-sided Hamming descent optimization and a noise-aware optimization pipeline that selects lower-cost equivalent circuits routable on target hardware.
AI.result: Across CSS LDPC encoder families (Bivariate Bicycle, hypergraph-product, entanglement-assisted codes), the pipeline cuts gate counts by 53.8% aggregate (68% on Bivariate Bicycle), reduces two-qubit depth by up to 71% after routing, and live-range scheduling further reduces routed preparation failure by up to 13.7%.
AI.conclusion: Encoder-matrix resynthesis combined with hardware-calibrated selection and scheduling is an effective compiler-level tool for preparing quantum LDPC code states with higher fidelity.

title: Trace-to-Hilbert-Schmidt Speed Ratio in Quantum Dynamics: Universal Bounds and Effective Rank
summary: We study the ratio between the trace speed and the Hilbert-Schmidt speed for differentiable finite-dimensional quantum states, $\mathcal R(φ)=\|\partial_φρ(φ)\|_1/\|\partial_φρ(φ)\|_2$. Because $\partial_φρ(φ)$ is always Hermitian and traceless, this ratio is constrained more strongly than for a generic operator. For any nonzero tangent operator $X=\partial_φρ$ of rank $r$, we prove the sharp bounds $\sqrt{2}\le \|X\|_1/\|X\|_2\le \sqrt r$. The lower bound is attained exactly for rank-two tangents, while the upper bound is attained exactly when all nonzero singular values are equal, which in the traceless Hermitian setting requires even rank. At every nonstationary point of a pure-state family, the tangent has rank two, implying $\mathcal R=\sqrt2$. For odd Hilbert-space dimension $d$, we further prove the sharp global maximum $\mathcal R\le \sqrt{d-1/d}$, with equality characterized by full-rank spectra whose positive and negative eigenvalues are separately degenerate and have multiplicities differing by one. We identify $\mathcal R^2$ as the inverse participation ratio of the singular-value distribution of the tangent operator, giving $\mathcal R$ a natural interpretation as an effective-rank diagnostic for local quantum dynamics. Furthermore, we decompose the effective rank into classical (eigenvalue) and quantum (eigenvector) contributions and prove the bound $r_{\mathrm{eff}}\le r_C + r_Q$, with equality guaranteed when either component vanishes. We establish a direct inequality linking the effective rank to the quantum Fisher information (QFI), which forces a large number of active singular modes when the QFI is small relative to the squared trace speed. Finally, we derive a hierarchy of quantum speed limits in which the effective rank controls the tightness of bounds expressed through the Hilbert-Schmidt speed.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes sharp bounds on the ratio of trace speed to Hilbert-Schmidt speed for differentiable quantum states, proving $\sqrt{2} \le \|X\|_1/\|X\|_2 \le \sqrt{r}$ for rank-$r$ tangent operators, with the ratio identified as an effective-rank diagnostic linked to quantum Fisher information and speed limits.
AI.motivation: To understand the fundamental constraints on the ratio between two important quantum state speed measures (trace speed and Hilbert-Schmidt speed) for differentiable finite-dimensional quantum states, and to characterize how this ratio serves as an effective-rank diagnostic for local quantum dynamics.
AI.method: The authors derive rigorous bounds using the properties of Hermitian traceless tangent operators $X = \partial_\phi \rho$, proving sharp lower and upper bounds via singular value analysis. They decompose the effective rank into classical (eigenvalue) and quantum (eigenvector) contributions and relate it to quantum Fisher information.
AI.result: Proved sharp bounds $\sqrt{2} \le \|X\|_1/\|X\|_2 \le \sqrt{r}$ for rank-$r$ tangents, with lower bound attained at rank-two tangents and upper bound when all nonzero singular values are equal (requiring even rank). For odd dimension $d$, global maximum $\mathcal{R} \le \sqrt{d-1/d}$. Established inequality linking effective rank to quantum Fisher information and derived a hierarchy of quantum speed limits.
AI.conclusion: The ratio $\mathcal{R}$ serves as an effective-rank diagnostic for quantum dynamics, with the effective rank decomposing into classical and quantum contributions. The results provide tighter quantum speed limits expressed through Hilbert-Schmidt speed and connect fundamental geometric quantities in quantum state space.

title: Schrodinger Oscillator and its Thermal Properties in a Dynamical Noncommutative Space
summary: In this paper, we study the two-dimensional Schrodinger oscillator within a dynamical noncommutative (DNC) space. By leveraging perturbation theory, we derive the energy eigenvalues and eigenvectors and systematically analyze the effects of both dynamical and non-dynamical noncommutative settings. First-order corrections to the eigensystem are obtained, revealing that the energy shift explicitly depends on the DNC parameter tau. Furthermore, we explore the thermal properties of the system by employing the partition function. Numerical results are presented to provide a comprehensive analysis of the system behavior under the considered effects. Notably, in the DNC framework, the commutation relations and the deformation parameter are position-dependent. Using the two-dimensional Bopp-shift, we effectively map the noncommutative problem to its commutative counterpart.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the two-dimensional Schrödinger oscillator in a dynamical noncommutative space, using perturbation theory to derive energy eigenvalues and eigenvectors, obtaining first-order corrections dependent on the DNC parameter τ, and studying thermal properties via the partition function with numerical results.
AI.motivation: To study the Schrödinger oscillator in a dynamical noncommutative (DNC) space where commutation relations and deformation parameters are position-dependent, extending beyond standard noncommutative frameworks.
AI.method: Perturbation theory is used to derive first-order energy corrections; a two-dimensional Bopp-shift maps the noncommutative problem to a commutative one; the partition function is employed to study thermal properties.
AI.result: Energy eigenvalues and eigenvectors are derived; first-order corrections show the energy shift depends explicitly on the DNC parameter τ; numerical results illustrate system behavior.
AI.conclusion: The DNC framework introduces position-dependent deformations that measurably impact energy eigenvalues and thermal properties of the Schrödinger oscillator.

title: Security of Quantum Conference Key Agreement with Two-Way Classical Communication
summary: Quantum conference key agreement (QCKA) enables multiple users to establish a common secret key with information-theoretic security and is regarded as a key primitive for secure communication in future quantum networks. However, practical implementations of QCKA typically suffer from higher noise levels than conventional bipartite quantum key distribution (QKD), making the improvement of the tolerable error threshold an important challenge. Gottesman and Lo proposed two preprocessing procedures for QKD with two-way classical communication, known as the B-step and the P-step, which enhance the tolerable error threshold. In this paper, we analyze the asymptotic security of QCKA with tripartite GHZ states and two measurement bases using two-way classical communication, including multiple B-steps and P-steps. We derive the corresponding secure key rate analytically and demonstrate that iterative B-steps can increase the tolerable error threshold beyond 20%, significantly improving upon the approximately 11% threshold achievable without two-way classical communication and the approximately 15% threshold obtained with only a single B-step. Our results show that two-way classical communication can substantially enhance the robustness of practical QCKA protocols.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the asymptotic security of quantum conference key agreement (QCKA) using tripartite GHZ states and two-way classical communication, showing that iterative B-steps can increase the tolerable error threshold beyond 20%, significantly improving upon the ~11% threshold without two-way communication and ~15% with a single B-step.
AI.motivation: Practical QCKA implementations suffer from higher noise levels than bipartite QKD, making improvement of the tolerable error threshold an important challenge.
AI.method: The authors analyze the asymptotic security of QCKA with tripartite GHZ states and two measurement bases using two-way classical communication, including multiple B-steps and P-steps, and derive the corresponding secure key rate analytically.
AI.result: Iterative B-steps can increase the tolerable error threshold beyond 20%, improving upon the ~11% threshold without two-way classical communication and the ~15% threshold with only a single B-step.
AI.conclusion: Two-way classical communication can substantially enhance the robustness of practical QCKA protocols.

title: Equiangular weighted frames and conical 2-designs with unequal traces
summary: Conical 2-designs are families of positive operators possessing crucial symmetry properties that allow them to efficiently characterize important quantum measures. However, little is known about their general structures and properties. We propose a construction method of conical 2-designs whose elements are not of equal traces, based on a generalization of equiangular weighted frames to non-projective operators. We provide a detailed analysis of their properties, relations to quantum measurements, and applications, together with examples that go beyond the known classes. This constitutes a major step toward a full characterization of informationally overcomplete quantum measurements.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a construction method for conical 2-designs with non-equal trace elements by generalizing equiangular weighted frames to non-projective operators, providing analysis of their properties, relations to quantum measurements, and applications, advancing toward full characterization of informationally overcomplete quantum measurements.
AI.motivation: Conical 2-designs are important for characterizing quantum measures, but their general structures and properties remain poorly understood, motivating a need for broader construction methods beyond existing classes.
AI.method: The authors propose a construction method based on generalizing equiangular weighted frames to non-projective operators, enabling the creation of conical 2-designs whose elements are not necessarily of equal traces.
AI.result: A detailed analysis of the properties of these generalized conical 2-designs, their relations to quantum measurements, and practical applications, along with examples extending beyond previously known classes.
AI.conclusion: This work represents a significant step toward a full characterization of informationally overcomplete quantum measurements.

title: Quantum random walks on d-regular graphs with Haar-random coin operators
summary: With unitary coin operator that is a random matrix drawn from a uniform distribution with respect to the Haar measure, we construct a variant of a discrete quantum random walk using a d-regular undirected connected simple graph. With each step of the walk, the coin operator random matrix is drawn independently from the distribution. The expectation value over the distribution of random unitaries for the associated quantum channel gives a depolarization channel for the coin subspace and resembles the associated classical random walk where the direction a walker steps depends upon the outcome of a fair coin or balanced d-sided dice. Remarkably, despite the fact that the averaged channel depolarizes the coin subspace, measurements in the vertex subspace can be designed that would reveal information about the initial quantum state, even after many iterations of the channel. We illustrate with examples of quantum walks on Cayley graphs of Abelian groups, such as the cycle and hypercube graphs. These quantum walks are examples of bipartite strongly interacting systems, where one subsystem is strongly perturbed, yet information about the initial state in the other subsystem is potentially measurable forever. Due to its decoherence, a quantum random walk with a Haar-random coin would not be useful in search algorithms but could aid in understanding quantum systems with strongly perturbed subsystems.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs a discrete quantum random walk on d-regular graphs using a Haar-random unitary coin operator drawn independently at each step. The averaged channel depolarizes the coin subspace and mimics a classical random walk, yet information about the initial quantum state in the vertex subspace can persist and be measured even after many iterations, as illustrated on cycle and hypercube graphs.
AI.motivation: To explore the behavior of quantum random walks when the coin operator is a Haar-random unitary (rather than a fixed unitary), and to understand how information about the initial quantum state survives despite strong depolarization in the coin subspace.
AI.method: The paper defines a discrete-time quantum walk on a d-regular undirected graph where each step uses a fresh Haar-random unitary coin operator. It analyzes the averaged quantum channel, showing it reduces to a depolarization channel on the coin and a classical random walk on the vertex space. Examples on Cayley graphs of Abelian groups (cycle and hypercube) are studied.
AI.result: The averaged channel depolarizes the coin subspace but does not fully erase information in the vertex subspace; measurements on vertices can reveal information about the initial quantum state even after many iterations. The walk resembles a classical random walk in expectation but retains quantum coherence in the vertex space.
AI.conclusion: Quantum walks with Haar-random coins are not useful for search algorithms due to decoherence, but they provide insight into quantum systems with strongly perturbed subsystems where information in one subsystem can persist and remain measurable.

title: QuTuner: Feature- and Learning-Guided Optimization Pass Tuning for Quantum Compilers
summary:
Quantum compilers play a key role in transforming quantum circuits into lower-cost implementations with improved execution fidelity. This process is commonly guided by circuit-level metrics, such as gate counts and circuit depth. Although compiler pass tuning has been widely studied in classical compilation, directly transferring these techniques to quantum compilers is challenging, because quantum programs are expressed as circuits and exhibit optimization behaviors that are shaped by quantum-specific structures. Prior quantum compiler tuning approaches have begun to use circuit features to guide pass selection, but they remain limited in two aspects: they search only a small portion of the optimization-pass space, and they mainly rely on static features that do not explicitly reflect how a circuit reacts to compiler optimizations.
  We present QuTuner, a feature-guided quantum compiler pass tuning framework that generalizes across compilers and tuning objectives. QuTuner first builds a large optimization dataset. It then characterizes each circuit from two complementary views: static circuit features that describe circuit structure, and optimization-aware pass embeddings that summarize the circuit's responses to individual optimization passes. Using these representations, QuTuner trains two offline models to retrieve and rank candidate pass sequences for unseen circuits, followed by lightweight refinement. We evaluate QuTuner on Qiskit and PyTKET using two benchmark suites. On Qiskit, QuTuner improves the evaluation-metric reduction by up to 84.85% over the strongest baseline while reducing tuning time by 73.59%. On PyTKET, it improves metric reduction by up to 18.68% with a 64.49% reduction in tuning time. These results show that QuTuner provides an effective approach to adaptive pass tuning for quantum compilers.

AI.tldr: QuTuner is a feature-guided quantum compiler pass tuning framework that uses both static circuit features and optimization-aware pass embeddings to efficiently select and rank pass sequences, achieving up to 84.85% better metric reduction and 73.59% faster tuning on Qiskit.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum compiler tuning approaches are limited because they search only a small portion of the optimization-pass space and rely mainly on static features that do not explicitly reflect how a circuit reacts to compiler optimizations.
AI.method: QuTuner builds a large optimization dataset, characterizes each circuit using static circuit features and optimization-aware pass embeddings, trains two offline models to retrieve and rank candidate pass sequences, and performs lightweight refinement.
AI.result: On Qiskit, QuTuner improves evaluation-metric reduction by up to 84.85% over the strongest baseline while reducing tuning time by 73.59%. On PyTKET, it improves metric reduction by up to 18.68% with a 64.49% reduction in tuning time.
AI.conclusion: QuTuner provides an effective approach to adaptive pass tuning for quantum compilers, generalizing across compilers and tuning objectives.

title: Breaking the One-Dimensional Expressibility-Trainability Tradeoff
summary: Expressive parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) are often designed under a dilemma: the growth of expressibility and entangling power (EP) that improves Hilbert-space coverage is also expected to randomize an ansatz and activate barren-plateau (BP) conditions. We show that this dilemma is not a one-dimensional tradeoff. The usual picture collapses three inequivalent objects -- parameter-ensemble coverage, fixed-circuit entangling response, and local gradient moments -- into one scalar narrative. For a fixed circuit probed by Haar-product inputs, EP is a global two-copy mean of the output-entanglement distribution, whereas entangling-power deviation (EPD) is a global four-copy fluctuation descriptor. Gradient variance, however, is a local two-copy contraction selected by a parameter light cone and a cost observable. This moment hierarchy yields an analytic separation: equal EP need not imply equal trainability, as witnessed by equal-EP circuits with different EPDs and different gradient variances. These separations turn EP and EPD into a two-dial design rule for PQC ansatzes: EP measures how far the circuit has moved along the coverage dial, while EPD monitors whether input-dependent variability remains. We find that ansatz routes can reach high, Haar-like coverage before EPD and gradient variance collapse, showing that coverage and BP activation are distinct crossover events. The EP/EPD framework thus breaks the apparent one-dimensional expressibility-trainability tradeoff into a practical design rule: search for highly expressive PQCs in the window where coverage is high but BP-like homogenization has not yet erased trainable structure.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the expressibility-trainability tradeoff in parameterized quantum circuits is not one-dimensional. By separating entangling power (EP) from entangling-power deviation (EPD), it demonstrates that high Hilbert-space coverage can be achieved without triggering barren plateaus, providing a two-dial design rule for constructing trainable, expressive PQCs.
AI.motivation: Existing literature presumes a one-dimensional tradeoff where increased expressibility inevitably leads to barren plateaus (BPs). The authors argue this conflates three distinct concepts—parameter-ensemble coverage, fixed-circuit entangling response, and local gradient moments—and seek to disentangle them.
AI.method: The authors introduce a moment hierarchy: EP is a global two-copy mean of output-entanglement distribution, EPD is a global four-copy fluctuation descriptor, and gradient variance is a local two-copy contraction selected by a parameter light cone and cost observable. They use this hierarchy to analytically and numerically separate coverage from trainability.
AI.result: Equal EP does not imply equal trainability; circuits with identical EP can have different EPDs and gradient variances. High Haar-like coverage can be reached before EPD and gradient variance collapse, indicating that coverage and BP activation are distinct crossover events.
AI.conclusion: The EP/EPD framework replaces the one-dimensional expressibility-trainability tradeoff with a practical two-dial design rule: search for highly expressive PQCs in the window where coverage is high but BP-like homogenization has not yet erased trainable structure.

title: Measurement Geometry as a Resource for Certifying Network Nonlocality
summary: Quantum networks can exhibit nonclassical correlations that cannot be explained by classical models with independent sources. While the role of entanglement is well understood, the impact of measurement design remains largely unexplored. Here we develop an operational framework for certifying network nonlocality in the bilocal Alice--Bob--Charlie network using ancilla-assisted meters to evaluate the nonlocal observables required for bilocal and fully network nonlocal (FNN) witnesses. The approach successfully reproduces both bilocal and FNN correlations in simulation. On the 156-qubit superconducting processor \textit{ibm\_kingston}, we observe bilocal nonlocality with $\mathcal{S}_{\rm BLHV}=1.067(6)>1$ after readout-error mitigation, while the FNN witnesses reach $99\%$ and $96\%$ of their certification thresholds, implying the substantially stronger requirements for FNN certification. We further show that Bob's joint measurement determines the accessible level of network nonlocality: bilocal and FNN certification are optimized by different measurement settings, while both violations can disappear even for maximally entangled states. These results identify measurement geometry as an independent resource for network nonlocality and provide a practical route toward its certification on programmable quantum processors.

AI.tldr: This paper develops an operational framework for certifying network nonlocality in bilocal quantum networks using ancilla-assisted meters, demonstrates it on a 156-qubit superconducting processor, and shows that the choice of measurement settings is an independent resource—optimization differs for bilocal vs. fully network nonlocal (FNN) certification, with FNN requiring substantially stronger conditions.
AI.motivation: While entanglement's role in quantum network nonlocality is well understood, the impact of measurement design remains largely unexplored. The authors aim to develop a framework for certifying network nonlocality and understand how measurement geometry affects certification.
AI.method: The authors develop an operational framework using ancilla-assisted meters to evaluate nonlocal observables for bilocal and fully network nonlocal (FNN) witnesses. They implement it on the ibm_kingston 156-qubit superconducting processor with readout-error mitigation.
AI.result: Bilocal nonlocality observed with S_BLHV = 1.067(6) > 1; FNN witnesses reached 99% and 96% of thresholds. Bob's joint measurement determines the accessible level of network nonlocality, with different settings optimizing bilocal vs. FNN certification. Violations can disappear even for maximally entangled states.
AI.conclusion: Measurement geometry is an independent resource for network nonlocality. The work provides a practical route toward certifying network nonlocality on programmable quantum processors, with FNN certification being substantially more demanding than bilocal certification.

title: Krylov complexity, mode-resolved complexity and entanglement entropy across phase transitions in the non-Hermitian extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model
summary: We investigate phase transitions in the extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model with next-nearest-neighbor hoppings and an imaginary staggered chemical potential. In the presence of small non-Hermiticity, exceptional points emerge in pairs from the gap-closing momenta near the topological phase boundaries of the Hermitian limit. Utilizing the Krylov spread complexity and entanglement entropy, we analyze two dynamical protocols: (i) preparing the non-Hermitian ground state via a unitary transformation, and (ii) evolving the system under the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian. We show that the spread complexity, and long-time spread complexity as well as entanglement entropy can effectively signal phase transitions in the first and second protocols, respectively. To unravel the detailed structure of the transitions, we introduce the momentum-resolved complexity that identifies the characteristic modes and tracks their evolution with the driving parameter. In the regime where the system possesses a purely imaginary spectrum, we further identify dynamical phases based on the saturation behavior of the spread complexity. The entanglement entropy is also found to exhibit similar saturation behavior, thereby providing a more experimentally accessible probe of the dynamical phases.

AI.tldr: The paper studies phase transitions in a non-Hermitian extended SSH model with next-nearest-neighbor hoppings and imaginary staggered chemical potential, using Krylov spread complexity and entanglement entropy in two dynamical protocols to detect topological phase transitions and dynamical phases.
AI.motivation: To understand how non-Hermiticity (via imaginary chemical potential) affects topological phase transitions in the SSH model, and to develop dynamical probes (spread complexity and entanglement entropy) that can effectively signal these transitions.
AI.method: The authors analyze two dynamical protocols: (i) preparing the non-Hermitian ground state via a unitary transformation; (ii) evolving the system under the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian. They use Krylov spread complexity, long-time spread complexity, momentum-resolved complexity, and entanglement entropy as diagnostics.
AI.result: Spread complexity and entanglement entropy effectively signal phase transitions in both protocols; momentum-resolved complexity identifies characteristic modes across transitions; in the purely imaginary spectrum regime, dynamical phases are identified via saturation behavior of spread complexity and entanglement entropy.
AI.conclusion: Krylov spread complexity and entanglement entropy are reliable probes of non-Hermitian topological phase transitions; momentum-resolved complexity reveals microscopic structural details; entanglement entropy offers an experimentally accessible alternative for detecting dynamical phases.

title: Estimation of a sparse multi-qubit Hamiltonian via compressed sensing
summary: Hamiltonian estimation is an effective approach in studying the structure and dynamical evolution of quantum systems. The difficulty in estimating the Hamiltonian is that an $N$-qubit Hamiltonian has $4^N-1$ unknown parameters, requiring exponentially many equations for information extraction. In this paper we develop a method based on compressed sensing to estimate the Hamiltonian of a multi-qubit system. We identify a problem where as $N$ increases, the common sufficient condition (Restricted Isometry Property) for compressed sensing often fails, obstructing the application of compressed sensing in ($N\geq 3$)-qubit Hamiltonian estimation. To solve this problem, we propose a ``scale transformation" technique to restore RIP and ensure a compressive estimation of a $k$-sparse Hamiltonian using only $O(k\log(4^N/k))$ equations. In the numerical examples, we estimate the Hamiltonians of two 6- and 30-qubit systems, demonstrating the effectiveness of the method.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a compressed sensing method for multi-qubit Hamiltonian estimation. It identifies that the standard Restricted Isometry Property (RIP) condition fails for N≥3 qubits, and proposes a "scale transformation" technique to restore RIP, enabling efficient estimation of k-sparse Hamiltonians using only O(k log(4^N/k)) equations. Numerical demonstrations on 6- and 30-qubit systems validate the approach.
AI.motivation: Hamiltonian estimation is crucial for studying quantum system structure and dynamics, but faces the challenge that an N-qubit Hamiltonian has 4^N-1 unknown parameters, requiring exponentially many equations. Compressed sensing offers a potential solution, but the standard RIP sufficient condition fails for N≥3 qubit systems, obstructing its application.
AI.method: The authors propose a "scale transformation" technique that restores the Restricted Isometry Property (RIP) condition, enabling compressed sensing to estimate k-sparse Hamiltonians using only O(k log(4^N/k)) equations.
AI.result: Numerical examples on 6-qubit and 30-qubit systems demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method for compressive Hamiltonian estimation.
AI.conclusion: The scale transformation technique successfully overcomes the RIP failure in multi-qubit Hamiltonian estimation, making compressed sensing viable for N≥3 qubit systems with significantly reduced measurement requirements.

title: A Path-Superposition Framework for Quantum Gate Teleportation
summary: Quantum gate teleportation enables distant parties to implement nonlocal quantum operations without physically transferring the participating qubits, making it a promising primitive for distributed quantum computing. We introduce a general framework for deterministic quantum gate teleportation based on path superposition, in which the target nonlocal operation is specified through the phase of a preshared maximally entangled resource and a suitable family of path-dependent local unitary operators. The framework establishes general design conditions that guarantee deterministic teleportation after measurement of the control qubits and the application of local correction operations. As representative realizations, we construct teleportation protocols for controlled-NOT (CNOT) and controlled-Z (CZ) gates, demonstrating that different nonlocal operations can be implemented within the same protocol architecture through appropriate choices of the design parameters. We further outline a proof-of-concept photonic realization based on spatial-path and polarization degrees of freedom. The proposed framework identifies path superposition as a versatile resource for quantum gate teleportation and distributed quantum information processing.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a general framework for deterministic quantum gate teleportation using path superposition, enabling nonlocal operations like CNOT and CZ gates without physically moving qubits, with a proof-of-concept photonic design.
AI.motivation: To enable distributed quantum computing by allowing distant parties to implement nonlocal quantum operations without physically transferring qubits, overcoming physical constraints in quantum networks.
AI.method: A general framework based on path superposition, where the target nonlocal operation is specified via the phase of a preshared maximally entangled resource and path-dependent local unitary operators. General design conditions ensure deterministic teleportation after control-qubit measurement and local corrections.
AI.result: Construction of deterministic teleportation protocols for CNOT and CZ gates within the same architecture, and a proof-of-concept photonic realization using spatial-path and polarization degrees of freedom.
AI.conclusion: Path superposition is a versatile resource for quantum gate teleportation and distributed quantum information processing.

title: Mapping open quantum dynamics onto graphs
summary: Graph-theoretic frameworks have been widely employed in quantum physics to address the high-dimensional complexity of quantum systems. Although open quantum dynamics incorporates system-bath coupling via numerous interacting operators, it has been formulated algebraically with a partial set of jump operators or statistically universal reservoirs, leaving the underlying connectivity structure largely unexplored. Here, we propose a universal graph-theoretic framework for Markovian quantum dynamics. The framework maps open quantum dynamics onto two uniquely defined graphs, where the quantum master equation is rigorously interpreted as the average wave characteristic of operator-valued signals across the graphs. Applying this framework to the open quantum Rabi model, we demonstrate an open-system generalization of Fock-state lattices, characterize graph-topological signatures of dissipation, and classify the weak-to-ultrastrong coupling transition. Building on these representations, graph pruning reveals the backbone of open quantum dynamics, which enables superior graph neural-network learning. Our results bridge graph theory and open quantum dynamics, achieving efficient data-driven analysis of high-dimensional complexity.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a universal graph-theoretic framework for Markovian open quantum dynamics, mapping the quantum master equation onto two uniquely defined graphs. Applying it to the open quantum Rabi model reveals dissipation signatures and coupling transitions, and enables graph pruning for efficient graph neural-network learning, bridging graph theory and open quantum dynamics for data-driven analysis of high-dimensional complexity.
AI.motivation: Existing open quantum dynamics approaches use algebraic formulations with partial jump operators or statistical universal reservoirs, leaving the underlying connectivity structure of system-bath coupling largely unexplored. A graph-theoretic framework is needed to reveal and leverage this structure.
AI.method: The authors propose a universal graph-theoretic framework that maps Markovian open quantum dynamics onto two uniquely defined graphs, where the quantum master equation is interpreted as the average wave characteristic of operator-valued signals across the graphs. They apply this framework to the open quantum Rabi model and use graph pruning to enable graph neural-network learning.
AI.result: The framework demonstrates an open-system generalization of Fock-state lattices, characterizes graph-topological signatures of dissipation, and classifies the weak-to-ultrastrong coupling transition. Graph pruning reveals the backbone of open quantum dynamics, enabling superior graph neural-network learning.
AI.conclusion: This work bridges graph theory and open quantum dynamics, achieving efficient data-driven analysis of high-dimensional complexity in quantum systems.

title: Magnetic graphs for cavity quantum electrodynamics
summary: Strengthening light-matter coupling has become a central challenge in cavity quantum electrodynamics (QED), enabling ultrafast gate operations, qubit protection, and deterministic nonlinear optics. As the coupling increases, even the simplest configuration, a two-level atom interacting with a quantized field, requires careful treatment, as exemplified by the gauge-invariant quantum Rabi model (QRM). Here we propose a magnetic graph model for single-atom cavity QED, which enables the interpretation of quantum dynamics across the ultrastrong coupling regime through graph connectivity. We demonstrate that the generalized QRM maps onto a complex bipartite graph of identical sites under Floquet boundary conditions. This framework captures the crossover from weak to deep-strong coupling via a single metric: the cost of disconnecting a nonmagnetic subgraph. We examine the mechanism underlying this connectivity transition, establishing phase frustration induced by subgraph topology as the primary driver. Scalable to many-body systems, this approach bridges graph theory and cavity QED, revealing highly complex-graph dynamics even in the simplest setting.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a magnetic graph model for single-atom cavity QED that maps the generalized quantum Rabi model onto a complex bipartite graph, using graph connectivity (specifically the cost of disconnecting a nonmagnetic subgraph) to capture the crossover from weak to deep-strong coupling, with phase frustration from subgraph topology as the key driver.
AI.motivation: Strengthening light-matter coupling is a central challenge in cavity QED for enabling ultrafast gate operations, qubit protection, and deterministic nonlinear optics, but even the simplest two-level atom interacting with a quantized field requires careful gauge-invariant treatment as coupling increases.
AI.method: The authors propose a magnetic graph model for single-atom cavity QED, mapping the generalized quantum Rabi model onto a complex bipartite graph with identical sites under Floquet boundary conditions. They use a single metric—the cost of disconnecting a nonmagnetic subgraph—to capture the coupling crossover.
AI.result: The framework captures the crossover from weak to deep-strong coupling via the graph connectivity metric. Phase frustration induced by subgraph topology is identified as the primary mechanism driving the connectivity transition.
AI.conclusion: This approach bridges graph theory and cavity QED, revealing highly complex-graph dynamics even in the simplest setting, and is scalable to many-body systems.

title: Quantum-Optical Bound States in the Continuum
summary: Bound states in the continuum (BICs) are counterintuitive localized states that lie within the continuum of extended states. While extensively realized and utilized in classical wave systems, it is still unclear what a close analog of BICs would be, and how to extract their experimental signature in quantum-optical settings -- where the wave field itself is quantized into bosonic excitations. Here, we present a paradigmatic quantum-optical model consisting of a driven multi-level Jaynes-Cummings (JC) system, featuring few quantum degrees of freedom yet capable of hosting a BIC. Using the concept of a Fock-state lattice (FSL), this model can be mapped to an extended structure comprising two semi-infinite inhomogeneous Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) chains coupled to a common continuum. An appropriate quantum superposition of two topological zero modes from the separate chains forms a BIC that remains perfectly localized in the Fock-state dimension within the continuum spectrum, due to complete decoupling from the common continuum via destructive quantum interference. We further develop a method to extract the spectroscopic signature of the BIC -- a discrete peak embedded in a continuous background -- by Fourier-transforming the time-dependent dynamics of the system's chiral-symmetry operator. A highly feasible experimental proposal using a single trapped ion is provided. Our work bridges BIC physics with quantum optics, opening a pathway to harnessing such exotic states at the quantum limit.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a quantum-optical model of a driven multi-level Jaynes-Cummings system that hosts a bound state in the continuum (BIC) via mapping to Fock-state lattices of SSH chains, and proposes experimental detection using a single trapped ion.
AI.motivation: While BICs are well-established in classical wave systems, their quantum-optical analog and experimental signature remain unclear, motivating the need to bridge BIC physics with quantum optics.
AI.method: The model maps a driven multi-level Jaynes-Cummings system to an extended Fock-state lattice comprising two semi-infinite inhomogeneous SSH chains coupled to a common continuum. A quantum superposition of two topological zero modes from the separate chains forms a BIC via destructive quantum interference. Spectroscopic signature extraction uses Fourier-transform of the chiral-symmetry operator's time-dependent dynamics.
AI.result: The BIC remains perfectly localized in the Fock-state dimension within the continuum spectrum due to complete decoupling from the common continuum. A spectroscopic signature (discrete peak embedded in a continuous background) is obtained. A feasible experimental proposal using a single trapped ion is provided.
AI.conclusion: This work bridges BIC physics with quantum optics, opening a pathway to harnessing such exotic states at the quantum limit.

title: Sector-memory obstruction to probe-level bath emergence in finite programmable qubit environments
summary: Finite quantum environments can relax local probes without acting as canonical baths. We study this distinction for a probe qubit coupled to a programmable bath of ($N$) qubits under excitation-number-conserving dynamics. The conserved charge partitions the Hilbert space into sectors. We characterize probe-level bath emergence using the sector-resolved late-time population ($p_e^{(q)}$), the sector-memory variance ($M_N$), and a global Gibbs-fit error ($Δ_G^{\mathrm{global}}$). Exact simulations with Haar-random pure states in each complete fixed-charge sector yield sector-dependent populations close to the maximally mixed-sector benchmark ($p_e^{(q)}=q/(N+1)$), producing a nonzero Gibbs obstruction. We then construct charge-preserving Floquet circuits using ($R_z$) phases and ($XX+YY$) exchange gates, validate them with ideal and noisy Qiskit simulations, and implement finite-depth experiments on IBM Fez. For ($N=4$) and ($ε=0$), the hardware data give ($M_N \simeq 0.044$), ($Δ_G^{\mathrm{global}} \simeq 0.558$), and charge preservation near 0.90 after readout mitigation. A paired symmetry-breaking scan using bath ($R_x(ε)$) rotations reduces both diagnostics while increasing charge leakage, but does not erase sector ordering over the accessible depths. These results show that equilibration within constrained sectors is insufficient to produce a single sector-independent Gibbs state for the probe.

AI.tldr: This paper studies a probe qubit coupled to a finite programmable bath of N qubits under excitation-number-conserving dynamics. Using sector-resolved population analysis, simulations with Haar-random states, and experiments on IBM quantum hardware, the authors show that equilibration within constrained charge sectors does not yield a single sector-independent Gibbs state, as evidenced by nonzero Gibbs obstruction and sector memory.
AI.motivation: To understand whether finite quantum environments with conserved quantities (like excitation number) can act as canonical baths for a local probe, and to characterize the deviation from thermal behavior due to Hilbert space fragmentation into charge sectors.
AI.method: The authors use sector-resolved late-time population (p_e^{(q)}), sector-memory variance (M_N), and global Gibbs-fit error (Δ_G^{global}) as diagnostics. They perform exact simulations with Haar-random pure states in fixed-charge sectors, construct charge-preserving Floquet circuits with R_z phases and XX+YY exchange gates, run ideal/noisy Qiskit simulations, and implement experiments on IBM Fez hardware with N=4 qubits.
