AI.result: Sector-dependent populations are close to the maximally mixed-sector benchmark p_e^{(q)}=q/(N+1), but produce nonzero Gibbs obstruction. Hardware data (N=4, ε=0) gives M_N≈0.044, Δ_G^{global}≈0.558, and charge preservation ~0.90. Symmetry-breaking R_x(ε) rotations reduce both diagnostics but increase charge leakage without erasing sector ordering.
AI.conclusion: Equilibration within constrained charge sectors is insufficient to produce a single sector-independent Gibbs state for the probe; conserved quantities fundamentally obstruct thermalization in finite quantum baths.

title: HamQASBench: A Hamiltonian-Informed Diagnostic Benchmark for Evaluating Quantum Architecture Search
summary: Quantum Architecture Search (QAS) automates the design of parameterized quantum circuits for variational quantum algorithms, yet existing benchmarks organize instances by molecular identity or qubit count -- criteria agnostic to Hamiltonian structure -- and rely solely on energy accuracy, which cannot detect structural failures such as over-parameterization on near-product ground states. We introduce HamQASBench, a Hamiltonian-informed diagnostic benchmark organizing 11 molecules into five structural tiers via fingerprints derived from the Pauli operator basis, computational basis representation, and ground-state entanglement. A post-hoc critical-structure extraction procedure identifies minimal circuits consistent with each tier's requirements, complementing energy-based evaluation with per-qubit entanglement analysis and pairwise state fidelity. Benchmarking five QAS methods across four paradigms reveals failure modes invisible to conventional metrics: over-parameterization in the minimalism regime, eigenstate commitment under degeneracy, a representation bottleneck in strongly correlated systems, topology-induced routing failure, and circuit search space growth as a scalability bottleneck.

AI.tldr: HamQASBench is a Hamiltonian-informed diagnostic benchmark for Quantum Architecture Search that organizes molecules into structural tiers, uses post-hoc critical-structure extraction, and reveals five failure modes invisible to conventional energy-based metrics.
AI.motivation: Existing QAS benchmarks organize instances by molecular identity or qubit count (agnostic to Hamiltonian structure) and rely solely on energy accuracy, which cannot detect structural failures like over-parameterization on near-product ground states.
AI.method: HamQASBench organizes 11 molecules into five structural tiers using fingerprints from the Pauli operator basis, computational basis representation, and ground-state entanglement. It employs post-hoc critical-structure extraction to find minimal circuits per tier, and evaluates using per-qubit entanglement analysis and pairwise state fidelity alongside energy.
AI.result: Benchmarking five QAS methods across four paradigms reveals five failure modes: over-parameterization in the minimalism regime, eigenstate commitment under degeneracy, representation bottleneck in strongly correlated systems, topology-induced routing failure, and circuit search space growth as a scalability bottleneck.
AI.conclusion: Hamiltonian structure-aware benchmarking is essential for diagnosing QAS failures that conventional energy-based metrics miss, and HamQASBench provides a systematic framework for detecting these structural failure modes.

title: Emergence of the Scrooge Ensemble in the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev Model
summary: The probabilistic nature of quantum measurement provides a direct window into the structure and complexity of many-body wave functions. When only part of a system is measured, the remaining degrees of freedom form an ensemble of post-measurement states whose statistical structure can reveal a stronger form of thermalization, known as deep thermalization. Recent numerical evidence suggests that this phenomenon is characterized by convergence of the projected ensemble to the Scrooge ensemble, a maximally random ensemble compatible with a given density matrix. In this Letter, we use the solvable Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model to unveil the mechanism by which the Scrooge ensemble emerges in many-body systems. By formulating measurement probabilities and post-measurement states in terms of path integrals, we analytically characterize all moments of the projected ensemble and show that they exactly match those of the Scrooge ensemble, even at short evolution times. We further connect this result to the saddle-point structure of the measurement path integral, which naturally generates the replica permutations underlying Scrooge statistics. Our results establish the solvable SYK model as a tractable setting for exploring universal statistics of quantum measurements in chaotic many-body dynamics.

AI.tldr: Using the solvable SYK model, the authors analytically prove that the projected ensemble from partial quantum measurements converges to the Scrooge ensemble, revealing the mechanism of deep thermalization in chaotic many-body systems.
AI.motivation: To uncover the mechanism by which the Scrooge ensemble emerges in many-body systems under partial measurement, and to provide an analytically tractable setting for studying deep thermalization.
AI.method: Formulating measurement probabilities and post-measurement states as path integrals in the SYK model, analytically characterizing all moments of the projected ensemble, and connecting to the saddle-point structure that generates replica permutations.
AI.result: All moments of the projected ensemble exactly match those of the Scrooge ensemble, even at short evolution times, with the saddle-point structure naturally producing the required replica permutations.
AI.conclusion: The SYK model provides a tractable setting for exploring universal statistics of quantum measurements in chaotic many-body dynamics, establishing deep thermalization as analytically accessible.

title: Photonic Cluster State Generation from a Quantum Dot Emitting in the Telecom C-band
summary: Photonic cluster states are a key resource for photonic quantum information processing. So far, deterministic generation of these states has been limited to the near-infrared wavelength range. To achieve quantum advantage in communication while maintaining compatibility with silicon photonics, operation in the telecom wavelength range is required. In this work, we demonstrate deterministic cluster state generation directly in the telecom C-band. This is achieved through repetitive excitation of a hole spin confined in an indium-arsenide quantum dot subjected to an external magnetic field. We characterize the quantum process that generates the cluster state by measuring its process map, obtaining a fidelity of $\mathrm{F} = 0.71 \pm 0.01$ to the ideal case. As part of this characterization, we observe spin--photon polarization entanglement with a negativity of $\mathrm{N} = 0.27 \pm 0.02$. The emitted photons exhibit indistinguishability of at least 83%, demonstrating the potential for future fusion gates necessary for photonic cluster state generation beyond linear connectivity.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates deterministic generation of photonic cluster states directly in the telecom C-band using a hole spin in an indium-arsenide quantum dot, achieving a process fidelity of 0.71, spin-photon entanglement negativity of 0.27, and photon indistinguishability of at least 83%.
AI.motivation: Prior work limited deterministic cluster state generation to near-infrared wavelengths; to enable quantum advantage in communication with silicon photonics compatibility, telecom-wavelength operation is required.
AI.method: Repetitive excitation of a hole spin confined in an indium-arsenide quantum dot under an external magnetic field; characterized via process map measurement and spin-photon polarization entanglement analysis.
AI.result: Process fidelity F = 0.71 ± 0.01; spin-photon entanglement negativity N = 0.27 ± 0.02; photon indistinguishability ≥ 83%.
AI.conclusion: Telecom C-band deterministic cluster state generation is feasible, and the demonstrated photon indistinguishability supports future fusion gates for cluster states beyond linear connectivity.

title: Quantum orientation, Noether structure, composition of systems and operations
summary: In this paper we argue that, in addition to the statistical structure of quantum theory, another structure, referred to here as the ``Noether structure," is necessary to describe the composition of systems and to define completely positive operations. A Noether structure reflects the dual role of Hermitian operators as observables on the one hand and as generators of symmetry transformations on the other. This idea has been expressed in a similar form in the works of Alfsen and Shultz, who investigated the conditions under which the Jordan product can be extended to an associative product of operator algebras. Our investigations into the Noether structure and the composition of systems are limited to the finite-dimensional case and establish a connection to completely positive operations. In the case of pure operations, the latter can be characterized as orientation-preserving maps.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a "Noether structure" alongside quantum theory's statistical structure to describe system composition and completely positive operations, linking it to Alfsen and Shultz's work on Jordan products extending to associative operator algebras, and characterizing pure operations as orientation-preserving maps in finite dimensions.
AI.motivation: To argue that the statistical structure of quantum theory alone is insufficient; an additional "Noether structure" reflecting the dual role of Hermitian operators (as observables and symmetry generators) is needed for composing systems and defining completely positive operations.
AI.method: The investigation is limited to finite-dimensional systems, connecting the Noether structure to Alfsen and Shultz's conditions for extending the Jordan product to an associative product of operator algebras, and linking it to completely positive operations.
AI.result: A connection is established between the Noether structure, system composition, and completely positive operations; pure operations are characterized as orientation-preserving maps.
AI.conclusion: The Noether structure is a necessary complement to the statistical structure of quantum theory for system composition and completely positive operations, with pure operations being orientation-preserving in finite dimensions.

title: Error Mitigation in Bosonic Systems via Virtual Distillation
summary: Virtual distillation is a promising error-mitigation technique that exploits multiple copies of a noisy quantum state to estimate observables as if measured on a purified state. Although originally introduced in the context of bosonic many-body systems under the name of virtual cooling, its development and applications have largely focused on qubit-based quantum computation. Here, we establish a framework for virtual distillation in bosonic quantum information processing and continuous-variable quantum computing. Building on a diagonalization of cyclic shift operators implemented with passive linear-optical interferometers, we derive experimentally accessible protocols for estimating virtually distilled expectation values of observables relevant to bosonic architectures. In particular, we show how to recover noise-mitigated expectation values of number operators, phase-shift operators, and arbitrary quadratures from multi-copy measurements. For number operators, we further demonstrate the estimation of virtually distilled correlators of arbitrary order through the characteristic function of the photon-number distribution. We apply the framework to states affected by photon loss and dephasing, two of the dominant noise mechanisms in bosonic quantum computation, and quantify the resulting suppression of noise contributions. Our results extend virtual distillation beyond its original setting and provide a practical route toward error-mitigated measurements in bosonic quantum processors using experimentally available linear-optical resources.

AI.tldr: The paper extends virtual distillation—an error-mitigation technique originally developed for qubit-based quantum computing—to bosonic (continuous-variable) quantum systems. The authors derive protocols using passive linear-optical interferometers to estimate noise-mitigated observables (number operators, phase-shift operators, quadratures) from multiple noisy copies, and demonstrate suppression of photon loss and dephasing errors.
AI.motivation: Virtual distillation has been highly successful for qubit-based quantum error mitigation but had not been systematically developed for bosonic quantum information processing and continuous-variable quantum computing, where dominant noise mechanisms (photon loss and dephasing) differ from those in qubit systems.
AI.method: The framework is built on diagonalizing cyclic shift operators using passive linear-optical interferometers. From multi-copy measurements, the authors derive protocols for estimating virtually distilled expectation values of bosonic observables, including number operators, phase-shift operators, arbitrary quadratures, and higher-order correlators via the characteristic function of the photon-number distribution.
AI.result: The authors show how to recover noise-mitigated expectation values for key bosonic observables, demonstrate estimation of arbitrarily ordered virtually distilled correlators for number operators, and quantify noise suppression for states affected by photon loss and dephasing.
AI.conclusion: Virtual distillation is successfully extended to bosonic quantum systems, providing a practical, experimentally accessible route to error-mitigated measurements in bosonic quantum processors using off-the-shelf linear-optical resources.

title: How Hard Is Quantum Advantage? A Cloud Microphysics Stress Test for Variational Quantum Models
summary: Quantum machine learning (QML) could have the potential to leverage advantages of quantum over classical computing but still lacks strong evidence of actual improvements and scalability, partly due to phenomena such as barren plateaus. In this paper, we employ a hybrid quantum neural network (QNN) on a dataset on cloud microphysics, containing processes for phase transitions of water in the atmosphere and its related temperature changes, which are highly relevant for accurate climate predictions and projections. To reach optimal performance of our QNNs, we employ a rich and trainable frequency spectrum together with expressivity enhancing classical postprocessing. We find that our QNNs strongly benefit from extensive hyperparameter optimization and thereby demonstrate the feasibility of applying QNNs to complex physical systems. At the same time, the QNNs are outperformed by classical baselines in the form of simple fully-connected neural networks. We discuss identified bottlenecks of this class of quantum models to learn the full complexity of the cloud microphysics dataset to show that there is a need to further understand and improve variational quantum models for machine learning such that they might fill the gap where classical models fail or are inefficient.

AI.tldr: Hybrid quantum neural networks were applied to a cloud microphysics dataset but were outperformed by simple classical fully-connected neural networks, despite extensive hyperparameter optimization and frequency spectrum enhancement.
AI.motivation: To explore whether quantum machine learning (QML) can provide advantages over classical computing on complex real-world problems, specifically cloud microphysics processes relevant to climate prediction, while addressing known challenges like barren plateaus.
AI.method: A hybrid quantum neural network (QNN) with a rich trainable frequency spectrum and expressivity-enhancing classical postprocessing, optimized via extensive hyperparameter optimization, applied to a cloud microphysics dataset describing water phase transitions and temperature changes in the atmosphere.
AI.result: The QNNs benefited from hyperparameter optimization and demonstrated feasibility for complex physical systems, but were outperformed by simple classical fully-connected neural networks serving as baselines.
AI.conclusion: Current variational quantum models have identified bottlenecks preventing them from learning the full complexity of the cloud microphysics dataset; further understanding and improvement are needed before QML can fill gaps where classical models fail or are inefficient.

title: Noise-limited secret key agreement with twin optical physically unclonable functions
summary: We investigate the use of twin optical fingerprints derived from correlated physical unclonable functions (PUFs), as a hardware-based platform for cryptographic key generation and distribution. Each fingerprint is associated with a random, yet reproducible speckle pattern, generated when coherent light is scattered by a disordered optical structure. We consider a pair of correlated optical PUFs, and study the conditions under which two honest parties can establish a common secret key, despite fabrication-induced variability and environmental noise. An explicit information-theoretic key-agreement protocol is developed, incorporating secure sketches, error reconciliation, and privacy amplification. We quantify information leakage due to public helper data, and derive lower bounds on the length of the final secret key. The analysis identifies the noise regimes in which secure key agreement is feasible, and examines the performance of both practical and near-capacity reconciliation schemes. Finally, we discuss how twin optical PUFs could be integrated into quantum key distribution (QKD) networks, as a mechanism for establishing an initial pre-shared secret key between two honest users, without relying on computational assumptions or trusted third parties.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using twin optical fingerprints from correlated physical unclonable functions (PUFs) for cryptographic key generation and distribution. It develops an information-theoretic key-agreement protocol with secure sketches, error reconciliation, and privacy amplification, analyzes noise regimes and information leakage, and discusses integration with QKD networks for assumption-free pre-shared key establishment.
AI.motivation: To enable hardware-based cryptographic key generation and distribution between two honest parties using correlated optical PUFs, without relying on computational assumptions or trusted third parties, while addressing fabrication-induced variability and environmental noise.
AI.method: Information-theoretic key-agreement protocol incorporating secure sketches, error reconciliation, and privacy amplification; analysis of information leakage from public helper data; derivation of lower bounds on secret key length; evaluation of practical and near-capacity reconciliation schemes across noise regimes.
AI.result: Identification of noise regimes where secure key agreement is feasible; quantification of information leakage due to public helper data; lower bounds on final secret key length; performance comparison of practical vs. near-capacity reconciliation schemes.
AI.conclusion: Twin optical PUFs can serve as a viable hardware platform for secret key establishment, and can be integrated into QKD networks to provide initial pre-shared keys without computational assumptions or trusted third parties.

title: Contraction and Expansion Values of Quantum Channels
summary: The contraction coefficient of the trace distance is a central tool in quantum information, quantifying how strongly a quantum channel degrades the distinguishability of states. However, being an extremal ratio, it captures only the most optimistic behaviour of the channel and is often trivial, even for very noisy channels. Moreover, a single scalar is poorly suited to describe how contraction accumulates under channel composition. In this work we introduce the \emph{contraction and expansion values}, two monotone sequences that refine the contraction and expansion coefficients in the same way singular values refine the operator norm. They arise from a min--max variational principle over subspaces of traceless Hermitian operators, admit an operational interpretation in terms of two state-discrimination games, and are shown to coincide with the Gel'fand or Bernstein numbers of the channel restricted to traceless operators. This identification places the sequences within Pietsch's theory of $s$-numbers and yields, in particular, bounds under channel composition that the contraction coefficient alone cannot provide. We establish their main structural properties and compute or estimate them for single-qubit channels, $d$-dimensional amplitude damping channels, and direct-sum channels.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces contraction and expansion values—two monotone sequences that refine the traditional contraction coefficient of the trace distance for quantum channels. These sequences arise from a min-max variational principle over traceless Hermitian operators, have an operational interpretation via state-discrimination games, and coincide with Gel'fand or Bernstein numbers in Pietsch's s-number theory. They provide tighter bounds under channel composition and are computed for single-qubit, amplitude damping, and direct-sum channels.
AI.motivation: The contraction coefficient of the trace distance is an extremal ratio that captures only the most optimistic behavior of a quantum channel and is often trivial even for noisy channels. A single scalar is poorly suited to describe how contraction accumulates under channel composition. The authors introduce refined sequences to overcome these limitations.
AI.method: The paper defines contraction and expansion values via a min-max variational principle over subspaces of traceless Hermitian operators. These values are identified as Gel'fand or Bernstein numbers (s-numbers in Pietsch's theory) of the channel restricted to traceless operators. Their properties are derived and computed/estimated for single-qubit channels, d-dimensional amplitude damping channels, and direct-sum channels.
AI.result: The contraction and expansion values refine the contraction/expansion coefficients analogously to how singular values refine the operator norm. They admit an operational interpretation in terms of two state-discrimination games, fit into Pietsch's s-number theory, and yield non-trivial bounds under channel composition. Explicit results are given for single-qubit, amplitude damping, and direct-sum channels.
AI.conclusion: The introduced sequences provide a more nuanced and informative characterization of how quantum channels contract distinguishability than the single contraction coefficient, especially under composition. They connect quantum information theory with classical s-number theory and open new avenues for analyzing channel discrimination tasks.

title: Extending the Bloch sphere model to an N-qubit system
summary: The Bloch sphere is an elegant tool for representing single-qubit states. However, a widely accepted generalization for multi-qubit systems with entanglement remains absent. We propose a novel geometric model extending the Bloch sphere representation to arbitrary $N$-qubit systems using $2^N-1$ spheres. We demonstrate that any pure 2-qubit state is uniquely described by three spheres: two for individual qubits and a third encapsulating bipartite entanglement. Generalizing this, we establish an $N$-qubit parameterization through the hierarchical application of controlled rotation gates along the $Z$ and $Y$ axes. We formally prove a strict bijection between the standard state vector representation and our model's angular parameters. This framework provides an intuitive visualization of multiple entanglement, offering potential computational advantages for quantum simulators and new analytical perspectives on quantum gates.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a geometric generalization of the Bloch sphere to N-qubit systems using 2^N-1 spheres, with a strict bijection to standard state vector representation, enabling intuitive visualization of entanglement.
AI.motivation: The Bloch sphere elegantly represents single-qubit states but lacks a widely accepted multi-qubit generalization that captures entanglement.
AI.method: The model represents any N-qubit pure state using 2^N-1 spheres, constructed via hierarchical controlled rotation gates along Z and Y axes, with a proven bijection between angular parameters and standard state vectors.
AI.result: A strict bijection is formally proven between the proposed angular parameterization and the standard state vector representation; 2-qubit states are uniquely described by three spheres (two individual, one for bipartite entanglement).
AI.conclusion: The framework offers intuitive visualization of multi-partite entanglement, potential computational advantages for quantum simulators, and new analytical perspectives on quantum gates.

title: Quantum Hashing via Constrained Rydberg Many-Body Dynamics
summary: In this Letter, we show that constrained many-body dynamics in Rydberg atom arrays naturally gives rise to a quantum hashing mechanism. By encoding ternary strings into deterministic trajectories in the state space, the classical information space is mapped onto a quantum state ensemble in the Hilbert space with an induced geometric structure. Statistical analysis reveals that this ensemble exhibits high probability near-orthogonality, random-like distribution, and broad geometric coverage. These geometric features naturally give rise to the essential cryptographic properties of quantum hashing, including low collision probability, one-wayness, tamper sensitivity, and privacy preservation. Our results demonstrate that the cryptographic functionality of quantum hashing need not rely on deliberately engineered algorithms, but can instead emerge naturally from constrained many-body dynamics, identifying quantum dynamics itself as a physical resource for cryptographic information processing.

AI.tldr: Constrained many-body dynamics in Rydberg atom arrays can naturally implement quantum hashing, where cryptographic properties emerge from physical dynamics rather than engineered algorithms.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that quantum cryptographic functionality, specifically quantum hashing, can emerge naturally from constrained many-body dynamics in Rydberg atom arrays, without requiring deliberately engineered algorithms.
AI.method: Encoding ternary strings into deterministic trajectories in Rydberg atom arrays, mapping classical information onto a quantum state ensemble with induced geometric structure, and statistically analyzing the resulting ensemble properties.
AI.result: The quantum state ensemble exhibits high probability near-orthogonality, random-like distribution, and broad geometric coverage, which naturally yield essential cryptographic properties: low collision probability, one-wayness, tamper sensitivity, and privacy preservation.
AI.conclusion: Quantum dynamics itself can serve as a physical resource for cryptographic information processing, as cryptographic functionality emerges naturally from constrained many-body dynamics rather than requiring engineered algorithms.

title: Canonical quantization of neurons
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, companion paper available at arXiv:2605.24386
summary: Canonical quantization provides a systematic procedure for constructing quantum models from classical Hamiltonians. Here, we apply this principle to a fundamental computational primitive of machine learning: the neuron. Specifically, by viewing a neuron as a composition of an energy function and an activation function, we quantize this model by replacing the energy function with a quantum Hamiltonian and applying the activation function to it through matrix functional calculus. This results in an activation observable that can be measured on an input quantum state. We investigate the use of these quantized neurons for function approximation, where the objective is to learn an unknown observable from labeled quantum data. For this purpose, we develop hybrid quantum-classical algorithms for training and evaluation, including procedures for measuring the activation observable and estimating gradients of the squared loss error. Our algorithms for gradient estimation rely on basic primitives like classical random sampling, the Hadamard test, and Hamiltonian simulation, and those for measuring an activation observable rely on quantum algorithms known as the power of one qumode and Schroedingerization. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our quantized neurons exhibit enhanced expressive capabilities relative to corresponding classical neurons on representative learning tasks. Our work establishes canonical quantization as a principled framework for constructing quantum machine learning primitives and provides a foundation for developing neural architectures tailored to quantum data.

AI.tldr: This paper applies canonical quantization from physics to the neuron computational primitive, creating quantized neurons where energy functions become quantum Hamiltonians and activation functions become observables measured on quantum states. The authors develop hybrid quantum-classical algorithms for training these quantized neurons, demonstrating enhanced expressive power over classical neurons in function approximation tasks with quantum data.
AI.motivation: To establish a principled framework for constructing quantum machine learning primitives by applying canonical quantization—a well-established physics principle—to the fundamental building block of neural networks (the neuron), thereby creating quantum neural models that can naturally process quantum data.
AI.method: The neuron is decomposed into an energy function and an activation function. Canonical quantization replaces the energy function with a quantum Hamiltonian, and the activation function is applied via matrix functional calculus to produce an activation observable. Hybrid quantum-classical algorithms are developed for training: gradient estimation uses classical random sampling, Hadamard test, and Hamiltonian simulation; activation measurement uses the power of one qumode and Schroedingerization techniques.
AI.result: Numerical experiments show quantized neurons exhibit enhanced expressive capabilities compared to classical neurons on representative learning tasks.
AI.conclusion: Canonical quantization provides a principled framework for constructing quantum machine learning primitives, laying a foundation for developing neural architectures specifically designed for quantum data.

title: Transmon Phase Gates Controlled by Superconducting Soliton DAC
summary: We introduce a superconducting digital-to-analog converter (DAC) that filters control noise, provides native multiplexing, performs quantum gates in nanoseconds, and can be controlled by CMOS. This is achieved by transducing a trapezoidal drive pulse into a superconducting soliton, which is then held in the DAC load loop, applying flux to a mutually-coupled superconducting qubit or gate coupler. The analog flux output by the DAC can be easily controlled by varying the soliton hold time, or with a DC-biased tunable DAC-qubit coupler, allowing the DAC to perform a fixed-time, high-fidelity gate that's robust to fabrication variance or flux offsets in the quantum circuit. Our initial demonstration shows that the DAC can successfully perform 5.6 ns S-gates on transmons. We measure the DAC-induced quantum state excitation probability per gate to be 0.05%, and find that the DAC-induced relaxation rate from the qubit 1 state is below the intrinsic T1 rate limit of the transmon. Quantum simulations show qualitative agreement with the measured data, and predict that the DAC excitation rate can be lowered 10 times further by overdamping the Josephson junction (JJ) in the DAC load loop. may be limited by a Interleaved Randomized Benchmarking (IRB) sequences on an observer qubit reveal that, when scaling to many qubits, the DAC's performance may be limited by a non-local, DAC-induced phase error of 1.6% per gate, appearing in ancilla qubits that are not directly coupled to any of the 30 DACs on the chip. We discuss strategies for future layouts of multi-DAC chips that focus on mitigating the source of these non-local, high-frequency electromagnetic interactions (EMI), and how to incorporate a DC-tunable coupler for phase correction.

AI.tldr: A superconducting DAC that transduces trapezoidal drive pulses into solitons for quantum gate control, demonstrated with 5.6 ns S-gates on transmons, showing 0.05% excitation probability and T1-limited relaxation, though non-local phase errors (1.6%) appear when scaling to many qubits.
AI.motivation: To develop a superconducting DAC that filters control noise, provides native multiplexing, performs fast quantum gates, and is CMOS-compatible, addressing the need for scalable, high-fidelity qubit control with reduced noise and hardware overhead.
AI.method: Transducing a trapezoidal drive pulse into a superconducting soliton held in a DAC load loop, which applies flux to a mutually-coupled qubit or gate coupler. Output flux is controlled by soliton hold time or a DC-biased tunable coupler. Demonstrated on transmons with 5.6 ns S-gates; quantum simulations with overdamped JJs used to predict performance improvements.
AI.result: 5.6 ns S-gates on transmons; DAC-induced excitation probability 0.05%; relaxation rate below intrinsic T1 limit; simulations predict 10× lower excitation with overdamped JJ; non-local phase error of 1.6% per gate observed in ancilla qubits when scaling to 30 DACs.
AI.conclusion: The superconducting DAC enables fast, low-noise, CMOS-controllable gates, but multi-DAC scaling introduces non-local EMI phase errors. Future mitigation strategies include improved chip layouts and DC-tunable couplers for phase correction.

title: Brownian Motion in Orthogonal and Symplectic Groups
summary: Matrix Brownian motion provides a powerful framework for studying crossover ensembles in quantum chaos and quantum transport, as well as thermalization and information scrambling in many-body dynamics. Here, we develop a unified diagrammatic framework to characterize Brownian ensembles for orthogonal and symplectic random matrices, which describe systems with particle-hole symmetry. We compute polynomial averages up to fourth order and construct an orthogonally invariant interpolation for the disconnected $\mathrm{SO}^-(q)$ sector of the orthogonal group. We consider applications relating to the fields of quantum information, quantum chaos, and quantum transport.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a unified diagrammatic framework for Brownian ensembles of orthogonal and symplectic random matrices (systems with particle-hole symmetry), computes polynomial averages up to fourth order, and constructs an orthogonally invariant interpolation for the disconnected SO^−(q) sector, with applications to quantum information, chaos, and transport.
AI.motivation: To extend the matrix Brownian motion framework, which has been powerful for studying crossover ensembles in quantum chaos, transport, and many-body dynamics, to systems with particle-hole symmetry described by orthogonal and symplectic random matrices.
AI.method: The authors develop a unified diagrammatic framework for Brownian ensembles of orthogonal and symplectic random matrices. They compute polynomial averages up to fourth order and construct an orthogonally invariant interpolation for the disconnected SO^−(q) sector of the orthogonal group.
AI.result: Polynomial averages up to fourth order are computed, and an orthogonally invariant interpolation for the SO^−(q) sector is constructed.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables applications in quantum information, quantum chaos, and quantum transport for systems with particle-hole symmetry.

title: Complementary 3D color codes for transversal quantum logic
summary: Transversal logical gates provide a direct route to fault-tolerant quantum computation, but the Eastin-Knill theorem forbids a universal transversal gate set within a single quantum error-correcting code. We propose a hybrid architecture based on the tetrahedral three-dimensional color code and its Hadamard-transformed counterpart, which we call the H-tetrahedral code. The two encodings support complementary transversal non-Clifford operations. Combined with bitwise Hadamard transformations that switch between the two encodings and a one-way transversal logical CNOT from the tetrahedral code to the H-tetrahedral code, these operations realize an almost-universal transversal logical gate set that enables both the creation of entanglement and logical states with magic. We complete a universal gate set through a pieceably fault-tolerant round-robin construction of a logical controlled-$Z$ gate between two H-tetrahedral codes. This logical entangling gate is interleaved with reduced-overhead Steane-type syndrome extraction using logical two-dimensional color-code auxiliary qubits. Our construction provides a new route toward implementing classically hard-to-simulate quantum algorithms where magic and most entangling operations are transversal while the resource overhead is concentrated in a small number of non-transversal Clifford entangling operations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hybrid quantum error-correcting architecture using tetrahedral and H-tetrahedral 3D color codes to achieve an almost-universal transversal logical gate set, completing universality via a fault-tolerant round-robin logical CZ gate with reduced-overhead syndrome extraction.
AI.motivation: The Eastin-Knill theorem forbids a universal transversal gate set in any single quantum error-correcting code, motivating the need for hybrid architectures that combine complementary transversal operations to approach universality while maintaining fault tolerance.
AI.method: The architecture combines tetrahedral 3D color code and its Hadamard-transformed (H-tetrahedral) code. Bitwise Hadamard transformations switch between encodings, a one-way transversal CNOT connects them, and a pieceably fault-tolerant round-robin construction implements a logical CZ gate between two H-tetrahedral codes using 2D color-code auxiliary qubits for syndrome extraction.
AI.result: The hybrid architecture realizes an almost-universal transversal logical gate set, enabling both entanglement creation and magic state generation. Universal gate completion is achieved with resource overhead concentrated only in a small number of non-transversal Clifford entangling operations.
AI.conclusion: This construction provides a new route toward implementing classically hard-to-simulate quantum algorithms where magic and most entangling operations are transversal, while overhead is confined to a minority of operations.

title: Characterisation of a satellite-to-ground channel for continuous variable quantum key distribution protocol
summary: In space based quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols, the quantum channel will be dynamic in nature and the channel loss will change with respect to the zenith angle. In the context of continuous variable (CV)-QKD, this will cause issues with parameter estimation and for a transmitted local oscillator in particular it will also fluctuate the shot noise. Therefore, it is vital to characterise this channel loss and the sources of this loss. In this paper the varying channel loss is characterised under practical assumptions. This is shown for various different scenarios, turbulence strengths, as well as wavelengths. This work shows, for the channel parameters considered, it is possible to generate a positive secret key if restricted Eve security assumptions are made.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes the dynamic channel loss in space-based continuous variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) as a function of zenith angle, showing that positive secret key generation is possible under restricted Eve security assumptions for various turbulence strengths and wavelengths.
AI.motivation: In space-based CV-QKD, the quantum channel is dynamic and loss varies with zenith angle, causing issues with parameter estimation and shot noise fluctuation for a transmitted local oscillator. Characterizing this loss and its sources is vital for system viability.
AI.method: The varying channel loss is characterized under practical assumptions across different scenarios, turbulence strengths, and wavelengths.
AI.result: For the considered channel parameters, a positive secret key can be generated when restricted Eve security assumptions are made.
AI.conclusion: Understanding and characterizing the dynamic channel loss in space-based CV-QKD is essential, and under certain restricted security assumptions, positive secret key rates are achievable.

title: Fragile single-cone Dirac quantum walks in two dimensions
summary: It is known that a one-dimensional (1D) quantum walk gives a local space-time discretization of the massless Dirac equation with a single quasi-energy cone (no fermion doubling at low energies), keeping the fundamental symmetries (chiral and time-reversal) of the continuum theory. We show that the analogous 2D construction is fundamentally more fragile. Local two-band quantum walks can have an unpaired Dirac cone, but the protecting symmetries then cease to be ordinary on-site symmetries: they become non-symmorphic, involving half-lattice translations, and are broken by generic spatial inhomogeneities. In particular, we demonstrate that the 2D Dirac quantum walk based on the Ho-Chalker network model can be gapped by potential scattering.

AI.tldr: 1D quantum walks discretize the massless Dirac equation without fermion doubling, but 2D analogs are more fragile: local two-band walks can have unpaired Dirac cones only when protected by non-symmorphic symmetries (involving half-lattice translations), which are broken by generic inhomogeneities—e.g., the Ho-Chalker network model's 2D Dirac walk can be gapped by potential scattering.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether the successful 1D construction of a quantum walk that discretizes the massless Dirac equation without fermion doubling can be extended to 2D, and to understand the role of symmetries in protecting the resulting Dirac cones.
AI.method: Analytical and symmetry-based analysis of local two-band quantum walks in 2D, examining the conditions under which unpaired Dirac cones exist and the nature of the protecting symmetries (non-symmorphic versus on-site).
AI.result: 2D constructions are fundamentally more fragile: unpaired Dirac cones require non-symmorphic symmetries (half-lattice translations), which are broken by generic spatial inhomogeneities; the Ho-Chalker network model's 2D Dirac quantum walk can be gapped by potential scattering.
AI.conclusion: Unlike the robust 1D case, 2D Dirac quantum walks lack protection from ordinary on-site symmetries, making them vulnerable to disorder and inhomogeneities.

title: Efficient classical simulation of two-dimensional long-range systems: Rydberg arrays and beyond
summary: In variational Monte Carlo (VMC) calculations of $N$-site quantum systems with arbitrary all-to-all two-body interactions, evaluating the local energy generally costs $O(N^3)$. We introduce a new framework that reduces this cost to $O(N)$ for tensor network states, capable of scalable and accurate computation of real-time dynamics and ground states. As a result, we obtain accurate simulations of the adiabatic real-time protocol of a $10\times10$ dipolar XY model realized in a Rydberg simulator [C. Chen et al., Nature 616, 691 (2023)], which was previously beyond the reach of classical simulation. Going beyond quantum experiments, we also directly perform ground state VMC to compare with the adiabatic state preparation. Our work demonstrates tensor network VMC as a powerful classical simulator for long-range quantum platforms such as Rydberg and ion-trap simulators, which are currently in urgent need of scalable classical benchmarking tools. As a separate technical contribution, we resolve the pathology of evolving from product states within of tensor network VMC.

AI.tldr: A new VMC framework reduces local energy evaluation cost from O(N³) to O(N) for tensor network states, enabling accurate classical simulation of a 10×10 Rydberg dipolar XY model previously beyond classical reach.
AI.motivation: Variational Monte Carlo calculations of N-site quantum systems with all-to-all two-body interactions have high computational cost (O(N³)), limiting scalability. There is an urgent need for scalable classical benchmarking tools for long-range quantum platforms like Rydberg and ion-trap simulators.
AI.method: Introduces a tensor network VMC framework that reduces local energy evaluation cost to O(N). Additionally resolves the pathology of evolving from product states within tensor network VMC.
AI.result: Achieves accurate simulations of the adiabatic real-time protocol of a 10×10 dipolar XY model realized in a Rydberg simulator, which was previously beyond reach of classical simulation. Enables ground state VMC for comparison with adiabatic state preparation.
AI.conclusion: Tensor network VMC is a powerful classical simulator for long-range quantum platforms (Rydberg, ion-trap), offering scalable classical benchmarking tools urgently needed by the field.

title: Quasi-holonomy in non-adiabatic quantum evolution
summary: We develop a framework for quasi-holonomy in non-adiabatic quantum time evolution of subspaces along loops in a complex Grassmannian. By factoring the Schrödinger evolution into dynamical and connection-induced contributions in a moving basis, we obtain an effective geometric generator that depends explicitly on the dynamical propagator. This quasi-connection does not define a genuine connection on the original Grassmann bundle, since its gauge transformation law acquires a history-dependent, nonlocal term. Other ways of factoring the Schrödinger evolution are briefly discussed. All these approaches suffer from the same type of history-dependence, thereby defining transport of subspaces in which geometric and dynamical effects are generally intertwined, just as in the case of the quasi-holonomy. Our work sheds light on the issue of separating quantum evolution of subspaces into holonomic and dynamical parts from an essentially gauge-theoretic perspective.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a framework for quasi-holonomy in non-adiabatic quantum evolution of subspaces in a complex Grassmannian, showing that factoring Schrödinger evolution into dynamical and geometric parts leads to a quasi-connection with history-dependent gauge transformations, where geometric and dynamical effects remain intertwined.
AI.motivation: To understand and formalize the separation of quantum evolution of subspaces into holonomic (geometric) and dynamical parts beyond the adiabatic regime, from a gauge-theoretic perspective.
AI.method: The authors factor the Schrödinger evolution into dynamical and connection-induced contributions using a moving basis, deriving an effective geometric generator (quasi-connection) that depends on the dynamical propagator. They examine its gauge transformation properties and compare alternative factorization approaches.
AI.result: The quasi-connection does not define a genuine connection on the Grassmann bundle because its gauge transformation law contains a history-dependent, nonlocal term. All alternative factorization approaches similarly suffer from history-dependence, preventing a clean separation of geometric and dynamical effects.
AI.conclusion: Non-adiabatic quantum evolution of subspaces inherently intertwines geometric and dynamical contributions, and a genuine holonomy (in the standard sense) cannot be defined outside the adiabatic limit using this approach.

title: Routing Anonymity and Identifiability of Noisy Quantum Hardware
summary: Present-day quantum computing is cloud-based, where a user submits a circuit to a service provider's proprietary backend hardware. While providers may wish to hide implementation details, scheduling choices, or even which physical device was used, noisy finite-shot outputs can carry backend-specific fingerprints: information imprinted in the classical output distribution that can reveal the backend identity. So far, such fingerprints have mostly been studied from a benchmarking perspective, with limited attention to privacy considerations for users and providers. This work develops the first formal framework for backend identifiability and its privacy implications. We introduce a backend-identifiability game and use it to formalise routing anonymity as a security notion for quantum cloud services. We show that backend identifiability is a hypothesis-testing problem and prove that, under passive i.i.d. access to a single backend, routing anonymity decays exponentially at the Chernoff rate. We also establish a utility-anonymity trade-off, imposing fundamental limits on how much backend-specific information can be removed from classical outputs without degrading their usefulness. In addition, we observe that, for noisy quantum hardware, identifying fingerprints are inherently an intermediate-depth phenomenon, and establish a depth principle using Pauli-transfer-matrix tools. We complement the theory with experiments on Amazon Braket on AWS, using ion-trap and superconducting quantum processors. We observe 87-90% classification between superconducting backends and 96-100% classification across physical platforms, and find that identifiability can survive natural forms of post-processing. Overall, these results establish routing anonymity as a distinct security requirement for quantum cloud computing, and provide a framework for quantifying and controlling the utility-anonymity trade-off.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes backend identifiability and routing anonymity in quantum cloud computing, showing that noisy quantum circuit outputs carry backend-specific fingerprints that can identify the physical hardware. The authors establish a hypothesis-testing framework, prove that routing anonymity decays exponentially, identify a utility-anonymity trade-off, and demonstrate that identifiability is an intermediate-depth phenomenon. Experiments on Amazon Braket achieve 87-100% classification accuracy across different quantum backends.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum cloud services allow providers to hide implementation details, but noisy finite-shot outputs inadvertently carry backend-specific fingerprints that can reveal the physical device identity. These fingerprints have been studied mainly for benchmarking, with little attention to privacy implications for both users and providers. This work aims to formalize the privacy risks arising from backend identifiability.
AI.method: The authors introduce a backend-identifiability game to formalize routing anonymity as a security notion. They treat backend identifiability as a hypothesis-testing problem and derive the Chernoff rate for exponential decay of anonymity under passive i.i.d. access. They establish a utility-anonymity trade-off using information-theoretic tools and analyze depth dependence via Pauli-transfer-matrix techniques. Experimental validation is performed on Amazon Braket using ion-trap and superconducting processors.
AI.result: 87-90% classification accuracy between superconducting backends and 96-100% classification across physical platforms. Identifiability survives natural post-processing. Routing anonymity decays exponentially at the Chernoff rate. A fundamental utility-anonymity trade-off exists. Fingerprints are inherently an intermediate-depth phenomenon.
AI.conclusion: Routing anonymity should be recognized as a distinct security requirement for quantum cloud computing. The framework provides tools for quantifying and controlling the utility-anonymity trade-off, enabling privacy-aware design of quantum cloud services.

title: Quantum Spectral Anomaly Detection
summary: A core task in quantum anomaly detection is to compute an anomaly score that quantifies how strongly a test quantum state deviates from a given quantum dataset assumed to be normal. Classically, principal component analysis (PCA) for centered data computes the anomaly score by evaluating the test sample relative to the subspace spanned by the selected leading eigenvectors. However, for quantum data that lack a standard centering, explicitly recovering principal eigenvectors, constructing full Gram matrices, or loading quantum-random-access-memory-style data can be more costly than estimating the anomaly score itself. To avoid these costs, we propose Quantum Spectral Anomaly Detection (QSPADE), which computes PCA-like anomaly scores directly from the spectrum of the average state of the normal dataset. By replacing hard PCA rank selection with a smooth, temperature-controlled spectral threshold, QSPADE makes near-threshold spectral components contribute partially to the anomaly score. This makes the score vary continuously rather than jump when a borderline component is included or excluded, and makes it less sensitive to noise or arbitrary hard cutoffs near the threshold. In the zero-temperature limit, QSPADE recovers the hard-projector PCA score. The proposed measurement-based quantum detector can be calibrated with a sample complexity independent of the data dimension. Numerical simulations show that QSPADE behaves like kernel-PCA on encoded classical data and detects changes across a transverse-field Ising transition without predefined order parameters. Consequently, QSPADE gives an efficient framework for both quantum-kernel anomaly detection on encoded classical data and the monitoring of quantum-native systems where diagnostic observables are unknown.

AI.tldr: QSPADE proposes a quantum anomaly detection method that computes PCA-like anomaly scores directly from the spectrum of the average state of normal data, using a smooth temperature-controlled spectral threshold instead of hard PCA rank selection, enabling efficient calibration independent of data dimension and applicability to both quantum-kernel classical data and quantum-native systems.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum anomaly detection methods rely on costly operations such as explicit principal eigenvector recovery, full Gram matrix construction, or QRAM-style data loading. Classical PCA for centered data is not directly applicable to quantum data lacking standard centering, motivating a more efficient direct spectral approach.
AI.method: QSPADE computes anomaly scores from the spectrum of the average state of the normal dataset. It replaces hard PCA rank selection with a smooth, temperature-controlled spectral threshold, allowing partial contributions from near-threshold components. The method is measurement-based and can be calibrated with sample complexity independent of data dimension.
AI.result: In the zero-temperature limit, QSPADE recovers the hard-projector PCA score. Numerical simulations demonstrate that QSPADE behaves like kernel-PCA on encoded classical data and can detect changes across a transverse-field Ising transition without predefined order parameters.
AI.conclusion: QSPADE provides an efficient framework for quantum-kernel anomaly detection on encoded classical data and for monitoring quantum-native systems where diagnostic observables are unknown, with reduced computational overhead and improved robustness near spectral thresholds.

title: Quantum Computational Resources and Conformal Field Theory: Unifying Spins, Bosons, and Fermions
summary: Characterizing a quantum state through the lens of quantum resources provides an information-theoretic perspective on many-body systems. While quantum entanglement serves as the paradigmatic example of a quantum resource, recent studies have shown that quantum magic, a resource for universal quantum computation, can capture aspects of many-body states complementary to those described by entanglement. For instance, in spin systems, conformal field theory (CFT) analysis of the stabilizer Rényi entropy has revealed universal features of nonstabilizerness that are qualitatively distinct from entanglement. In bosonic and fermionic systems, however, a comparable formulation for their computational resource, non-Gaussianity, has yet to be established. In this work, we introduce a unified measure, the magic Rényi entropy (MRE), to quantify computational resources in spins, bosons, and fermions on an equal footing. This allows us to reveal common universal aspects of nonstabilizerness and non-Gaussianity in critical many-body states. In particular, our CFT analysis shows that the universal contribution to the MRE appears as the size-independent term determined by the Affleck-Ludwig boundary entropy. We find that non-Gaussianity can continuously renormalize this universal contribution or drive a boundary phase transition through bulk-induced boundary renormalization-group flows. As a concrete demonstration, we present a detailed CFT analysis of non-Gaussianity in interacting spinless fermions described by the Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid, showing boundary transitions at the Luttinger parameters $K=1/3$ and $K=3$. We perform numerical calculations that confirm our field-theoretical predictions. These results provide a unified field-theoretical understanding of many-body magic across spins, bosons, and fermions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a unified measure called the magic Rényi entropy (MRE) to quantify computational resources (nonstabilizerness and non-Gaussianity) in spins, bosons, and fermions, revealing universal features in critical many-body systems through CFT analysis, particularly the Affleck-Ludwig boundary entropy, and demonstrating boundary phase transitions in Tomonaga-Luttinger liquids.
AI.motivation: While quantum magic (nonstabilizerness) has been studied in spin systems via CFT analysis of stabilizer Rényi entropy, a comparable formulation for bosonic and fermionic computational resources (non-Gaussianity) has been lacking. This work aims to establish a unified measure applicable across all three types of systems.
AI.method: The authors introduce the magic Rényi entropy (MRE) as a unified measure, perform CFT analysis to identify universal contributions (Affleck-Ludwig boundary entropy), analyze boundary renormalization-group flows, and numerically simulate interacting spinless fermions described by the Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid model.
AI.result: The universal contribution to MRE is the size-independent Affleck-Ludwig boundary entropy. Non-Gaussianity can renormalize this contribution or drive boundary phase transitions. In Tomonaga-Luttinger liquids, boundary transitions occur at Luttinger parameters K=1/3 and K=3. Numerical calculations confirm field-theoretical predictions.
AI.conclusion: The MRE provides a unified field-theoretical understanding of many-body magic across spins, bosons, and fermions, establishing common universal features of nonstabilizerness and non-Gaussianity in critical systems.

title: Coherent Control of Energy Transport at Room Temperature in a Noisy Bath
summary: Coherent control of energy transport in a non-equilibrium steady-state (NESS) in a reaction-center-connected donor-acceptor pair is proposed. The pigments are considered to be continuously interacting with incoherent radiation and a phonon bath while being driven by phase-controlled coherent fields. Coherent excitation of the donor-acceptor pair is shown to induce interference between excitation pathways, resulting in phase dependent modulation of the flux. As a consequence one can enhance or suppress energy transfer via interference, e.g. an optical energy switch. The persistence of such interference enables coherent control at a NESS in dissipative regime suggests an extension of the operational scope of quantum control from traditional transient domain with low dissiaption to noisy environment NESS at room temperature.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes coherent control of energy transport in a non-equilibrium steady-state (NESS) within a reaction-center-connected donor-acceptor pair, demonstrating phase-dependent flux modulation via interference of excitation pathways, enabling an optical energy switch that persists even in dissipative, room-temperature environments.
AI.motivation: To extend quantum coherent control from traditional transient, low-dissipation regimes to noisy, room-temperature non-equilibrium steady-state environments, enabling persistent control of energy transport.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of a donor-acceptor pair connected to a reaction center, continuously interacting with incoherent radiation and a phonon bath, while being driven by phase-controlled coherent fields to induce pathway interference.
AI.result: Phase-dependent modulation of energy flux is observed, allowing enhancement or suppression of energy transfer via interference, effectively functioning as an optical energy switch.
AI.conclusion: Coherent control persists at a non-equilibrium steady-state even in dissipative, room-temperature conditions, expanding the operational scope of quantum control to noisy environments.

title: Logical Spectroscopy: Lifted-Product Codes with Addressable Bases
summary:
Quantum LDPC memories can encode many logical qubits, but dimension alone does not make them usable: applications need explicit conjugate logical operators with structured labels and physical representatives. For hypergraph-product (HGP) codes this structure is transparent, since the input matrices are binary and can be row-reduced over $\mathbb{F}_2$. Abelian lifted-product codes are subtler. Their seed entries are shifts, or sparse sums of shifts, in a group-algebra ring rather than a field, so pivot blocks need not be invertible and global row reduction can fail.
  We address this with \emph{logical spectroscopy}, a spectral construction that replaces global row reduction by finite-field computations in the Frobenius character packets of the Abelian lift group. The Chinese remainder theorem (CRT) decomposes the group algebra into these packets. In each packet, we compute kernels, quotients, and product-complex homology; we then lift the resulting representatives back with CRT idempotents and pair $X$ and $Z$ logicals through reciprocal trace-dual packets. This gives complete addressable conjugate logical bases for finite Abelian lifted products $\mathsf{LP}(A,B)$.
  The same packet data also gives design diagnostics. Packet ranks show how logical sectors split, the lifted representatives give certified upper bounds on the width of the constructed conjugate basis, and whole-orbit erasures decompose into packet-attributed erased-logical dimensions. Thus, CRT packets also serve as working coordinates: they label logical sectors, certify the constructed basis width, and attribute structured erasure failures. Under bounded seed-shape and group-basis-support assumptions, this construction gives Abelian lifted-product qLDPC families an HGP-like feature while preserving the layout freedom of group-algebra lifts.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces logical spectroscopy, a method using Frobenius character packets and CRT to construct explicit conjugate logical bases for Abelian lifted-product quantum LDPC codes, overcoming the non-invertibility issues in group-algebra row reduction that arise compared to hypergraph-product codes.
AI.motivation: Hypergraph-product (HGP) codes have transparent logical structure because their input matrices are binary and can be row-reduced over 𝔽₂. However, Abelian lifted-product codes use group-algebra entries (shifts or sums of shifts) where pivot blocks may not be invertible, making global row reduction fail. A method to systematically construct explicit conjugate logical operators for these codes is needed.
AI.method: Logical spectroscopy replaces global row reduction with finite-field computations within Frobenius character packets of the Abelian lift group. The CRT decomposes the group algebra into these packets. Kernels, quotients, and product-complex homology are computed per packet; representatives are lifted back via CRT idempotents, and X and Z logicals are paired through reciprocal trace-dual packets.
AI.result: Complete addressable conjugate logical bases for finite Abelian lifted products LP(A,B) are obtained. Packet ranks reveal how logical sectors split, lifted representatives give certified upper bounds on basis width, and whole-orbit erasures are decomposed into packet-attributed erased-logical dimensions.
AI.conclusion: CRT packets serve as working coordinates that label logical sectors, certify basis width, and attribute structured erasure failures. Under bounded seed-shape and group-basis-support assumptions, this construction gives Abelian lifted-product qLDPC families an HGP-like feature while preserving the layout freedom of group-algebra lifts.
